###### Abstract.

Gaussian empirical Bayes methods usually maintain a _precision independence_ assumption: The unknown parameters of interest are independent from the known standard errors of the estimates. This assumption is often theoretically questionable and empirically rejected. This paper proposes to model the conditional distribution of the parameter given the standard errors as a flexibly parametrized location-scale family of distributions, leading to a family of methods that we call close. The close framework unifies and generalizes several proposals under precision dependence. We argue that the most flexible member of the close family is a minimalist and computationally efficient default for accounting for precision dependence. We analyze this method and show that it is competitive in terms of the regret of subsequent decisions rules. Empirically, using close leads to sizable gains for selecting high-mobility Census tracts.

JEL codes. C10, C11, C44

Keywords. Empirical Bayes, g\-modeling, regret, heteroskedasticity, nonparametric maximum likelihood, Opportunity Atlas, Creating Moves to Opportunity

### 1\. Introduction

Applied economists often use empirical Bayes methods to shrink noisy parameter estimates, in hopes of accounting for the imprecision in the estimates and improving subsequent decisions. Many such settings1 can be described by a heteroskedastic Gaussian sequence model with known variances. That is, researchers obtain statistical estimates Yi and accompanying standard errors σi for parameters θi associated with units i\=1,…,n. Motivated by the central limit theorem, we model Yi as unbiased Gaussian signals on θi with known variances σi2:

<table id="S1.Ex1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table"><tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline"><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S1.Ex1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Y_{i}\mid\theta_{i},\sigma_{i}\sim\mathcal{N}(\theta_{i},\sigma_{i}^{2})\hskip 10.00002pti=1,\ldots,n." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>Y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo fence="false">|</mo><mrow><msub><mi>θ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>σ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>∼</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒩</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>θ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>σ</mi><mi>i</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mspace style="width:1em;" width="1em"></mspace><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow></semantics></math></td><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody></table>

Loosely speaking, empirical Bayes methods improve decisions—e.g., estimating θi or identifying units with high θi—by pooling strength across the many estimates (Yi,σi)i\=1n and accounting for differing levels of noise σi.

Commonly used empirical Bayes methods often assume _precision independence_—that the known standard errors σi do not predict the underlying parameters θi (i.e., σi𝑦θi). However, precision independence is economically questionable and empirically rejected in many contexts. Inappropriately imposing it can harm empirical Bayes decisions, possibly even making them underperform decisions without shrinkage. Motivated by these concerns, this paper introduces and analyzes empirical Bayes methods that allow for precision dependence.

To be concrete, our empirical application ([Bergman et al., 2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib65)) uses empirical Bayes methods to shrink raw economic mobility estimates (Yi,σi) of low-income children, curated by [Chetty et al. (forthcoming)](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib66). Here, θi represents true unobserved economic mobility of low-income children from Census tract i. In this context, precision independence assumes that the standard errors of these estimates do not predict true economic mobility. However, more upwardly mobile Census tracts tend to have noisier estimates, in part because they contain fewer low-income households. Consequently, the standard errors σi and true mobility θi are positively correlated.

In this context, imposing precision independence can be costly for decision-making. [Bergman et al. (2024)](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib65) select high-mobility Census tracts by choosing those with high empirical Bayes posterior means (i.e., shrinkage estimates). Under precision independence, empirical Bayes methods shrink all estimates to their _unconditional_ mean (i.e., 𝔼⁡\[θi\]) and shrink noisier estimates more aggressively. If θi and σi are positively correlated, such shrinkage tends to systematically _underestimate_ true mobility of high-σi tracts. This can harm subsequent selection decisions, if we wish to target high-mobility—hence disproportionately high-σi\---tracts.2 In contrast, screening on shrinkage estimates computed by our methods selects substantially more mobile tracts.

To introduce empirical Bayes methods, let us return to the Gaussian model ([1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#S1.Ex1 "1. Introduction ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters")). Under this setup, empirical Bayes methods are rationalized as approximations of unknown optimal decisions. Assume that (θi,σi) are drawn randomly from some distribution. Then the optimal, infeasible decisions take the form of Bayes decision rules for an _oracle Bayesian_, whose prior is the unknown distribution of (θi,σi). Empirical Bayes methods emulate these oracle decisions by estimating the oracle’s prior from the data. For instance, _shrinkage estimation_, discussed so far, corresponds to using the estimated posterior means of θi given (Yi,σi) as a decision rule for predicting θ1,…,θn. Under this backdrop, precision independence further simplifies the problem of estimating the oracle’s prior, but introduces poor performance when it fails to hold.

This paper has two contributions. First, we propose a flexible but tractable framework for modeling precision dependence that nests various proposals in the literature. Our methods are then natural estimation strategies under this framework. [Section 2](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#S2 "2. Model and proposed method ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters") models θi|σi as a conditional location-scale family,3 controlled by σi\-dependent location hyperparameter m0​(σ)\=𝔼⁡\[θ∣σ\] and scale hyperparameter s02​(σ)\=Var⁡(θ∣σ). Under this assumption, different values of σi translate, compress, or dilate the distribution θi|σi, but the underlying shape G0 of this distribution is constant over σi. This model subsumes precision independence as the special case where the location and scale parameters are constant functions of σi.

This model naturally gives rise to a family of conditional location-scale empirical Bayes methods—which we call close—by estimating the hyperparameters (m0​(σ),s0​(σ),G0). The close framework also makes estimating these objects highly tractable. The location and scale hyperparameters m0​(⋅),s0​(⋅) can be written as conditional moments of Y|σ, reducing their estimation to learning conditional expectation functions. Subsequently, given (m0​(⋅),s0​(⋅)), it is possible to normalize the data (Yi,σi) so as to remove precision dependence. After normalization, one could then apply conventional empirical Bayes methods to estimate the remaining hyperparameter G0.

The close framework unifies and generalizes several proposals in the literature (among others, [Kline et al., 2023](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib14); [Weinstein et al., 2018](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib88); [George et al., 2017](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib9); [Ignatiadis and Wager, 2019](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib64)). These proposals can be viewed as specific modeling and estimation choices for (m0,s0,G0). Various subsets of these proposals emphasize a nonparametric perspective for modeling and estimating various components of (m0,s0,G0); thus, a natural way to generalize is to adopt a nonparametric perspective for all of them. In particular, we advocate for using nonparametric regression to estimate (m0​(⋅),s0​(⋅)) and for using _nonparametric maximum likelihood_ (npmle) to estimate G0 ([Kiefer and Wolfowitz, 1956](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib83); [Jiang and Zhang, 2009](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib89); [Koenker and Mizera, 2014](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib82)). We refer to this variant as close\-npmle. We view close\-npmle as a flexible, minimalist, and computationally efficient default, in the absence of substantive knowledge that motivates further restrictions on (m0,s0,G0).

The second contribution of the paper is a theoretical analysis of close\-npmle in [Section 3](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#S3 "3. Theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters"). Our main result ([Theorems 1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#Thmtheorem1 "Theorem 1. ‣ 3.1.2. MSE regret results ‣ 3.1. Regret rate in squared error ‣ 3. Theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters") and [2](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#Thmtheorem2 "Theorem 2. ‣ 3.1.2. MSE regret results ‣ 3.1. Regret rate in squared error ‣ 3. Theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters")) establishes that, under the close assumptions, close\-npmle emulates the oracle Bayesian as well as possible in terms of squared error loss. Specifically, we establish upper and lower bounds for the squared error _Bayes regret_ for close\-npmle. These upper and lower bounds match up to logarithmic factors in the number of observations, indicating that close\-npmle attains a regret rate that is approximately minimax optimal. These results extend existing regret guarantees for npmle\-based empirical Bayes to account for precision dependence ([Soloff et al., 2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib86); [Jiang, 2020](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib85); [Jiang and Zhang, 2009](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib89); [Saha and Guntuboyina, 2020](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib77)). The key technical difficulty is accounting for estimation error in m0 and s0, which feed into npmle estimation.

We enrich our main result in two additional ways. First, to assess robustness of close\-npmle to the close assumption, we study a population version of close\-npmle under misspecification of the location-scale model. [Theorem 3](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#Thmtheorem3 "Theorem 3. ‣ 3.2. Robustness to the location-scale assumption () ‣ 3. Theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters") finds that its worst-case risk—under arbitrarily different shapes of θi|σi as a function of σi—is within a bounded multiple of the risk of a minimax procedure. Second, we also extend our guarantee for squared error regret to the Bayes regret for two ranking-related decision problems, including the problem of selecting high-mobility tracts in [Bergman et al. (2024)](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib65). [Theorem 4](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#Thmtheorem4 "Theorem 4. ‣ 3.3. Other decision objectives and relation to squared-error loss ‣ 3. Theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters") shows that the Bayes regret in squared error dominates the Bayes regret for these other decision problems. Coupled with [Theorem 1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#Thmtheorem1 "Theorem 1. ‣ 3.1.2. MSE regret results ‣ 3.1. Regret rate in squared error ‣ 3. Theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters"), this implies that close\-npmle has good performance for these ranking-related problems as well.

To illustrate our method, [Section 4](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#S4 "4. Empirical illustration ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters") applies close to two empirical exercises ([Chetty et al., forthcoming](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib66); [Bergman et al., 2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib65)). The first exercise is a simulation calibrated to the Opportunity Atlas, the dataset published by [Chetty et al. (forthcoming)](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib66). For all 15 measures of economic mobility that we consider, close\-npmle improves over all alternative methods and captures over 90% of possible mean-squared error (MSE) gains relative to no shrinkage, whereas conventional empirical Bayes methods capture only 70% on average and as little as 50% for some.

The second exercise evaluates the out-of-sample performance of various procedures for selecting high-mobility Census tracts ([Bergman et al., 2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib65)), using an out-of-sample validation procedure based on the coupled bootstrap that we introduce ([Oliveira et al., 2021](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib37)). [Bergman et al. (2024)](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib65) use empirical Bayes procedures to select high-mobility Census tracts in Seattle. In an exercise that mimics theirs, we find that close\-npmle selects more economically mobile tracts than conventional methods. Conventional methods, on the other hand, frequently select less mobile tracts than screening based on the noisy estimates directly. The improvements of close\-npmle over the standard method are on median 2.6 times the _value of basic empirical Bayes_—that is, the improvements the standard method delivers over screening on the raw estimates Yi directly. Therefore, for this application, if one finds using the standard empirical Bayes method a worthwhile methodological investment, then the additional gain of using close is likewise meaningful.

### 2\. Model and proposed method

#### 2.1. Empirical Bayes assumptions

We observe estimates Yi and their standard errors σi for parameters θi, over populations i∈{1,…,n}. We maintain two assumptions that are standard in the empirical Bayes literature ([Gilraine et al., 2020](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib60); [Jiang, 2020](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib85); [Soloff et al., 2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib86); [Gu and Koenker, 2023](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib34); [Gu and Walters, 2022](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib70); [Walters, 2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib4)).

First, we assume throughout that the estimates are conditionally Gaussian with known variances equal to σi2 and are independent across i ([1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#S1.Ex1 "1. Introduction ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters")). The Gaussian model ([1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#S1.Ex1 "1. Introduction ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters")) is heuristically motivated by a central limit theorem applied to the underlying micro-data. This assumption is not without loss: We ignore the fact that the central limit theorem is only an approximation and treat the Normality as exact. As a concrete example (cf. Example 2 in [Walters, 2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib4)), suppose θi\=𝔼Qi​\[Yi​j\] is the population mean of some variable Yi​j∼Qi drawn from population Qi. A natural estimator Yi of θi is the sample mean of Yi​1,…,Yi​ni. A natural estimate for the variance of Yi is σi2\=ni−2​∑j\=1ni(Yi​j−Yi)2. By standard arguments, as ni→∞, σi−1​(Yi−θi)​⟶𝑑​𝒩​(0,1). This heuristically motivates ([1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#S1.Ex1 "1. Introduction ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters")) by replacing “⟶𝑑” with “∼.’’4

Second, we assume that (θi,σi) are random and sampled i.i.d. from some distribution. Since empirical Bayes methods estimate the distribution of (θi,σi), it is natural to think of (θi,σi) as random. For minor technical reasons, throughout, we condition on σ1:n\=(σ1,…,σn) and treat them as fixed. Thus, we think of θi as drawn independently but not necessarily identically:

<table id="S2.Ex1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table"><tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline"><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.Ex1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta_{i}\mid\sigma_{i}\overset{\mathrm{i.n.i.d.}}{\sim}G_{(i)}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>θ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo fence="false">|</mo><mrow><msub><mi>σ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mover accent="true"><mo>∼</mo><mrow><mrow><mi mathsize="0.700em">i</mi><mo lspace="0em" mathsize="0.700em" rspace="0.167em">.</mo><mi mathsize="0.700em">n</mi><mo lspace="0em" mathsize="0.700em" rspace="0.167em">.</mo><mi mathsize="0.700em">i</mi><mo lspace="0em" mathsize="0.700em" rspace="0.167em">.</mo><mi mathsize="0.700em">d</mi></mrow><mo lspace="0em" mathsize="0.700em">.</mo></mrow></mover><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>G</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msub></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow></semantics></math></td><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody></table>

Let P0≡(G(1),…,G(n)) denote the conditional distribution θ1:n∣σ1:n.

Throughout, we focus on a setting without additional covariates Xi, returning to accommodating for covariates in the empirical application ([Section 4](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#S4 "4. Empirical illustration ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters")). Our methods generalize immediately to settings with covariates Xi—as long as Yi|Xi,θi,σi∼𝒩⁡(θi,σi2)—by treating Xi symmetrically as σi. We focus on σi since it is always present in heteroskedastic empirical Bayes settings, and it enters the likelihood of Yi unlike other covariates. Likewise, for simplicity, we focus on a setting where (Yi,θi,σi) are independently distributed: We briefly discuss dependence across i in [Section OA2.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A2.SS1 "OA2.1. Correlated 𝑌_𝑖 and correlated 𝜃_𝑖 ‣ Appendix OA2 Additional discussions ‣ Part II Additional discussions and empirical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters").

Under these assumptions, empirical Bayes methods are desirable for decision-making: They approximate optimal but infeasible decision rules. To see this, consider a decision problem with loss function L(𝜹,θ1:n), which evaluates an action 𝜹 at a vector of parameters θ1:n. The optimal decision—in terms of expected loss 𝔼P0\[L(⋅,θ1:n)∣σ1:n\] over (Yi,θi)|σi—chooses actions that minimize the posterior expected loss under prior P0:

<table id="S2.Ex3" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table"><tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline"><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.Ex3.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\bm{\delta}^{\star}(Y_{1:n},\sigma_{1:n};P_{0})\in\argmin_{\bm{\delta}}\mathbb{E}_{P_{0}}[L(\bm{\delta},\theta_{1:n})\mid Y_{1:n},\sigma_{1:n}]." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>𝜹</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>Y</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>σ</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><mo>;</mo><msub><mi>P</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>∈</mo><msub><mrow><mi>arg</mi><mo lspace="0.150em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>min</mi></mrow><mi>𝜹</mi></msub><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><msub><mi>P</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>L</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝜹</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>θ</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">∣</mo><msub><mi>Y</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>σ</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow></semantics></math></td><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody></table>

For this reason, we refer to 𝜹⋆ as the oracle Bayes decision rule, and think of it as the Bayes decision rule for an oracle whose prior is P0. 𝜹⋆ is infeasible since we do not know P0. To remedy, empirical Bayes methods seek to approximate the oracle Bayes rule 𝜹⋆. Naturally, one recipe is to plug an estimate P^ for P0 into ([2.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#S2.Ex3 "2.1. Empirical Bayes assumptions ‣ 2. Model and proposed method ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters")):5

<table id="S2.Ex5" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table"><tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline"><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.Ex5.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\bm{\delta}_{\mathrm{EB}}(Y_{1:n},\sigma_{1:n};\hat{P})\in\argmin_{\bm{\delta}}\mathbf{E}_{\hat{P}}[L(\bm{\delta},\theta_{1:n})\mid Y_{1:n},\sigma_{1:n}]." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝜹</mi><mi>EB</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>Y</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>σ</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><mo>;</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>P</mi><mo mathsize="0.900em">^</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>∈</mo><msub><mrow><mi>arg</mi><mo lspace="0.150em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>min</mi></mrow><mi>𝜹</mi></msub><msub><mi>𝐄</mi><mover accent="true"><mi>P</mi><mo mathsize="1.280em">^</mo></mover></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>L</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝜹</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>θ</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">∣</mo><msub><mi>Y</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>σ</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow></semantics></math></td><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody></table>

For the decision problem where L(𝜹,θ1:n)\=1n∑i\=1n(δi−θi)2 is mean-squared error, ([2.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#S2.Ex5 "2.1. Empirical Bayes assumptions ‣ 2. Model and proposed method ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters")) generates empirical Bayes posterior means 𝐄P^\[θi∣Yi,σi\], often referred to as shrinkage estimates ([James and Stein, 1961](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib39); [Efron and Morris, 1973](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib91)).

To simplify the estimation of P0, popular empirical Bayes methods often assume _precision independence_: θi𝑦σi, or, equivalently, G(1)\=⋯\=G(n) in ([2.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#S2.Ex1 "2.1. Empirical Bayes assumptions ‣ 2. Model and proposed method ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters")) and equal to some distribution G(0). For instance, the standard parametric empirical Bayes method models G(i) as i.i.d. Gaussian, G(0)∼𝒩⁡(m0,s02) ([Morris, 1983](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib90)). State-of-the-art empirical Bayes methods relax the parametric assumptions on G(0) and estimate G(0) with _nonparametric maximum likelihood_, or npmle ([Jiang, 2020](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib85); [Gilraine et al., 2020](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib60); [Soloff et al., 2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib86)). Henceforth, we refer to these methods as independent-gauss and independent-npmle, respectively. The “independent” here emphasizes precision independence.

#### 2.2. Precision independence and its violation

Despite its convenience, precision independence may be economically implausible; imposing it may cause empirical Bayes methods to underperform. We illustrate this with an application to the Opportunity Atlas ([Chetty et al., forthcoming](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib66)). There, one published measure of economic mobility θi of tract i defines it as the probability that a Black individual becomes relatively high-income (i.e., having family income in the top 20 percentiles nationally) after growing up relatively poor in tract i (i.e., with parents at the 25th percentile nationally).

Intuitively, Census tracts with more low-income Black households should have more precise estimates of θi, simply because there is a larger sample size to estimate θi. However, it is likely that these tracts are also on average poorer and are thus less economically mobile. Thus, these Census tracts should have smaller σi but also lower θi, meaning that (σi,θi) are positively correlated.

  

###### Notes.

All tracts within the largest 20 Commuting Zones are shown. Due to the regression specification in [Chetty et al. (forthcoming)](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib66), point estimates of θi∈\[0,1\] do not always lie within \[0,1\]. The orange line plots nonparametric regression estimates of the conditional mean 𝔼⁡\[Y∣σ\]\=𝔼⁡\[θ∣σ\]≡m0​(σ), estimated via local linear regression implemented by [Calonico et al. (2019)](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib63). The orange shading shows a 95% uniform confidence band, constructed by the max-t confidence set over 50 equally spaced evaluation points. See [Appendix SM3](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A3a "Appendix SM3 Estimating 𝜂_0 by local linear regression ‣ Part IV Additional theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters") for details on estimating conditional moments of θi given σi. ∎

Figure 1. Scatter plot of Yi against log10⁡(σi) in [Chetty et al. (forthcoming)](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib66)

As this economic intuition predicts, precision independence is readily rejected for this measure of economic mobility. [Figure 1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#S2.F1 "In 2.2. Precision independence and its violation ‣ 2. Model and proposed method ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters") plots the estimates Yi against their standard errors, overlaying an estimate of the conditional mean function m0​(σi)≡𝔼⁡\[θi∣σi\]\=𝔼⁡\[Yi∣σi\]. If θi were independent of σi, then the true conditional mean function m0​(σi) should be constant. [Figure 1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#S2.F1 "In 2.2. Precision independence and its violation ‣ 2. Model and proposed method ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters") shows the contrary—tracts with more imprecisely estimated Yi indeed tend to have higher θi.

  

###### Notes.

The top left panel shows posterior mean estimates with independent-gauss. The top right panel shows the same with independent-npmle. The bottom panel displays posterior mean estimates from our preferred procedure, close\-npmle. In the top panels, the estimates for the unconditional mean and variance of θi are weighted by the precision 1/σi2, following [Bergman et al. (2024)](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib65). ∎

Figure 2. Posterior mean estimates under precision independence

What happens if we apply empirical Bayes methods that assume precision independence here? [Figure 2](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#S2.F2 "In 2.2. Precision independence and its violation ‣ 2. Model and proposed method ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters") overlays empirical Bayes posterior means on the scatterplot. In the top left panel, independent-gauss shrinks Yi towards a common estimated mean m^0, depicted as the black line. When σi and θi are positively correlated, estimated posterior means under independent-gauss systematically undershoot θi for tracts with imprecise estimates. Similarly, the top right panel of [Figure 2](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#S2.F2 "In 2.2. Precision independence and its violation ‣ 2. Model and proposed method ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters") shows that independent-npmle suffers from the same undershooting. In contrast, the bottom panel of [Figure 2](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#S2.F2 "In 2.2. Precision independence and its violation ‣ 2. Model and proposed method ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters") previews our preferred procedure, close\-npmle, which shrinks towards the conditional mean 𝔼⁡\[θi∣σi\], thus avoiding the undershooting.

Nonetheless, posterior means from independent-gauss or independent-npmle may still be better predictors, on average, for θi in mean-squared error than the noisy Yi ([James and Stein, 1961](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib39); [Efron and Morris, 1975](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib30)). However, the undershooting for large σi is particularly problematic if one hopes instead to _select_ high-mobility Census tracts based on these posterior means, as do [Bergman et al. (2024)](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib65). On average, high-mobility tracts are exactly those with high σi. Underestimating mobility for these tracts thus leads to suboptimal selections that may even underperform screening directly based on Yi (see, also, [Mehta, 2019](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib40)).

  

###### Notes.

This plot shows a subregion of [Figure 1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#S2.F1 "In 2.2. Precision independence and its violation ‣ 2. Model and proposed method ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters") and highlights two Census tracts. The two tracts are those with log10⁡(σi)<−1.1 with the highest Yi, for which the selection decisions from independent-gauss and close\-npmle disagree. Like [Bergman et al. (2024)](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib65), the selection decisions aim to select 1/3 of Census tracts so as to maximize the average θi selected, by screening for the top 1/3 of empirical Bayes posterior means (formally, see [Decision Problem 3](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#Thmprob3 "Decision Problem 3 (top-𝑚 selection). ‣ 3.3. Other decision objectives and relation to squared-error loss ‣ 3. Theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters")). ∎

Figure 3. Ranking decisions for two Census tracts

To see this, [Figure 3](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#S2.F3 "In 2.2. Precision independence and its violation ‣ 2. Model and proposed method ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters") zooms into a subregion of [Figure 1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#S2.F1 "In 2.2. Precision independence and its violation ‣ 2. Model and proposed method ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters") and highlights two Census tracts, one in Englewood, NJ, and one in Richmond, CA—referring to them by tracts A and B, respectively. Demographically, tract A is 77% nonwhite according to the 2010 Census, and tract B is 57% nonwhite, contributing to different σi’s. Tract A has a lower raw estimate Yi than tract B (YA<YB); and tracts with similar σi to tract A, on average, also have lower estimates than those similar to tract B (i.e., m^​(σA)<m^​(σB)). Either gap between the two tracts is substantial.6 These observations are compelling evidence in favor of θB\>θA: If one would like to select a Census tract to recommend, then, between A and B, one is probably better off recommending tract B.

However, independent-gauss shrinks both to an estimate of the unconditional mean, which results in a higher posterior mean estimate for tract A. In doing so—fooled by an excessively low shrinkage target for tract B—independent-gauss recommends tract A over B instead. In contrast, our preferred method (close\-npmle) computes posterior means that preserve the more plausible ordering of the two tracts. We do so by modeling the conditional distribution of θi|σi more flexibly, which we turn to now.

#### 2.3. Conditional location-scale modeling of precision dependence

We propose the following _conditional location-scale model_ as a relaxation: For a distribution G0 normalized to have zero mean and unit variance, θi has the following representation

([2.4](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#S2.Ex7 "Equation 2.4 ‣ 2.3. Conditional location-scale modeling of precision dependence ‣ 2. Model and proposed method ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters")) states that the conditional distribution θ|σ depends on σ via m0​(σ) and s0​(σ). The function m0​(⋅) translates the _location_ of the distribution and the function s0​(⋅) controls the _scaling_. The underlying _shape_ of the distribution is governed by τi∼G0 and is restricted by ([2.4](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#S2.Ex7 "Equation 2.4 ‣ 2.3. Conditional location-scale modeling of precision dependence ‣ 2. Model and proposed method ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters")) to be invariant across different σi values. By the normalization of G0, we can think of m0​(⋅) as the conditional mean of θi|σi and s02​(⋅) as the conditional variance.

Applying the empirical Bayes recipe ([2.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#S2.Ex5 "2.1. Empirical Bayes assumptions ‣ 2. Model and proposed method ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters")) amounts to estimating the unknown hyperparameters (η0,G0). Estimating η0\=(m0​(⋅),s0​(⋅)) is straightforward, as η0 can be written as conditional moments of Yi|σi:

<table id="S2.Ex8" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table"><tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline"><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.Ex8.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m_{0}(\sigma)=\mathbb{E}[\theta\mid\sigma]=\mathbb{E}[Y\mid\sigma]\hskip 10.00002pt\text{ and }\hskip 10.00002pts_{0}^{2}(\sigma)=\operatorname{Var}(\theta\mid\sigma)=\operatorname{Var}(Y\mid\sigma)-\sigma^{2}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>m</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>σ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>𝔼</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mi>θ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">∣</mo><mi>σ</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>𝔼</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mi>Y</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">∣</mo><mi>σ</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mspace style="width:1em;" width="1em"></mspace><mtext>&nbsp;and&nbsp;</mtext><mspace style="width:1em;" width="1em"></mspace><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi>s</mi><mn>0</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>σ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>Var</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mi>σ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>Var</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mi>σ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><msup><mi>σ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow></semantics></math></td><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody></table>

Estimating η0 thus reduces to estimating conditional expectation functions.

Estimating G0 is more complicated. We do so by normalizing away the precision dependence. Consider transforming (Yi,σi) into (Zi,νi), defined by Zi≡Yi−m0​(σi)s0​(σi) and νi≡σis0​(σi). Note that ([2.4](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#S2.Ex7 "Equation 2.4 ‣ 2.3. Conditional location-scale modeling of precision dependence ‣ 2. Model and proposed method ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters")) implies that

<table id="S2.Ex10" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table"><tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline"><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.Ex10.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Z_{i}\mid\tau_{i},\nu_{i}^{2}\sim\mathcal{N}(\tau_{i},\nu_{i}^{2})\hskip 10.00002pt\tau_{i}\mid\sigma_{i},\nu_{i}\overset{\mathrm{i.i.d.}}{\sim}G_{0}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>Z</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo fence="false">|</mo><mrow><msub><mi>τ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>ν</mi><mi>i</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo>∼</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒩</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>τ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>ν</mi><mi>i</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mspace style="width:1em;" width="1em"></mspace><mrow><msub><mi>τ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo fence="false">|</mo><msub><mi>σ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>ν</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mover accent="true"><mo>∼</mo><mrow><mrow><mi mathsize="0.700em">i</mi><mo lspace="0em" mathsize="0.700em" rspace="0.167em">.</mo><mi mathsize="0.700em">i</mi><mo lspace="0em" mathsize="0.700em" rspace="0.167em">.</mo><mi mathsize="0.700em">d</mi></mrow><mo lspace="0em" mathsize="0.700em">.</mo></mrow></mover><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>G</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow></semantics></math></td><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody></table>

([2.3](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#S2.Ex10 "2.3. Conditional location-scale modeling of precision dependence ‣ 2. Model and proposed method ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters")) makes clear that, first, the transformed triplet (Zi,τi,νi) obeys an analogue of the Gaussian model ([1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#S1.Ex1 "1. Introduction ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters")), where Zi is a noisy Gaussian signal on τi with variance νi2. Second, precision independence holds in ([2.3](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#S2.Ex10 "2.3. Conditional location-scale modeling of precision dependence ‣ 2. Model and proposed method ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters")), since τi|νi​∼i.i.d.​G0.

This observation motivates the following strategy: First, estimate m0 and s0 with m^​(⋅) and s^​(⋅) so as to transform (Yi,σi) into (Z^i,ν^i):

<table id="S2.Ex12" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table"><tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline"><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.Ex12.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{Z}_{i}=\frac{Y_{i}-\hat{m}(\sigma_{i})}{\hat{s}(\sigma_{i})}\hskip 10.00002pt\text{and }\hskip 10.00002pt\hat{\nu}_{i}=\frac{\sigma_{i}}{\hat{s}(\sigma_{i})}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>Z</mi><mo mathsize="0.900em">^</mo></mover><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>Y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>m</mi><mo mathsize="0.900em">^</mo></mover><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>σ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>s</mi><mo mathsize="0.900em">^</mo></mover><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>σ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac></mrow><mspace style="width:1em;" width="1em"></mspace><mtext>and&nbsp;</mtext><mspace style="width:1em;" width="1em"></mspace><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>ν</mi><mo mathsize="0.900em">^</mo></mover><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mfrac><msub><mi>σ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>s</mi><mo mathsize="0.900em">^</mo></mover><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>σ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow></semantics></math></td><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody></table>

Second, apply empirical Bayes methods that assume precision independence on (Z^i,ν^i) to estimate G0. This leads to a family of empirical Bayes strategies that we refer to as conditional location-scale empirical Bayes, or close:

1.  close–step 1
    
    Estimate m0​(σ),s02​(σ) according to ([2.3](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#S2.Ex8 "2.3. Conditional location-scale modeling of precision dependence ‣ 2. Model and proposed method ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters")).
    
2.  close–step 2
    
    With the estimates η^\=(m^,s^), transform the data according to ([2.3](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#S2.Ex12 "2.3. Conditional location-scale modeling of precision dependence ‣ 2. Model and proposed method ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters")). Apply empirical Bayes methods under precision independence to estimate G0 with some G^n on the transformed data (Z^i,ν^i).
    
3.  close–step 3
    
    Having estimated (η^,G^n) and hence having obtained P^, we then form empirical Bayes decision rules following ([2.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#S2.Ex5 "2.1. Empirical Bayes assumptions ‣ 2. Model and proposed method ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters")).
    

This framework produces a family of empirical Bayes strategies, since [close–step 1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#S2.I1.i1 "In 2.3. Conditional location-scale modeling of precision dependence ‣ 2. Model and proposed method ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters") and  [close–step 2](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#S2.I1.i2 "Item 
close–step 2 ‣ 2.3. Conditional location-scale modeling of precision dependence ‣ 2. Model and proposed method ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters") can take different forms that practitioners can plug and play. When there are additional covariates Xi (independent of the noise Yi−θiσi), researchers can choose instead to model m0​(σi,Xi) and s0​(σi,Xi) that include these covariates, and estimate G0 after normalizing by m0​(σi,Xi) and s0​(σi,Xi).

This paper focuses on a particular implementation which we call close\-npmle. It uses nonparametric regression for [close–step 1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#S2.I1.i1 "In 2.3. Conditional location-scale modeling of precision dependence ‣ 2. Model and proposed method ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters") and npmle for [close–step 2](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#S2.I1.i2 "In 2.3. Conditional location-scale modeling of precision dependence ‣ 2. Model and proposed method ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters") . We recommend this method as a flexible default and primarily analyze it in [Section 3](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#S3 "3. Theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters"). We conclude this section with several self-contained discussions on implementations of these two steps, the rationale for ([2.4](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#S2.Ex7 "Equation 2.4 ‣ 2.3. Conditional location-scale modeling of precision dependence ‣ 2. Model and proposed method ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters")) and close\-npmle, and other miscellaneous issues.

#### 2.4. Discussions

##### 2.4.1. Implementation

For [close–step 1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#S2.I1.i1 "In 2.3. Conditional location-scale modeling of precision dependence ‣ 2. Model and proposed method ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters") , one can exploit ([2.3](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#S2.Ex8 "2.3. Conditional location-scale modeling of precision dependence ‣ 2. Model and proposed method ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters")) by plugging in estimates of conditional expectation functions. For 𝔼^\[⋅∣σ\] an estimator of conditional means, we may let m^​(σ)\=𝔼^​\[Y∣σ\] and s^2​(σ)\=𝔼^​\[(Y−m^​(σ))2∣σ\]−σ2. The estimator 𝔼^\[⋅∣σ\] itself may be nonparametric or based on judiciously chosen parametric models (see [Walters, 2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib4), for suggestions of the latter). The estimation of η0 should also impose known support restrictions on η0. For instance, the conditional variance estimate s^0 should be nonnegative (see [Remark 1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#Thmrmk1 "Remark 1 (Negative 𝑠̂^2 estimates). ‣ 2.4.3. Additional remarks ‣ 2.4. Discussions ‣ 2. Model and proposed method ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters")), and the conditional mean estimate should be within the support of θi. Our subsequent theoretical results simply assume that the estimators for m0​(⋅),s0​(⋅) are well-behaved and are uniformly accurate.

For [close–step 2](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#S2.I1.i2 "In 2.3. Conditional location-scale modeling of precision dependence ‣ 2. Model and proposed method ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters") , one could again model G0 nonparametrically or parametrically. As a flexible, performant, and minimalist default in the absence of stronger views on the shape G0, we focus on using npmle to estimate G0 ([Koenker and Gu, 2019](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib41)). Formally, the npmle G^n maximizes the log-likelihood of Z^i, whose marginal distribution is the convolution G0⋆𝒩⁡(0,ν^i2): For φ⁡(⋅) the Gaussian probability density function and 𝒫⁡(ℝ) the set of all distributions supported on ℝ, we maximize

In practice, we approximate 𝒫⁡(ℝ) with finitely-supported distributions on a grid in order to compute ([2.4.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#S2.Ex14 "2.4.1. Implementation ‣ 2.4. Discussions ‣ 2. Model and proposed method ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters")) ([Koenker and Mizera, 2014](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib82)).7

On the other hand, a default _parametric_ model for G0 is to simply assume that G0∼𝒩⁡(0,1), which we refer to as close\-gauss. This approach amounts to using independent-gauss on the transformed estimates (Zi,νi), with knowledge that the prior G0 has zero mean and unit variance. Under this model, the oracle Bayes posterior means are:

Despite being rationalized under the assumption θi|σi∼𝒩⁡(m0​(σi),s02​(σi)), this oracle ([2.4.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#S2.Ex16 "2.4.1. Implementation ‣ 2.4. Discussions ‣ 2. Model and proposed method ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters")) enjoys strong robustness properties8 even without the location-scale model ([2.4](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#S2.Ex7 "Equation 2.4 ‣ 2.3. Conditional location-scale modeling of precision dependence ‣ 2. Model and proposed method ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters")) and the assumption that G0∼𝒩⁡(0,1). First, ([2.4.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#S2.Ex16 "2.4.1. Implementation ‣ 2.4. Discussions ‣ 2. Model and proposed method ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters")) is the optimal linear-in-Y decision rule for estimating θi in squared error ([Weinstein et al., 2018](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib88)); second, ([2.4.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#S2.Ex16 "2.4.1. Implementation ‣ 2.4. Discussions ‣ 2. Model and proposed method ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters")) is minimax in the sense that it minimizes the worst-case mean squared error over choices of G(1),…,G(n) among all decision rules (see [Lemmas SM4.2](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A4.Thmlemma2 "Lemma SM4.2. ‣ Appendix SM4 Auxiliary lemmas for and ‣ Part IV Additional theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters") and [SM4.3](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A4.Thmlemma3 "Lemma SM4.3. ‣ Appendix SM4 Auxiliary lemmas for and ‣ Part IV Additional theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters") for formal statements, respectively). This method performs almost as well as close\-npmle in our empirical exercises.

##### 2.4.2. The location-scale assumption and close\-npmle

Table 1. Various existing methods fit into the close framework

|  | Step 1 | Step 2 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [Weinstein et al. (2018)](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib88) | Partition-based nonparametric estimator for m0,s02 | G0∼𝒩⁡(0,1) |
| [George et al. (2017)](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib9) | Parametric models for m0,s02 | G0∼𝒩⁡(0,1) |
| [Chamberlain (1984)](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib42) | Parametric models for m0,s02 | G0∼𝒩⁡(0,1) |
| [Efron (2016)](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib31) | Constant m0,s02 | G0 nonparametric (log-spline sieves) |
| [Kline et al. (2023)](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib14) | m0\=c1​s​(⋅), s0\=c2​s​(⋅) for parametric s⁡(⋅) | G0 nonparametric (log-spline sieves) |
| independent-npmle | Constant m0,s02 | G0 nonparametric |
| independent-gauss | Constant m0,s02 | G0∼𝒩⁡(0,1) |
| [Ignatiadis and Wager (2019)](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib64) | Nonparametric m0, constant s02 | G0∼𝒩⁡(0,1) |
| [Jiang and Zhang (2010)](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib33) | Constant m0, s0​(σ)\=σ (see [Remark 2](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#Thmrmk2 "Remark 2 (Other transformations). ‣ 2.4.3. Additional remarks ‣ 2.4. Discussions ‣ 2. Model and proposed method ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters")) | G0 nonparametric |

We argue that the location-scale assumption provides a unifying framework for a number of existing methods, and close\-npmle is a natural generalization of these methods within this framework. We also briefly speculate how to generalize beyond close\-npmle.

Several existing methods can be thought of as implementations of close by making different choices in [close–step 1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#S2.I1.i1 "In 2.3. Conditional location-scale modeling of precision dependence ‣ 2. Model and proposed method ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters") and [close–step 2](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#S2.I1.i2 "In 2.3. Conditional location-scale modeling of precision dependence ‣ 2. Model and proposed method ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters") . [Table 1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#S2.T1 "In 2.4.2. The location-scale assumption and close-npmle ‣ 2.4. Discussions ‣ 2. Model and proposed method ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters") summarizes how these methods fit into the close framework. Among these methods, some choose nonparametric models for [close–step 1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#S2.I1.i1 "In 2.3. Conditional location-scale modeling of precision dependence ‣ 2. Model and proposed method ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters") and some choose nonparametric models for [close–step 2](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#S2.I1.i2 "In 2.3. Conditional location-scale modeling of precision dependence ‣ 2. Model and proposed method ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters") . For instance, [Weinstein et al. (2018)](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib88) propose close\-gauss, with a partition-based nonparametric estimator for m0,s02. [Kline et al. (2023)](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib14) consider a scale family θi\=s0​(σi,β)​τi for some τi|σi​∼i.i.d.​G0; they model s0​(σi,β) parametrically, but model G0 flexibly using a log-spline sieve ([Efron, 2016](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib31)). [George et al. (2017)](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib9) propose a fully Bayesian model whose components feature parametric choices for m0,s0 with G0∼𝒩⁡(0,1).

While the right modeling approach likely depends on the particular empirical context, various subsets of these proposals emphasize being flexible in at least one of the two steps. Thus, absent substantive knowledge that motivates more restrictive assumptions, a natural default that unifies these approaches is to be flexible in both steps. Among nonparametric methods, close\-npmle may be particularly attractive due to its minimalism: The npmle is free of tuning parameters ([Koenker and Gu, 2019](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib41)), and tuning parameter choices for nonparametric regression are relatively well-understood ([Calonico et al., 2019](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib63); [Armstrong and Kolesár, 2018](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib8)). That said, at a high level, when precision dependence is an issue, any approach that models and estimates m0,s0,G0 well is likely to perform well.

While close\-npmle naturally generalizes the existing methods in [Table 1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#S2.T1 "In 2.4.2. The location-scale assumption and close-npmle ‣ 2.4. Discussions ‣ 2. Model and proposed method ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters"), one might consider methods that do not impose ([2.4](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#S2.Ex7 "Equation 2.4 ‣ 2.3. Conditional location-scale modeling of precision dependence ‣ 2. Model and proposed method ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters")) and are even more flexible. These methods are potentially more theoretically and computationally cumbersome: For instance, we can show that these flexible methods can no longer transform Yi into some Zi\=h⁡(Yi,σi) so as to exploit precision independence on the transformed model Zi|τ⁡(θi,σi),σi.9 In this sense, these methods must depart substantially from those that impose precision independence.

A natural approach is to estimate npmle locally around σ values, and we consider these approaches important venues of future work. One might consider discretizing observed σi values into bins and apply independent-npmle within each bin.10 A smoother—but more computationally intensive—alternative is to estimate the posterior at some given σ by considering only observations with σi∈\[σ−h,σ+h\] and again use independent-npmle for these observations. For these methods, the number of bins and bandwidth h are tuning parameters. While we anticipate ad hoc choices of tuning parameters to perform well, a proper theoretical analysis likely needs to link tuning choices to smoothness in the conditional distribution σ↦fY|σ(⋅∣σ) with respect to certain distributional distances. The corresponding regularity conditions thus seem more complex than smoothness conditions for conditional expectations required by close\-npmle.

##### 2.4.3. Additional remarks

###### Remark 1 (Negative s^2 estimates).

Analogue estimators for s02​(σi)\=Var⁡(Yi∣σi)−σi2 may take negative values.11 In our experience, truncating s^ at zero does not seem to cause bad performance when computing posterior means. Nevertheless, in [Appendix SM3](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A3a "Appendix SM3 Estimating 𝜂_0 by local linear regression ‣ Part IV Additional theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters") and the software implementation, we propose a heuristic but data-driven truncation rule that produces strictly positive s^, borrowing from a statistics literature on estimating non-centrality parameters for non-central χ2 distributions ([Kubokawa et al., 1993](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib62)). ■

###### Remark 2 (Other transformations).

We summarize and compare close to two methodological alternatives, deferring a detailed discussion on these and on several others to [Section OA2.2](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A2.SS2 "OA2.2. Alternatives to close ‣ Appendix OA2 Additional discussions ‣ Part II Additional discussions and empirical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters"). First, [Jiang and Zhang (2010)](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib33) propose applying npmle on the t\-ratio Zi\=Yi/σi∼𝒩⁡(θi/σi,1); similar approaches are used in [Efron (2016)](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib31); [Kline et al. (2022)](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib52). For estimating θi, one then uses θ^i\=σi⋅𝐄G^n​\[θi/σi∣Zi\]. Interpreting θ^i as an estimated posterior mean 𝔼P0\[θi∣Yi,σi\] requires that θi/σi𝑦σi—meaning that ([2.4](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#S2.Ex7 "Equation 2.4 ‣ 2.3. Conditional location-scale modeling of precision dependence ‣ 2. Model and proposed method ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters")) holds with s0​(σi)\=σi and constant m0​(⋅). Thus this t\-ratio approach can be viewed as a particular instance of close, if we wish to imbue it with an empirical Bayesian interpretation.

Second, when Yi and θi are sample and population means of binary outcomes, the estimated variance of Yi is mechanically correlated with θi: σi2\=Yi​(1−Yi)ni. A variance-stabilizing transform, e.g. Zi\=arcsin⁡Yi ([Brown, 2008](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib6)), results in _approximately_ Gaussian Zi∼𝒩⁡(arcsin⁡θi,14​ni) without the mechanical dependence. However, it is still possible that ni predicts θi, and when that happens, proper modeling of θi|ni—e.g., via an analogue of ([2.4](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#S2.Ex7 "Equation 2.4 ‣ 2.3. Conditional location-scale modeling of precision dependence ‣ 2. Model and proposed method ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters"))—can continue to improve performance. ■

### 3\. Theoretical results

As a review, we observe (Yi,σi)i\=1n, where (θi,σi) satisfies ([2.4](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#S2.Ex7 "Equation 2.4 ‣ 2.3. Conditional location-scale modeling of precision dependence ‣ 2. Model and proposed method ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters")) and (Yi,θi,σi) obeys ([1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#S1.Ex1 "1. Introduction ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters")). The procedure close\-npmle transforms the data (Yi,σi) into (Z^i,ν^i), with estimated conditional moments η^\=(m^,s^) for η0\=(m0,s0) in [close–step 1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#S2.I1.i1 "In 2.3. Conditional location-scale modeling of precision dependence ‣ 2. Model and proposed method ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters") . It then estimates G0 via npmle ([2.4.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#S2.Ex14 "2.4.1. Implementation ‣ 2.4. Discussions ‣ 2. Model and proposed method ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters")) on (Z^i,ν^i)i\=1n. This section introduces a few statistical guarantees on the performance of close\-npmle in terms of _regret_. To unify presentation, we first review decision theory primitives and introduce regret.

Let 𝜹(Y1:n,σ1:n) be a _decision rule_ mapping the data (Y1:n,σ1:n) to _actions_. Recall that L(𝜹,θ1:n) denotes a _loss function_ mapping actions and parameters to a scalar. Let RB(𝜹;P0)\=𝔼P0\[L(𝜹,θ1:n)∣σ1:n\] be the _Bayes risk_ of 𝜹 under P0. The oracle Bayes decision rule 𝜹⋆ ([2.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#S2.Ex3 "2.1. Empirical Bayes assumptions ‣ 2. Model and proposed method ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters")) is optimal in the sense that it minimizes RB. Thus, a natural performance measure for the empirical Bayesian ([2.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#S2.Ex5 "2.1. Empirical Bayes assumptions ‣ 2. Model and proposed method ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters")) is the gap between the Bayes risks of 𝜹EB and 𝜹⋆. We refer to this quantity as _Bayes regret_:

<table id="S3.EGx2" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table"><tbody id="S3.Ex1"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline"><td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_left"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_left">(3.1)</span></td><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td><td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.Ex1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\mathrm{BayesRegret}_{n}(\bm{\delta}_{\mathrm{EB}})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>BayesRegret</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝜹</mi><mi>EB</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></semantics></math></td><td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.Ex1.m2" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{P_{0}}[L(\bm{\delta}_{\mathrm{EB}},\theta_{1:n})-L(\bm{\delta}^{\star},\theta_{1:n})\mid\sigma_{1:n}]," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><msub><mi>P</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>L</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝜹</mi><mi>EB</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>θ</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>L</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>𝜹</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msup><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>θ</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">∣</mo><msub><mi>σ</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow></semantics></math></td><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody></table>

where the right-hand side integrates over the randomness in θ1:n,Y1:n, and, by extension, P^. If an empirical Bayes method achieves low Bayes regret, then it successfully imitates the decisions of the oracle Bayesian, and its decisions are thus approximately optimal. Our results show that Bayes regret for close\-npmle vanishes quickly as a function of n.

###### Remark 3 (Fixed vs. random θ).

Our results consider asymptotic optimality, in terms of ([3.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#S3.Ex1 "Equation 3.1 ‣ 3. Theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters")), of the empirical Bayes decision rule when θi|σi is randomly sampled from P0, following a recent literature on nonparametric empirical Bayes ([Jiang, 2020](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib85); [Soloff et al., 2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib86)). A separate literature considers instead the frequentist risk RF(θ1:n;σ1:n)≡𝔼\[L(𝜹,θ1:n)∣θ1:n,σ1:n\] under fixed (θ1:n,σ1:n) ([Robbins, 1956](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib81)). For instance, [James and Stein (1961)](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib39); [Bock (1975)](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib7); [Brown (2008)](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib6); [Weinstein et al. (2018)](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib88) consider shrinkage estimators that dominate δi\=Yi uniformly for all configurations of θ1:n. [Xie et al. (2012)](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib67); [Kwon (2023)](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib68) consider choosing decision rules within a restricted class that minimize an unbiased estimate of RF. In particular, [Xie et al. (2012)](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib67) can be thought of as implementing independent-gauss with different ways of estimating the hyperparameters in θi|σi​∼i.i.d.​𝒩​(m0,s02), and [Weinstein et al. (2018)](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib88) can be thought of as implementing close\-gauss.

While these guarantees for RF are preserved even if we further average the frequentist risk over θ1:n∣σ1:n∼P0, they are distinct from upper bounding ([3.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#S3.Ex1 "Equation 3.1 ‣ 3. Theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters")).12 In particular, they may leave much on the table if RB is targeted. Moreover, these guarantees in RF are typically restricted to MSE. Our example in [Figure 3](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#S2.F3 "In 2.2. Precision independence and its violation ‣ 2. Model and proposed method ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters") shows that reasonable decisions for MSE may not be reasonable for subsequent selection decisions. As a simple example, [Bock (1975)](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib7) considers spherical shrinkage rules of the form δi\=c⁡(∑jYj2)​Yi for some function c⁡(⋅). However, despite dominating no-shrinkage in MSE, δi does not change the ranking of different units, and hence does not improve on ranks over Yi. ■

In what follows, we use the symbol C to denote a generic positive and finite constant which does not depend on n. We use the symbol Cx to denote a generic positive and finite constant that depends only on x, some parameter(s) that describe the problem. Occurrences of the same symbol C,Cx may not refer to the same constants. Since all expectation or probability statements are with respect to the conditional distribution P0 of θ1:n∣σ1:n, going forward, we treat σ1:n as fixed and simply write 𝔼⁡\[⋅\],P⁡(⋅) to denote the expectation and probability over θ1:n∣σ1:n∼P0; we may omit the subscript P0 or the conditioning on σ1:n.

#### 3.1. Regret rate in squared error

Our main result concerns the canonical statistical problem of estimating the parameters θ1:n under MSE.

###### Decision Problem 1 (Squared-error estimation of θ1:n).

The action 𝜹\=(δ1,…,δn) collects estimates δi for θi, evaluated with MSE: L(𝜹,θ1:n)\=1n∑i\=1n(δi−θi)2. The oracle Bayes decision rule 𝜹⋆\=(θ1∗,…,θn∗) here is the posterior mean under P0, where θi∗≡𝔼P0\[θi∣Yi,σi\]. The empirical Bayesian counterpart is θ^i,P^\=𝐄P^\[θi∣Yi,σi\]. ■

For [Decision Problem 1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#Thmprob1 "Decision Problem 1 (Squared-error estimation of 𝜃_{1:𝑛}). ‣ 3.1. Regret rate in squared error ‣ 3. Theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters"), define MSERegretn as the excess loss of the empirical Bayes posterior means relative to that of the oracle Bayes posterior means:

##### 3.1.1. Assumptions for regret upper bound

We first assume that G^n is an approximate maximizer of the log-likelihood on the transformed data (Z^i,ν^i) satisfying some support restrictions. This is not restrictive, as the actual maximizers of the log-likelihood function satisfy it (Proposition 4, [Soloff et al. (2024)](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib86)). This assumption also accommodates for the fact that the npmle is approximated by a discrete distribution on a grid.

###### Assumption 1.

Let ψi​(Zi,η^,G)≡log⁡(∫−∞∞φ⁡(Z^i−τν^i)​G​(𝑑τ)) be the objective function in ([2.4.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#S2.Ex14 "2.4.1. Implementation ‣ 2.4. Discussions ‣ 2. Model and proposed method ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters")), ignoring the factor 1/ν^i that does not involve G. We assume that G^n satisfies

We now state further assumptions on 𝒫0 beyond ([2.4](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#S2.Ex7 "Equation 2.4 ‣ 2.3. Conditional location-scale modeling of precision dependence ‣ 2. Model and proposed method ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters")). First, we assume that G0 is sufficiently thin-tailed such that its moments grow slowly.14 The thickness of its tail is parametrized by α∈(0,2\], which subsequently affects the log factors in [Theorem 1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#Thmtheorem1 "Theorem 1. ‣ 3.1.2. MSE regret results ‣ 3.1. Regret rate in squared error ‣ 3. Theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters").

###### Assumption 2.

The distribution G0 has zero mean, unit variance, and admits simultaneous moment control: For some α∈(0,2\] and A0\>0 such that for all p\>0, (𝔼τ∼G0​\[|τ|p\])1/p≤A0​p1/α.

Next, [Assumption 3](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#Thmas3 "Assumption 3. ‣ 3.1.1. Assumptions for regret upper bound ‣ 3.1. Regret rate in squared error ‣ 3. Theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters") imposes that members of 𝒫0 have various variance parameters uniformly bounded away from zero and ∞. This is a standard assumption in the literature, maintained likewise by [Jiang (2020)](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib85) and [Soloff et al. (2024)](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib86).

###### Assumption 3.

The variances (σ1:n,s0) admit lower and upper bounds: There are positive reals σℓ,σu,s0​ℓ,s0​u\>0 such that, for all i and all σ∈(σℓ,σu), σℓ<σi<σu and s0​ℓ<s0​(σ)<s0​u.

Lastly, we require that m0​(⋅) and s0​(⋅) satisfy some smoothness restrictions. We also require that m^​(⋅) and s^​(⋅) satisfy some corresponding regularity conditions. Let CA1p​(\[σℓ,σu\]) denote the Hölder class of order p≥1 with maximal Hölder norm A1\>0 supported on \[σℓ,σu\] (Section 2.7.1, [van der Vaart and Wellner, 1996](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib78)).

    where ∥η∥∞≡max⁡(∥m∥∞,∥s∥∞) for η\=(m,s).
    
2.  (3)
    
    η^ takes values in 𝒱 almost surely: P⁡(m^∈𝒱,s^∈𝒱)\=1, where 𝒱 is a set of functions supported on \[σℓ,σu\] that (i) is uniformly bounded supf∈𝒱∥f∥∞≤CA1 and (ii) admits the metric entropy bound log⁡N⁡(ϵ,𝒱,∥⋅∥∞)≤CA1,p,σℓ,σu​(1/ϵ)1/p.
    
3.  (4)
    
    The conditional variance estimator respects the conditional variance bounds in [Assumption 3](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#Thmas3 "Assumption 3. ‣ 3.1.1. Assumptions for regret upper bound ‣ 3.1. Regret rate in squared error ‣ 3. Theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters"): P⁡(s0​ℓ2<s^<2​s0​u)\=1.
    

[Assumption 4](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#Thmas4 "Assumption 4. ‣ 3.1.1. Assumptions for regret upper bound ‣ 3.1. Regret rate in squared error ‣ 3. Theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters") is a Hölder smoothness assumption on the conditional moments m0 and s0, which is a standard regularity condition for nonparametric regression. Moreover, it is also a high-level assumption on the quality of the estimation procedure for (m^,s^). It expects that m^ and s^ are accurate in ∥⋅∥∞, belong to a class with manageable metric entropy, and obey the bounds for s0.15

[2](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#Thmas2 "Assumption 2. ‣ 3.1.1. Assumptions for regret upper bound ‣ 3.1. Regret rate in squared error ‣ 3. Theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters"), [4](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#Thmas4 "Assumption 4. ‣ 3.1.1. Assumptions for regret upper bound ‣ 3.1. Regret rate in squared error ‣ 3. Theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters"), and [3](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#Thmas3 "Assumption 3. ‣ 3.1.1. Assumptions for regret upper bound ‣ 3.1. Regret rate in squared error ‣ 3. Theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters") specify a class of distributions 𝒫0 and estimators η^\=(m^​(⋅),s^​(⋅)) regulated by a set of hyperparameters ℋ\=(σℓ,σu,sℓ,su,A0,A1,α,β0,p). Our subsequent theoretical results are uniform over 𝒫0 for a fixed ℋ.

##### 3.1.2. MSE regret results

Our main result is a non-asymptotic upper bound for ([3.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#S3.Ex3 "3.1. Regret rate in squared error ‣ 3. Theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters")): The MSE regret of close\-npmle converges to zero no slower than n−2​p2​p+1​(log⁡n)C.
