[Theorem 1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#Thmtheorem1 "Theorem 1. ‣ 3.1.2. MSE regret results ‣ 3.1. Regret rate in squared error ‣ 3. Theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters") continues a recent statistics literature on empirical Bayes methods via npmle, by characterizing the effect of an estimated first-step parameter η^. Our theory hews closely to—and extends—the results in [Jiang (2020)](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib85) and [Soloff et al. (2024)](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib86), which themselves extend earlier results in the homoskedastic setting ([Jiang and Zhang, 2009](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib89); [Saha and Guntuboyina, 2020](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib77)). In particular, [Soloff et al. (2024)](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib86) show that the MSE regret rate is of the form C​(log⁡n)β​1n under precision independence and assumptions similar to ours. In this context, we show that first-step estimation error degrades this regret rate gracefully, and we link the corresponding regret rate to the smoothness of η0. The proof of [Theorem 1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#Thmtheorem1 "Theorem 1. ‣ 3.1.2. MSE regret results ‣ 3.1. Regret rate in squared error ‣ 3. Theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters") is deferred to the Online Appendix, but its main ideas are outlined in [Appendix A](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A1 "Appendix A Proof outline for ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters").

[Theorem 2](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#Thmtheorem2 "Theorem 2. ‣ 3.1.2. MSE regret results ‣ 3.1. Regret rate in squared error ‣ 3. Theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters") shows that the rate ([1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#S3.Ex8 "Theorem 1. ‣ 3.1.2. MSE regret results ‣ 3.1. Regret rate in squared error ‣ 3. Theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters")) is optimal up to logarithmic factors. These logarithmic factors partly reflect inefficiencies in the proof of [Theorem 1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#Thmtheorem1 "Theorem 1. ‣ 3.1.2. MSE regret results ‣ 3.1. Regret rate in squared error ‣ 3. Theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters"), but in any case the gap is not large. We prove [Theorem 2](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#Thmtheorem2 "Theorem 2. ‣ 3.1.2. MSE regret results ‣ 3.1. Regret rate in squared error ‣ 3. Theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters") by showing that any good posterior mean estimate θ^i implies a good estimate m^​(σi) for m0 for some particular choice of G0,σ1:n,s02(⋅). Minimax lower bounds for estimation of m0 ([Tsybakov, 2008](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib72)) then imply lower bounds for estimation of the oracle posterior means θi∗ (see [Ignatiadis and Wager, 2019](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib64), for a similar argument in a related setting).

We additionally note that these regret upper bounds readily extend to the case where covariates are present and the location-scale assumption ([2.4](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#S2.Ex7 "Equation 2.4 ‣ 2.3. Conditional location-scale modeling of precision dependence ‣ 2. Model and proposed method ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters")) is specified with respect to the additional covariates Xi:

<table id="S3.Ex11" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table"><tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline"><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.Ex11.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta_{i}\mid\sigma_{i},X_{i}\sim G_{0}\left({\frac{\cdot-m_{0}(X_{i},\sigma_{i})}{s_{0}(X_{i},\sigma_{i})}}\right)," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>θ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo fence="false">|</mo><mrow><msub><mi>σ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>X</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>∼</mo><mrow><msub><mi>G</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><msub><mi>m</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>X</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>σ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>X</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>σ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow></semantics></math></td><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody></table>

under smoothness assumptions on (m0,s0,m^,s^) analogous to [Assumption 4](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#Thmas4 "Assumption 4. ‣ 3.1.1. Assumptions for regret upper bound ‣ 3.1. Regret rate in squared error ‣ 3. Theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters"). The resulting convergence rate would reflect the dimensionality of the covariates, and the term n−2​p2​p+1 would be replaced with n−2​p2​p+1+d, where d is the dimension of X.

Taken together, [Theorems 1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#Thmtheorem1 "Theorem 1. ‣ 3.1.2. MSE regret results ‣ 3.1. Regret rate in squared error ‣ 3. Theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters") and [2](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#Thmtheorem2 "Theorem 2. ‣ 3.1.2. MSE regret results ‣ 3.1. Regret rate in squared error ‣ 3. Theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters") are statistical optimality guarantees for close\-npmle in terms of [Decision Problem 1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#Thmprob1 "Decision Problem 1 (Squared-error estimation of 𝜃_{1:𝑛}). ‣ 3.1. Regret rate in squared error ‣ 3. Theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters"). That is, the worst-case MSE performance gap of close\-npmle relative to the oracle contracts at the best possible rate, meaning that close\-npmle mimics the oracle as well as possible.

#### 3.2. Robustness to the location-scale assumption ([2.4](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#S2.Ex7 "Equation 2.4 ‣ 2.3. Conditional location-scale modeling of precision dependence ‣ 2. Model and proposed method ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters"))

We prove [Theorems 1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#Thmtheorem1 "Theorem 1. ‣ 3.1.2. MSE regret results ‣ 3.1. Regret rate in squared error ‣ 3. Theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters") and [2](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#Thmtheorem2 "Theorem 2. ‣ 3.1.2. MSE regret results ‣ 3.1. Regret rate in squared error ‣ 3. Theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters") imposing the location-scale model ([2.4](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#S2.Ex7 "Equation 2.4 ‣ 2.3. Conditional location-scale modeling of precision dependence ‣ 2. Model and proposed method ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters")). This is an optimistic assessment of the performance of close\-npmle. While ([2.4](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#S2.Ex7 "Equation 2.4 ‣ 2.3. Conditional location-scale modeling of precision dependence ‣ 2. Model and proposed method ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters")) nests precision independence, it may still be misspecified. This subsection explores the worst-case behavior of close\-npmle without ([2.4](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#S2.Ex7 "Equation 2.4 ‣ 2.3. Conditional location-scale modeling of precision dependence ‣ 2. Model and proposed method ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters")).

We do so by considering an idealized version of close\-npmle. So long as θi|σi has two moments, η0​(⋅)\=(m0​(⋅),s0​(⋅)) are well-defined as conditional moments. We will assume that m0,s0 are known. Without ([2.4](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#S2.Ex7 "Equation 2.4 ‣ 2.3. Conditional location-scale modeling of precision dependence ‣ 2. Model and proposed method ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters")), G0 is ill-defined, but we assume that we obtain some pseudo-true value G0∗ that has zero mean and unit variance. Thus, for estimating τi\=θi−m0​(σi)s0​(σi), whose distribution is τi|σi∼Gi, this idealized procedure uses some misspecified prior G0∗≠Gi, where G0∗ agrees with Gi in the first two moments. The worst-case performance of the procedure that uses G0∗ depends on how far posterior means under G0∗ differs from posterior means under Gi.

We show in [Appendix SM5](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A5 "Appendix SM5 Maximum posterior discrepancy of priors satisfying moment constraints ‣ Part IV Additional theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters") that this difference is bounded uniformly for all G0∗ satisfying an additional tail assumption. This result implies that the maximum risk of this procedure is at most a constant multiple of the minimax risk; here, the minimaxity is defined with respect to a game between an analyst and an adversary, where the analyst knows m0,s0 and hopes to estimate θ1:n, and the adversary chooses the shape of the distribution τi|σi. In this game, the oracle version of close\-gauss ([2.4.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#S2.Ex16 "2.4.1. Implementation ‣ 2.4. Discussions ‣ 2. Model and proposed method ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters")) is a minimax procedure ([Lemma SM4.3](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A4.Thmlemma3 "Lemma SM4.3. ‣ Appendix SM4 Auxiliary lemmas for and ‣ Part IV Additional theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters")).

Specifically, let 𝒫⁡(m0,s0) denote the set of distributions of θ1:n∣σ1:n where 𝔼⁡\[θi∣σi\]\=m0​(σi) and Var⁡(θi∣σi)\=s02​(σi). Let

#### 3.3. Other decision objectives and relation to squared-error loss

So far, our regret guarantees are only about estimation in MSE ([Decision Problem 1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#Thmprob1 "Decision Problem 1 (Squared-error estimation of 𝜃_{1:𝑛}). ‣ 3.1. Regret rate in squared error ‣ 3. Theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters")). We now turn to two decision problems that involve ranking or selection and show similar guarantees for close\-npmle in terms of regret for these decision problems. These decision problems are likely more economically relevant for, e.g., replacing low value-added teachers, recommending high-mobility tracts, or treatment choice ([Gilraine et al., 2020](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib60); [Bergman et al., 2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib65); [Manski, 2004](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib24); [Stoye, 2009](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib21); [Kitagawa and Tetenov, 2018](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib20); [Athey and Wager, 2021](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib19)).

###### Decision Problem 2 (utility maximization by selection).

Suppose 𝜹\=(δ1,…,δn) consists of binary selection decisions δi∈{0,1}. For each population, selecting that population has net benefit θi. The decision maker wishes to maximize utility (i.e., negative loss): −L(𝜹,θ1:n)\=1n∑i\=1nδiθi. The oracle Bayes rule selects all whose posterior mean net benefit θi is nonnegative: δi⋆\=𝟙​(θi,P0∗≥0). One natural empirical Bayes decision rule replaces θi,P0∗ with θi,P^∗, following ([2.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#S2.Ex5 "2.1. Empirical Bayes assumptions ‣ 2. Model and proposed method ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters")). ■

###### Decision Problem 3 (top-m selection).

Similar to utility maximization by selection, suppose 𝜹 consists of binary selection decisions, with the additional constraint that exactly m populations are chosen: ∑iδi\=m. The decision maker’s utility is the average θi of the selected set:

<table id="S3.Ex16" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table"><tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline"><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.Ex16.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="-L(\bm{\delta},\theta_{1:n})=\frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\delta_{i}\theta_{i}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>L</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝜹</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>θ</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>m</mi></mfrac><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></munderover><msub><mi>δ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><msub><mi>θ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow></semantics></math></td><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody></table>

The oracle Bayesian selects the populations corresponding to the m largest posterior means θi,P0∗: δi⋆\=𝟙(θi,P0∗ is among the top-m of θ1:n,P0∗). Again, the empirical Bayes recipe ([2.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#S2.Ex5 "2.1. Empirical Bayes assumptions ‣ 2. Model and proposed method ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters")) replaces P0 with the estimate P^. ■

###### Remark 4.

The utility function ([3](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#S3.Ex16 "Decision Problem 3 (top-𝑚 selection). ‣ 3.3. Other decision objectives and relation to squared-error loss ‣ 3. Theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters")) rationalizes the widespread practice of screening based on empirical Bayes posterior means ([Gilraine et al., 2020](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib60); [Chetty et al., 2014](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib92); [Kane and Staiger, 2008](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib56); [Hanushek, 2011](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib18); [Bergman et al., 2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib65)). In [Bergman et al. (2024)](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib65), for instance, where housing voucher holders are incentivized to move to Census tracts selected according to economic mobility, ([3](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#S3.Ex16 "Decision Problem 3 (top-𝑚 selection). ‣ 3.3. Other decision objectives and relation to squared-error loss ‣ 3. Theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters")) represents the expected economic mobility of a mover were they to move randomly to one of the selected tracts. Our theoretical results can accommodate slightly less restrictive mover behavior ([Remark B.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A2.Thmrmk1 "Remark B.1 (Mover interpretation of ). ‣ Appendix B Proofs of other results stated in the main text ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters")). ■

The oracle Bayes decision rules 𝜹⋆ in [Decision Problems 2](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#Thmprob2 "Decision Problem 2 (utility maximization by selection). ‣ 3.3. Other decision objectives and relation to squared-error loss ‣ 3. Theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters") and [3](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#Thmprob3 "Decision Problem 3 (top-𝑚 selection). ‣ 3.3. Other decision objectives and relation to squared-error loss ‣ 3. Theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters") depend solely on the vector of oracle Bayes posterior means θ1:n∗. Therefore, for these problems, the natural empirical Bayes decision rules simply replace oracle Bayes posterior means (θi∗) with empirical Bayes ones (θ^i). It stands to reason that as θ^i is close to θi∗ in squared error, even when θ^i implies the wrong selection decision, this decision is not too costly for the empirical Bayesian. We formalize this intuition in the following theorem, showing that if θ^i are close to θi∗ in MSE, then decisions plugging in θ^i are also close to their oracle counterparts in terms of Bayes risk.

To specialize, let UMRegretn denote BayesRegretn for the loss function in [Decision Problem 2](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#Thmprob2 "Decision Problem 2 (utility maximization by selection). ‣ 3.3. Other decision objectives and relation to squared-error loss ‣ 3. Theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters") and let TopRegretn(m) denote BayesRegretn for [Decision Problem 3](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#Thmprob3 "Decision Problem 3 (top-𝑚 selection). ‣ 3.3. Other decision objectives and relation to squared-error loss ‣ 3. Theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters").

In particular, for m/n→c∈(0,1), both regret rates ([1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#S3.Ex18 "Item 1 ‣ Theorem 4. ‣ 3.3. Other decision objectives and relation to squared-error loss ‣ 3. MSE regret results ‣ 3.1. Regret rate in squared error ‣ 3. Theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters"). Thus, the performance of the empirical Bayes decision rule approximates that of the oracle at least as fast as O(n−p/(2p+1)), up to log factors.

###### Remark 5 (Tightness of [Theorem 4](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#Thmtheorem4 "Theorem 4. ‣ 3.3. Other decision objectives and relation to squared-error loss ‣ 3. Theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters")).

We suspect that the actual performance of close\-npmle for [Decision Problems 2](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#Thmprob2 "Decision Problem 2 (utility maximization by selection). ‣ 3.3. Other decision objectives and relation to squared-error loss ‣ 3. Theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters") and [3](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#Thmprob3 "Decision Problem 3 (top-𝑚 selection). ‣ 3.3. Other decision objectives and relation to squared-error loss ‣ 3. Theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters") may be better than predicted by [Theorem 4](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#Thmtheorem4 "Theorem 4. ‣ 3.3. Other decision objectives and relation to squared-error loss ‣ 3. Theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters"). The proof of [Theorem 4](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#Thmtheorem4 "Theorem 4. ‣ 3.3. Other decision objectives and relation to squared-error loss ‣ 3. Theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters") exploits the fact that when the empirical Bayesian makes a selection mistake, the size of the mistake is not large if the square-error regret is low. It does not exploit the fact that if squared error regret is low, then the empirical Bayesian may be unlikely to make mistakes in the first place.19 Nevertheless, [Theorem 4](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#Thmtheorem4 "Theorem 4. ‣ 3.3. Other decision objectives and relation to squared-error loss ‣ 3. Theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters") is competitive with recent results. For instance, in nonparametric settings, the rate in [Theorem 4](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#Thmtheorem4 "Theorem 4. ‣ 3.3. Other decision objectives and relation to squared-error loss ‣ 3. Theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters") is more favorable than the upper bound derived in [Coey and Hung (2022)](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib80), who also study [Decision Problem 3](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#Thmprob3 "Decision Problem 3 (top-𝑚 selection). ‣ 3.3. Other decision objectives and relation to squared-error loss ‣ 3. Theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters"). ■

We close this section with a procedure that provides unbiased estimates of the loss of _arbitrary_ decision rules for [Decision Problems 1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#Thmprob1 "Decision Problem 1 (Squared-error estimation of 𝜃_{1:𝑛}). ‣ 3.1. Regret rate in squared error ‣ 3. The conditional independence allows us to use Yi(2) as an out-of-sample validation for decision rules computed based on Yi(1). We denote their variances by σi,(1)2 and σi,(2)2.

The coupled bootstrap can be thought of as approximating sample-splitting the micro-data without needing access. We could imagine splitting the micro-data into training and testing sets, and think of Yi(1) as training-set estimates and Yi(2) as testing-set estimates. We might compute decisions based on Yi(1) and evaluate them honestly with fresh data Yi(2). The coupled bootstrap precisely emulates this sample-splitting procedure.20

The following proposition formalizes how to use coupled bootstrap to provide unbiased estimators for the loss of a generic decision rule.21

### 4\. Empirical illustration

How does close\-npmle perform in the field? We now consider two empirical exercises related to [Chetty et al. (forthcoming)](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib66) and [Bergman et al. (2024)](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib65). Using Census micro-data, [Chetty et al. (forthcoming)](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib66) estimate a suite of tract-level children’s outcomes in adulthood and publish an ‘‘Opportunity Atlas’’ of the estimates and the corresponding standard errors.22 Taking these estimates, [Bergman et al. (2024)](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib65) conducted a program called Creating Moves to Opportunity. [Bergman et al. (2024)](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib65) provided assistance to treated low-income individuals to move to Census tracts with estimated posterior means in the top third. We view [Bergman et al. (2024)](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib65)’s objectives as top-m selection, for m equal to one third of the number of tracts in Seattle and King County, WA.

The Opportunity Atlas published by [Chetty et al. (forthcoming)](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib66) also includes tract-level covariates, a complication that we have so far abstracted away from. In the ensuing empirical exercises, following [Bergman et al. (2024)](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib65), the estimates are residualized against the covariates as a preprocessing step ([Fay and Herriot, 1979](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib32)).23 We now let Y~i denote the raw Opportunity Atlas estimates for a pre-residualized parameter ϑi and let (Yi,θi) be their residualized counterparts against a vector of tract-level covariates Xi, with regression coefficient β.24 We can apply the empirical Bayes procedures in this paper to (Yi,σi2) and obtain an estimated posterior for θi. This estimated posterior for the residualized parameter θi then implies an estimated posterior for the original parameter ϑi\=θi+Xi′​β, by adding back the fitted values Xi′​β. When there are no covariates, ϑi\=θi and Yi\=Y~i.

The covariates we use are included in the publicly available data from [Chetty et al. (forthcoming)](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib66) and cross-referenced with their labels in [Table OA3.2](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A3.T2 "In OA3.2. Simulation exercises setup ‣ Appendix OA3 Additional empirical exercises ‣ Part II Additional discussions and empirical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters"). They include: poverty rate in 2010, share of Black individuals in 2010, mean household income in 2000, log wage growth for high school graduates, fraction with college or post-graduate degrees in 2010, mean parent family income rank, mean parent family income rank for Black individuals, number of all and Black children under 18 with parents whose household income is below median in 2000 (in both levels and logs).

We consider 15 measures of economic mobility ϑi. Each ϑi is the population mean of _some_ outcome for individuals of _some_ demographic subgroup growing up in tract i, whose parents are at the 25th income percentile.25 We will consider three types of outcomes: (i) percentile rank of adult income (mean rank), (ii) an indicator for whether the individual has incomes in the top 20 percentiles (top-20 probability), and (iii) an indicator for whether the individual is incarcerated (incarceration) for the following five demographic subgroups: all individuals (pooled), white individuals, white men, Black individuals, and Black men. Under these shorthands, the outcome in [Section 2](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#S2 "2. Model and proposed method ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters") is top-20 probability (Black), while [Bergman et al. (2024)](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib65) consider mean rank pooled.

The remainder of this section compares several methods on two exercises. In the first exercise, a calibrated simulation, we compare MSE performance of various methods to that of the oracle posterior. The second exercise is an empirical application to a scale-up of the exercise in [Bergman et al. (2024)](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib65). It uses the coupled bootstrap ([Section 3.4](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#S3.SS4 "3.4. Validating performance by coupled bootstrap ‣ 3. Theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters")) to evaluate whether close\-npmle selects more economically mobile tracts than alternatives.

#### 4.1. Calibrated simulation

We draw from a data-generating process estimated from the data. This data-generating process does not impose the location-scale assumption. On the data (Yi,σi), we estimate m^​(⋅),s^2​(⋅) via local linear regression. We then transform to obtain Z^i\=Yi−m^​(σi)s^​(σi) and ν^i\=σis^​(σi). We partition σi into vingtiles. For the data (Z^i,ν^i) whose σi falls in a given vingtile v∈{1,2,3,4,5}, we estimate a vingtile-specific G^n,v via npmle. We then normalize this estimated npmle to have mean zero and variance one, by affinely transforming the estimated distribution. Finally, to generate synthetic data, for a σi corresponding to the v⁡(σi)th vingtile, we draw τi∗|σi∼G^n,v⁡(σi)normalized, and set θi∗\=τi∗​s^​(σi)+m^​(σi), Yi∗|θi∗,σi∼𝒩⁡(θi∗,σi2) and Y~i∗\=Yi∗+Xi′​β. Additional details for the sampling process and simulation setup are documented in [Section OA3.2](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A3.SS2 "OA3.2. Simulation exercises setup ‣ Appendix OA3 Additional empirical exercises ‣ Part II Additional discussions and empirical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters").

On the simulated data, we then implement various empirical Bayes strategies. We consider the feasible procedures: naive, independent-gauss, independent-npmle, close\-gauss (parametric), close\-gauss, and close\-npmle, as well as the infeasible oracle. Here,

-   •
    
    naive sets θ^i\=Yi.
    
-   •
    
    independent-gauss weighs the estimation of the hyperparameters (m0,s0) with 1/σi2, following [Bergman et al. (2024)](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib65).
    
-   •
    
    close\-gauss (parametric) implements close\-gauss, where [close–step 1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#S2.I1.i1 "In 2.3. Conditional location-scale modeling of precision dependence ‣ 2. Model and proposed method ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters") models the conditional moments parametrically as m0​(σi,a)\=a1+a2​log⁡σi and s02​(σi,b)\=exp⁡(b1+b2​log⁡σi), and estimates m0,s0 via least-squares.26
    
-   •
    
    The conditional moments η0\=(m0​(⋅),s0​(⋅)) in close\-gauss and close\-npmle are estimated via local linear regression, where bandwidth is selected via plug-in IMSE-optimal bandwidth, as implemented in [Calonico et al. (2019)](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib63).27
    
-   •
    
    Since we know the ground truth data-generating process, we can also compute the oracle procedure that uses posterior means under the true P0.
    
-   •
    
    None of the feasible procedures have access to β, which they must estimate in the same way using weighted least squares with weight 1/σi2, following [Bergman et al. (2024)](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib65).

The table shows relative performance, defined as the squared error improvement over naive, normalized as a percentage of the improvement of oracle over naive. The last row shows the column median. Results are averaged over 1,000 Monte Carlo draws. ∎

Figure 4. Relative squared error Bayes risk for various empirical Bayes posterior means

[Figure 4](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#S4.F4 "In 4.1. Calibrated simulation ‣ 4. Empirical illustration ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters") plots the results from this calibrated simulation, focusing on MSE performance. For each method and each target variable, we display a relative measure of MSE gain. For each method, we calculate its MSE gain over naive, normalized by the MSE gain of oracle over naive. If we think of the oracle–naive difference as the total size of the “statistical pie,” then [Figure 4](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#S4.F4 "In 4.1. Calibrated simulation ‣ 4. Empirical illustration ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters") shows how much of this pie each method captures.

The first five columns show the relative mean-squared error performance without residualizing against covariates, applying empirical Bayes methods directly on (Y~i,σi). We see that methods which assume precision independence perform worse than methods based on close.28 Across the 15 variables, the median proportion of possible gains captured by independent-gauss is only 31%. This value is 50% for independent-npmle, and 86% for close\-npmle. Among the first five columns, close\-npmle uniformly dominates all three other methods. This indicates that the standard error σi is highly predictive of θi, and using that information can be very helpful in the absence of additional covariates.

The next five columns show performance when the methods do have access to covariate information. For mean rank, after covariate residualization, the dependence between θi and σi does not appear to substantially affect shrinkage decisions. independent-npmle and close\-methods perform similarly, capturing almost all of the available gains. For the other two outcome variables, top-20 probability and incarceration, the dependence between θi and σi is stronger, and close\-based methods display substantial improvements over methods that assume precision independence. Among close\-methods, those that are more flexible appear to reap a small benefit, though simple parametric models for (m0,s0,G0) remain competitive and significantly improve upon methods that assume precision independence. The most flexible method, close\-npmle, achieves near-oracle performance across the different definitions of θi and again uniformly dominates all other feasible methods.29

#### 4.2. Validation exercise via coupled bootstrap

  

###### Notes.

Each column is an empirical Bayes strategy that we consider, and each row is a different definition of ϑi. The table shows coupled-bootstrap estimates of average ϑi among the Census tracts selected by each method—in terms of either percentage points or percentile ranks—over 1,000 draws of coupled bootstrap. All decision rules are estimated separately within CZs and select the top third of Census tracts within each CZ. The color scheme within each row treats the performance of naive as zero (grey) and close\-npmle as one (dark green), and is hence not comparable across rows. On this scale, a method that overperforms naive is colored green; otherwise it is colored magenta. The best performer for each row is additionally marked with an orange star. ∎

Figure 5. Performance of decision rules in top-m selection exercise

Our second empirical exercise uses the coupled bootstrap described in [Section 3.4](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#S3.SS4 "3.4. Validating performance by coupled bootstrap ‣ 3. Theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters") for the policy problem in [Bergman et al. (2024)](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib65). Viewing the policy problem in [Bergman et al. (2024)](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib65) as top-m selection, can close\-npmle make better selections?

Specifically, we imagine scaling up [Bergman et al. (2024)](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib65)’s exercise and perform empirical Bayes procedures for all Census tracts in the largest 20 Commuting Zones (CZs). We then select the top third of tracts _within_ each CZ, according to empirical Bayesian posterior means for ϑi. Additionally, to faithfully mimic [Bergman et al. (2024)](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib65), here we perform all empirical Bayes procedures _within CZ_. Throughout, we choose ω to emulate a 90-10 train-test split on the micro-data. See [Section OA3.2](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A3.SS2 "OA3.2. Simulation exercises setup ‣ Appendix OA3 Additional empirical exercises ‣ Part II Additional discussions and empirical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters") for details on the policy exercise setup.

[Figure 5](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#S4.F5 "In 4.2. Validation exercise via coupled bootstrap ‣ 4. Empirical illustration ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters") shows the estimated performance of various methods. According to these estimates, close\-npmle generally improves over independent-gauss.30 Strikingly, independent-gauss with covariates underperforms naive for four of the 15 variables, and independent-gauss without covariates underperforms for nearly all variables.

For the mean rank variables, using close\-npmle generates substantial gains for mobility measures for Black individuals (0.63 percentile ranks for Black men and 0.43 percentile ranks for Black individuals). To put these gains in dollar terms, at the income level for experiment participants in [Bergman et al. (2024)](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib65), an incremental percentile rank amounts to about $1,000 per annum. Thus, the estimated gain in terms of mean income rank is roughly $400–600. For the other two outcomes, top-20 probability and incarceration, the gains are even more sizable. These gains are as high as 2–3 percentage points on average. Among close\-methods, we again find that close\-npmle generally performs the best, though by small margins.31 While close\-npmle is a simple default that works uniformly well, in this case, simple parametric models that allow for dependence also appear competitive.

We can think of the performance gap between independent-gauss and naive as the _value of basic empirical Bayes_. If practitioners find using the standard empirical Bayes method a worthwhile investment over screening on the raw estimates directly, perhaps they reveal that the value of basic empirical Bayes is economically significant. Across the 15 measures, the improvement of close\-npmle over independent-gauss is on median 260% of the value of basic empirical Bayes, where the median is attained by mean rank for Black individuals. Thus, the additional gain of close\-npmle over independent-gauss is substantial compared to the value of basic empirical Bayes. If the latter is economically significant, then it is similarly worthwhile to use close\-npmle instead.

### 5\. Conclusion

This paper studies empirical Bayes methods in the heteroskedastic Gaussian location model. We argue that precision independence—the assumption that the precision of estimates does not predict the true parameter—is often empirically rejected. Empirical Bayes methods that rely on precision independence can generate worse posterior mean estimates. Screening decisions based on these estimates can suffer as a result. They may even be worse than the selection decisions made with the unshrunk estimates directly.

Instead of treating θi as independent from σi, we model its conditional distribution as a location-scale family in σ\-dependent location and scale parameters. This assumption leads naturally to a family of empirical Bayes strategies that we call close. The close\-framework naturally subsumes and generalizes several existing proposals for accommodating precision dependence. We prove that close\-npmle attains minimax-optimal rates in Bayes regret, extending previous theoretical results. That is, it approximates infeasible oracle Bayes posterior means as competently as statistically possible. Additionally, we show that an idealized version of close\-npmle is robust, with finite worst-case Bayes risk. Finally, we further connect our main theoretical results to ranking-type decision problems in [Bergman et al. (2024)](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib65).

Simulation and validation exercises demonstrate that close\-npmle generates sizable gains relative to the standard parametric empirical Bayes shrinkage method. Across calibrated simulations, close\-npmle attains close-to-oracle mean-squared error performance. In a hypothetical, scaled-up version of [Bergman et al. (2024)](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib65), across a wide range of economic mobility measures, close\-npmle consistently selects more mobile tracts than does the standard empirical Bayes method. The gains in the average economic mobility among selected tracts, relative to the standard empirical Bayes procedure, are often comparable to—or even multiples of—the value of basic empirical Bayes.

Loosely speaking, [Soloff et al. (2024)](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib86), following [Jiang and Zhang (2009)](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib89), show that

1.  (1)
    
    With high probability, all approximate maximizers of the likelihood have low average Hellinger distance:

    for some rate function δn2≲1n​(log⁡n)C (Theorem 7 in [Soloff et al. (2024)](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib86)).
    
2.  (2)
    
    For a given G, 𝔼⁡\[(τi∗−τ^i,G,η0)2\]≲(log⁡n)C​(h¯2​(fG,⋅,fG0,⋅)) (Theorem 9 in [Soloff et al. (2024)](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib86)).
    

Therefore, an approximate maximizer G^n∗ of the likelihood Subn​(G) should have low average Hellinger distance to G0 and thus should output similar posterior means.

#### A.2. Step 2: show G^n is an approximate maximizer of the true likelihood

To use this argument for [Theorem A.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A1.Thmtheorem1 "Theorem A.1. ‣ Appendix A Proof outline for ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters"), a key challenge is that G^n only maximizes the _approximate_ likelihood 1n​∑iψi​(Zi,η^,G), which only has η^≈η0 on An, but η^≠η0. A key result is an oracle inequality for the likelihood ([Corollary SM1.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A1.Thmcor1a "Corollary SM1.1. ‣ Appendix SM1 An oracle inequality for the likelihood ‣ Part III Important preliminary results for ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters")), where, loosely speaking,

#### A.3. Step 3: adapt Hellinger distance bound

[Corollary SM1.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A1.Thmcor1a "Corollary SM1.1. ‣ Appendix SM1 An oracle inequality for the likelihood ‣ Part III Important preliminary results for ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters") makes sure that G^n probably achieves high likelihood, but the bound depends on h¯2. Since ([1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A1.Ex9 "Item 1 ‣ A.1. Step 1: convert regret on 𝜃_𝑖 to regret on 𝜏_𝑖 ‣ Appendix A Proof outline for ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters")) uses a likelihood bound for G to control h¯2, we need to additionally finesse ([1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A1.Ex9 "Item 1 ‣ A.1. Step 1: convert regret on 𝜃_𝑖 to regret on 𝜏_𝑖 ‣ Appendix A Proof outline for ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters")) to accommodate the fact that the likelihood bound depends on h¯2.

Second, we adapt ([1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A1.Ex9 "Item 1 ‣ A.1. Step 1: convert regret on 𝜃_𝑖 to regret on 𝜏_𝑖 ‣ Appendix A Proof outline for ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters")) to show that, loosely speaking, with high probability G^n has low average Hellinger distance to G0 ([Corollary OA1.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A1.Thmcor1 "Corollary OA1.1. ‣ OA1.1. Proof of ‣ Appendix OA1 Review of notation and proofs of and ‣ Part I Proof of ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters")):

<table id="A1.Ex16" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table"><tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline"><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A1.Ex16.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\operatorname{P}\left[{A_{n},\overline{h}^{2}(f_{\hat{G}_{n},\cdot},f_{G_{0},\cdot})\gtrsim_{\mathcal{H}}n^{-p/(2p+1)}(\log n)^{C}}\right]=O\left({\frac{(\log n)^{C}}{n}}\right)." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mrow><mo>[</mo><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msup><mover accent="true"><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="true">¯</mo></mover><mn>2</mn></msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>f</mi><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>G</mi><mo mathsize="1.280em">^</mo></mover><mi>n</mi></msub><mo rspace="0em">,</mo><mo lspace="0em">⋅</mo></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>f</mi><mrow><msub><mi>G</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo rspace="0em">,</mo><mo lspace="0em">⋅</mo></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><msub><mo>≳</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℋ</mi></msub><msup><mi>n</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>/</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>p</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>log</mi><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mi>C</mi></msup><mo>]</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>O</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mfrac><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mi>C</mi></msup><mi>n</mi></mfrac><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow></semantics></math></td><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody></table>

Thus, this allows us to show that 𝔼⁡\[(τi∗−τ^i,G,η0)2​𝟙​(An)\] is small, after additional empirical process arguments in [Appendix OA1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A1a "Appendix OA1 Review of notation and proofs of and ‣ Part I Proof of ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters").

This section concludes with a proof for [Theorem 1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#Thmtheorem1 "Theorem 1. ‣ 3.1.2. MSE regret results ‣ 3.1. Regret rate in squared error ‣ 3. Theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters") given these results.

###### Proof of [Theorem 1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#Thmtheorem1 "Theorem 1. ‣ 3.1.2. MSE regret results ‣ 3.1. Regret rate in squared error ‣ 3. Theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters").

### Appendix B Proofs of other results stated in the main text

###### Proof of [Theorem 2](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#Thmtheorem2 "Theorem 2. ‣ 3.1.2. MSE regret results ‣ 3.1. Regret rate in squared error ‣ 3. Theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters").

We consider a specific choice of G0,σ1:n, and s0. Namely, suppose G0∼𝒩⁡(0,1), σ1:n are equally spaced in \[σℓ,σu\], and s0​(σ)\=(sℓ+su)/2≡s0 is constant. With these choices, the oracle posterior means θi∗ are equal to

Using classical minimax results, [Lemma SM4.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A4.Thmlemma1 "Lemma SM4.1. ‣ Appendix SM4 Auxiliary lemmas for and ‣ Part IV Additional theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters") shows that the right-hand side is lower bounded by n−2p/(2p+1), which completes the proof. ∎

Note that θ^i,G0∗,η0\=s0​(σi)​τ^i,G0∗,η0+m0​(σi), where τi,G,η∗ is the posterior mean for τi under (G,η), and θi\=s0​(σi)​τi+m0​(σi). Thus,

###### Proof of [Theorem 4](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#Thmtheorem4 "Theorem 4. ‣ 3.3. Other decision objectives and relation to squared-error loss ‣ 3. Theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters").

1.  (1)
    
    By the law of iterated expectations, since θ^i,θi∗ are both measurable with respect to the data,33

    Note that, for 𝟙​(θi∗≥0)−𝟙​(θ^i≥0) to be nonzero, 0 is between θ^i and θi∗. Hence, |θi∗|≤|θi∗−θi| and thus by Jensen’s inequality

The last step follows from the observation that the sorted difference is dominated by the unsorted difference, ∑i\=1n(θ(i)∗−θ^σ⁡(i))2≤∑i\=1n(θ^i−θi∗)2, which is true by the rearrangement inequality.34 ∎

###### Remark B.1 (Mover interpretation of [Theorem 4](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#Thmtheorem4 "Theorem 4. ‣ 3.3. Other decision objectives and relation to squared-error loss ‣ 3. Theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters")).

Recall that we can think of top-m selection as the decision problem in [Bergman et al. (2024)](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib65) ([Remark 4](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#Thmrmk4 "Remark 4. ‣ 3.3. Other decision objectives and relation to squared-error loss ‣ 3. Theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters")). The utility function represents the expected mobility of a mover, assuming that the mover moves randomly into one of the high mobility Census tracts. Our proof of [Theorem 4](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#Thmtheorem4 "Theorem 4. ‣ 3.3. Other decision objectives and relation to squared-error loss ‣ 3. Theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters") allows for a slightly more general decision problem. Suppose the decision now is to provide a full ranking of Census tracts for potential movers and maximize the expected mobility for a mover. Suppose that the probability that a mover moves to a tract depends decreasingly and solely on the tract’s rank. To be more concrete, suppose the mover has probability π1 of moving to the highest-ranked tract, π2≤π1 to the second-highest, and so forth. Then, with the same argument, the corresponding regret is dominated by 2​n​∑i\=1nπi2⋅(𝔼⁡\[1n​∑i\=1n(θ^i−θi∗)2\])1/2, which generalizes ([2](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#S3.Ex20 "Item 2 ‣ Theorem 4. ‣ 3.3. Other decision objectives and relation to squared-error loss ‣ 3. Theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters")). ■

Here, we define 𝐄G,ν​\[h​(τ,Z)∣z\] as the function of z that equals the posterior mean for h⁡(τ,Z) under the data-generating model τ∼G and Z|τ∼𝒩⁡(τ,ν). Explicitly,

<table id="A1.Ex7a" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table"><tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline"><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A1.Ex7a.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{E}_{G,\nu}\left[{h(\tau,Z)\mid z}\right]=\frac{1}{f_{G,\nu}(z)}\int h(\tau,z)\varphi\left({\frac{z-\tau}{\nu}}\right)\frac{1}{\nu}\,G(d\tau)." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>𝐄</mi><mrow><mi>G</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>ν</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>[</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>τ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>Z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">∣</mo><mi>z</mi></mrow><mo>]</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mrow><mi>G</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>ν</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>∫</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>τ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>φ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>z</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>τ</mi></mrow><mi>ν</mi></mfrac><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>ν</mi></mfrac><mo lspace="0.150em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>G</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">𝑑</mo><mi>τ</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow></semantics></math></td><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody></table>

so that φ⁡(φ+​(ρ))\=ρ. Observe that φ+​(ρ)≲log⁡(1/ρ).

Recall the event An and the quantity Z¯n in ([A.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A1.E1 "Equation A.1 ‣ Appendix A Proof outline for ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters")). Many of the following statements are true for An defined with generic Δn,Mn. However, to obtain our rate expression in the end, recall that we set Δn,Mn to be of the following form:

The main theorem of this part in the Online Appendix is stated and proved in the following section. It characterizes regret behavior on the event An, for Δn,Mn chosen as in ([OA1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A1.Ex14a "Appendix OA1 Review of notation and proofs of and ‣ Part I Proof of ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters")).

#### OA1.1. Proof of [Theorem A.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A1.Thmtheorem1 "Theorem A.1. ‣ Appendix A Proof outline for ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters")

We first state a result that is key to our remaining arguments, which we verify in the Supplementary Material ([Appendix SM2](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A2b "Appendix SM2 A large-deviation inequality for the average Hellinger distance ‣ Part III Important preliminary results for ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters")).

###### Corollary OA1.1.

Assume [Assumptions 1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#Thmas1 "Assumption 1. ‣ 3.1.1. Assumptions for regret upper bound ‣ 3.1. Regret rate in squared error ‣ 3. We have that ([OA1.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A1.Ex30 "Proof. ‣ OA1.1. Proof of ‣ Appendix OA1 Review of notation and proofs of and ‣ Part I Proof of ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters"))≤4​(𝔼​ξ1+𝔼​ξ2+𝔼​ξ3+𝔼​ξ4)\=4​(𝔼​ξ1+𝔼​ξ3+𝔼​ξ4).

The individual ξj’s are bounded by the arguments in the remainder of this section. The key term leading to the final rate is 𝔼⁡\[ξ3\]:

-   •
    
    We show in [Lemma OA1.3](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A1.Thmlemma3 "Lemma OA1.3. ‣ OA1.1. Proof of ‣ Appendix OA1 Review of notation and proofs of and ‣ Part I Proof of ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters") that ξ1≲ℋMn2(logn)2Δn2, and thus 𝔼ξ1≲ℋMn2(logn)2Δn2.
    
-   •
    
    [Lemma OA1.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A1.Thmlemma1 "Lemma OA1.1. ‣ Appendix OA1 Review of notation and proofs of and ‣ Part I Proof of ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters")(2) implies that, given the choice ρn in ([OA1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A1.Ex16a "Appendix OA1 Review of notation and proofs of and ‣ Part I Proof of ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters")), the regularized posterior means and the unregularized posterior means are equal θ^G^n,η0,ρn\=θ^G^n,η0, since the truncation does not bind. Therefore, ξ2\=0.
    
-   •
    
    We show in [Section OA1.2](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A1.SS2a "OA1.2. Controlling 𝜉_3 ‣ Appendix OA1 Review of notation and proofs of and ‣ Part I Proof of ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters") that 𝔼ξ3≲ℋ(logn)3δn2. Here, δn is the rate in ([OA1.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A1.Ex24 "Corollary OA1.1. ‣ OA1.1. Proof of ‣ Appendix OA1 Review of notation and proofs of and ‣ Part I Proof of ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters")).
    
-   •
    
    Finally, we show in [Lemma OA1.4](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A1.Thmlemma4 "Lemma OA1.4. ‣ OA1.1. Proof of ‣ Appendix OA1 Review of notation and proofs of and ‣ Part I Proof of ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters") that 𝔼ξ4≲ℋ1n.
    

Lastly, we observe that by the definition of δn in ([OA1.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A1.Ex24 "Corollary OA1.1. ‣ OA1.1. Proof of ‣ Appendix OA1 Review of notation and proofs of and ‣ Part I Proof of ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters")), the upper bound for 𝔼⁡\[ξ3\] is the dominating rate. Plugging the definition of δn2 yields that

###### Remark OA1.1 (Remainder of proof).

The proof for [Theorem A.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A1.Thmtheorem1 "Theorem A.1. ‣ Appendix A Proof outline for ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters") hinges on the key result in [Section OA1.2](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A1.SS2a "OA1.2. Controlling 𝜉_3 ‣ Appendix OA1 Review of notation and proofs of and ‣ Part I Proof of ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters") for bounding ξ3. Effectively, the argument first relates ξ3 to the corresponding regret for the transformed parameters τi ([OA1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A1.Ex12 "Appendix OA1 Review of notation and proofs of and ‣ Part I Proof of ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters")):

<table id="A1.Ex34" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table"><tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline"><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A1.Ex34.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lVert\tau_{\hat{G}_{n},\eta_{0},\rho_{n}}-\tau_{\rho_{n}}^{*}\rVert^{2}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mrow><mo fence="true" mathsize="0.900em" rspace="0em">∥</mo><mrow><msub><mi>τ</mi><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>G</mi><mo mathsize="1.280em">^</mo></mover><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>η</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>ρ</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><msubsup><mi>τ</mi><msub><mi>ρ</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>∗</mo></msubsup></mrow><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" mathsize="0.900em">∥</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow></semantics></math></td><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody></table>

To prove a bound for this object, we truncate to the event where h¯2​(fG^n,⋅,fG0,⋅) is small and use the fact that, loosely speaking, the ∥τG^n,η0,ρn−τρn∗∥2 can be bounded by h¯2​(fG^n,⋅,fG0,⋅). For this argument to work, the key is that the event where h¯2​(fG^n,⋅,fG0,⋅) is small has high probability, which is shown in [Corollary OA1.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A1.Thmcor1 "Corollary OA1.1. ‣ OA1.1. Proof of ‣ Appendix OA1 Review of notation and proofs of and ‣ Part I Proof of ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters"). Lastly, to prove [Corollary OA1.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A1.Thmcor1 "Corollary OA1.1. ‣ OA1.1. Proof of ‣ Appendix OA1 Review of notation and proofs of and ‣ Part I Proof of ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters"), we need to first establish that G^n—estimated off (Z^i,ν^i)—does not have high likelihood suboptimality Subn​(G^n). This is the most laborious part of the proof ([Corollary SM1.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A1.Thmcor1a "Corollary SM1.1. ‣ Appendix SM1 An oracle inequality for the likelihood ‣ Part III Important preliminary results for ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters")). ■

###### Lemma OA1.3.

Under the assumptions of [Theorem A.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A1.Thmtheorem1 "Theorem A.1. ‣ Appendix A Proof outline for ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters"), in the proof of [Theorem A.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A1.Thmtheorem1 "Theorem A.1. ‣ Appendix A Proof outline for ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters"), ξ1≲ℋMn2(logn)2Δn2.

Under the assumptions of [Theorem A.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A1.Thmtheorem1 "Theorem A.1. ‣ Appendix A Proof outline for ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters"), in the proof of [Theorem A.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A1.Thmtheorem1 "Theorem A.1. ‣ Appendix A Proof outline for ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters"), 𝔼ξ4≲ℋ1n.

#### OA1.2. Controlling ξ3

###### Lemma OA1.5.

Under the assumptions of [Theorem A.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A1.Thmtheorem1 "Theorem A.1. ‣ Appendix A Proof outline for ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters"), in the proof of [Theorem A.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A1.Thmtheorem1 "Theorem A.1. ‣ Appendix A Proof outline for ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters"), 𝔼ξ3≲ℋ(logn)3δn2, where δn is defined in ([OA1.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A1.Ex24 "Corollary OA1.1. ‣ OA1.1. Proof of ‣ Appendix OA1 Review of notation and proofs of and ‣ Part I Proof of ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters")).

###### Proof.

Observe that |θ^i,G^n,η0,ρn−θi,ρn∗|\=s0​i​|τ^i,G^n,η0,ρn−τi,ρn∗| where τ^i,G^n,η0,ρn is the regularized posterior with prior G^n at conditional moments η0 and τi,ρn∗\=τ^i,G0,η0,ρn, where we recall ([OA1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A1.Ex12 "Appendix OA1 Review of notation and proofs of and ‣ Part I Proof of ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters")).

Thus, we shall focus on controlling

Fix the rate function δn in ([OA1.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A1.Ex24 "Corollary OA1.1. ‣ OA1.1. Proof of ‣ Appendix OA1 Review of notation and proofs of and ‣ Part I Proof of ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters")) and the constant Bℋ in [Corollary OA1.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A1.Thmcor1 "Corollary OA1.1. ‣ OA1.1. Proof of ‣ Appendix OA1 Review of notation and proofs of and ‣ Part I Proof of ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters") (which in turn depends on Cℋ∗ in [Corollary SM1.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A1.Thmcor1a "Corollary SM1.1. ‣ Appendix SM1 An oracle inequality for the likelihood ‣ Part III Important preliminary results for ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters")). Let Bn\={h¯(fG^n,⋅,fG0,⋅)<Bℋδn} be the event of a small average squared Hellinger distance. Let G1,…,GN be a finite set of prior distributions (chosen to be a net of {G:h¯​(fG,⋅,fG0,⋅)≤δn} in some distance), and let τρn(j) be the posterior mean vector corresponding to prior Gj with conditional moments η0 and regularization ρn.

The decomposition ζ1 through ζ4 is exactly analogous to Section D.3 in the supplementary materials to [Soloff et al. (2024)](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib86) and to the proof of Theorem 1 in [Jiang (2020)](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib85). In particular, ζ1 is the gap on the “bad event” where the average squared Hellinger distance is large, which is manageable since 𝟙​(An∩BnC) has small probability by [Corollary OA1.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A1.Thmcor1 "Corollary OA1.1. ‣ OA1.1. Proof of ‣ Appendix OA1 Review of notation and proofs of and ‣ Part I Proof of ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters"). ζ2 is the distance from the posterior means at G^n to the closest posterior mean generated from the net G1,…,GN; ζ2 is small if we make the net {G1,…,GN} very fine. ζ3 measures the distance between ∥τρn(j)−τρn∗∥ and its expectation; ζ3 can be controlled by (i) a large-deviation inequality and (ii) controlling the metric entropy of the net ([Proposition SM1.2](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A1.Thmprop2 "Proposition SM1.2. ‣ SM1.8.4. Putting together ‣ SM1.8. Complexity of 𝒫(ℝ) under moment-based distance ‣ Appendix SM1 An oracle inequality for the likelihood ‣ Part III Important preliminary results for ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters")). Lastly, ζ4 measures the expected distance between τρn(j) and τρn∗; it is small since Gj are fixed priors with small average squared Hellinger distance.

However, our argument for ζ3 is slightly different and avoids an argument in [Jiang and Zhang (2009)](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib89) which appears to not apply in the heteroskedastic setting. See [Remark OA1.2](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A1.Thmrmk2 "Remark OA1.2. ‣ OA1.2.3. Controlling 𝜁_3 ‣ OA1.2. Controlling 𝜉_3 ‣ Appendix OA1 Review of notation and proofs of and ‣ Part I Proof of ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters").

The subsequent subsections control ζ1 through ζ4, and find that ζ4≲ℋ(logn)3δn2 is the dominating term. ∎

##### OA1.2.1. Controlling ζ1

First, we note that,

Proof of ‣ Appendix OA1 Review of notation and proofs of and ‣ Part I Proof of ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters"), P⁡(An∩BnC)≤(log⁡log⁡nlog⁡2+9)​1n, and hence 1n𝔼ζ12≲ℋlog⁡n​log⁡log​nn.

##### OA1.2.3. Controlling ζ3

We first observe that Vi​j≡|τi,ρn(j)−τi,ρn∗|≲ℋlog⁡n, by [Lemma SM1.8](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A1.Thmlemma8a "Lemma SM1.8 (Lemma 2, ( ) ). ‣ SM1.9. Auxiliary lemmas ‣ Appendix SM1 An oracle inequality for the likelihood ‣ Part III Important preliminary results for ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters"). Let Vj\=(V1​j,…,Vn​j)′, we have that ζ3\=maxj⁡(∥Vj∥−𝔼⁡∥Vj∥)+. Let Kn\=Cℋ​log⁡n≥maxi​j⁡|Vi​j|. Since Gj,G0 are both fixed, V1​j,…,Vn​j are mutually independent, and Vi​j/Kn∈\[0,1\]. Then, observe that by [Lemma OA1.8](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A1.Thmlemma8 "Lemma OA1.8. ‣ OA1.3. Auxiliary lemmas ‣ Appendix OA1 Review of notation and proofs of and ‣ Part I Proof of ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters"),

###### Remark OA1.2.

For the analogous term under homoskedasticity, [Jiang and Zhang (2009)](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib89) observe that ∥τρn(j)−τρn∗∥ is a Lipschitz function of the noise component Zi−τi. As a result, a Gaussian isoperimetric inequality (Theorem 5.6 in [Boucheron et al. (2013)](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib76)) bounds

<table id="A1.Ex64" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table"><tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline"><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A1.Ex64.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\operatorname{P}\left({\lVert\tau_{\rho_{n}}^{(j)}-\tau_{\rho_{n}}^{*}\rVert\geq\mathbb{E}\left[{\lVert\tau_{\rho_{n}}^{(j)}-\tau_{\rho_{n}}^{*}\rVert\mid\tau_{1},\ldots,\tau_{n}}\right]+x}\right)," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" mathsize="0.900em" rspace="0em">∥</mo><msubsup><mi>τ</mi><msub><mi>ρ</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>j</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>−</mo><msubsup><mi>τ</mi><msub><mi>ρ</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>∗</mo></msubsup><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" mathsize="0.900em" rspace="0.1389em">∥</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0.1389em">≥</mo><mi>𝔼</mi><mrow><mo>[</mo><mrow><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" mathsize="0.900em" rspace="0em">∥</mo><msubsup><mi>τ</mi><msub><mi>ρ</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>j</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>−</mo><msubsup><mi>τ</mi><msub><mi>ρ</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>∗</mo></msubsup><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" mathsize="0.900em" rspace="0em">∥</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">∣</mo><msub><mi>τ</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>τ</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>]</mo></mrow><mo>+</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow></semantics></math></td><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody></table>

independently of n—a fact used in Proposition 4 of [Jiang and Zhang (2009)](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib89). Note that the concentration of ∥τρn(j)−τρn∗∥ is towards its conditional mean

where G0,n\=1n​∑iδτi is the empirical distribution of the τ’s. However, ([OA1.2](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A1.Ex66 "Remark OA1.2. ‣ OA1.2.3. Controlling 𝜁_3 ‣ OA1.2. Controlling 𝜉_3 ‣ Appendix OA1 Review of notation and proofs of and ‣ Part I Proof of ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters")) no longer holds in the heteroskedastic setting, and to adapt this argument, we need to additionally control the difference between 𝔼\[∥τρn(j)−τρn∗∥∣τ1,…,τn\] and 𝔼⁡\[∥τρn(j)−τρn∗∥\]. The argument in [Jiang (2020)](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib85) (p.2289) appears to use the Gaussian concentration of Lipschitz functions argument without this additional step. Instead, we establish control of ζ3 by observing that entries of τρn(j)−τρn∗ are bounded and applying the convex Lipschitz concentration inequality. ■

##### OA1.2.4. Controlling ζ4

#### OA1.3. Auxiliary lemmas

###### Lemma OA1.6.

Let θ^i,G^,η^ be the posterior mean at prior G^ and conditional moments estimate at η^. Let θi∗\=θ^i,G0,η0 be the oracle posterior mean. Assume that G^ is supported within \[−M¯n,M¯n\] where M¯n\=maxi⁡|Z^i​(η^)∨1|. Recall that ∥η^−η0∥∞\=max⁡(∥m^−m0∥∞,∥s^−s0∥∞). Suppose

1.  (1)
    
    ∥η^−η0∥∞≲ℋ1;
    
2.  (2)
    
    [2](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#Thmas2 "Assumption 2. ‣ 3.1.1. Assumptions for regret upper bound ‣ 3.1. Regret rate in squared error ‣ 3. Theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters") and [3](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#Thmas3 "Assumption 3. ‣ 3.1.1. Assumptions for regret upper bound ‣ 3.1. Regret rate in squared error ‣ 3. Theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters") holds;
    
3.  (3)
    
    s^≳ℋsℓ​n for some fixed sequence sℓ​n\>0.
    

Then, letting Z¯n\=maxi⁡|Zi|∨1,

###### Lemma OA1.7.

Let Z¯n\=maxi⁡|Zi|∨1. Under [Assumption 2](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#Thmas2 "Assumption 2. ‣ 3.1.1. Assumptions for regret upper bound ‣ 3.1. Regret rate in squared error ‣ 3. Theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters"), for t\>1

Moreover, if Mn\=(Cℋ+1)​(C2,ℋ−1​log⁡n)1/α as in ([OA1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A1.Ex14a "Appendix OA1 Review of notation and proofs of and ‣ Part I Proof of ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters")), then for all sufficiently large choices of Cℋ, P⁡(Z¯n\>Mn)≤n−2.

###### Proof.

The first claim is immediate under [Lemma SM1.12](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A1.Thmlemma12 "Lemma SM1.12. ‣ SM1.9. Auxiliary lemmas ‣ Appendix SM1 An oracle inequality for the likelihood ‣ Part III Important preliminary results for ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters") and a union bound. The second claim follows from the observation that

## Part II Additional discussions and empirical results

### Appendix OA2 Additional discussions

#### OA2.1. Correlated Yi and correlated θi

The assumptions ([1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#S1.Ex1 "1. Introduction ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters")) and ([2.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#S2.Ex1 "2.1. Empirical Bayes assumptions ‣ 2. Model and proposed method ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters")) imply that (Yi,θi,σi) are i.i.d. across i. In general, we may consider a joint distribution on θ1:n∣Σ, conditional on which the estimates may also be correlated Y1:n∣θ1:n∼𝒩(θ1:n,Σ) (see, among others, [Bonhomme and Denis, 2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib2); [Müller and Watson, 2022](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib26), for settings in which the non-independence appears natural). In principle, given a flexible model for the distribution θ1:n∣Σ, we would estimate this model from the data (Y1:n,Σ), and likewise compute an estimated posterior. In particular, if θ1:n∣Σ is described by ([2.4](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#S2.Ex7 "Equation 2.4 ‣ 2.3. Conditional location-scale modeling of precision dependence ‣ 2. Model and proposed method ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters")) but Y1:n may be correlated conditional on θ1:n,Σ, then [close–step 1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#S2.I1.i1 "In 2.3. Conditional location-scale modeling of precision dependence ‣ 2. Model and proposed method ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters") and  [close–step 2](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#S2.I1.i2 "Item 
close–step 2 ‣ 2.3. Conditional location-scale modeling of precision dependence ‣ 2. Model and proposed method ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters") continue to estimate θ1:n∣Σ, and one can adapt [close–step 3](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#S2.I1.i3 "In 2.3. Conditional location-scale modeling of precision dependence ‣ 2. Model and proposed method ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters") accordingly to exploit the correlation between Yi’s.

Modeling the joint distribution of (Y1:n,θ1:n,Σ) may be difficult. Interestingly, modeling only the marginal distributions of each coordinate (Yi,θi,σi)—as we have done—turns out to be sufficient for optimal decision-making, if we restrict the class of decision rules. For a compound decision problem, where L(𝜹,θ1:n)\=1n∑i\=1nℓ(δi,θi), consider restricting to _separable_ decision rules δi\=δi​(Yi,σi), where we make decisions about θi using only (Yi,σi). In that case, the best decision δi​(⋅,⋅) minimizes the posterior risk 𝔼\[ℓ(δ(Yi,σi),θi)∣Yi,σi\]. This result provides some reassurance that ignoring the dependence across coordinates is inefficient but may not be harmful, since naive decisions are often separable, and the optimal separable rule would dominate it. Restricting to separable decision rules can also be motivated by practical or fairness considerations: For instance, it may be unfair to base human resource decisions about a given teacher on the value-added estimate of another.

We formalize the above paragraph in [Lemma OA2.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A2.Thmlemma1 "Lemma OA2.1. ‣ OA2.1. Correlated 𝑌_𝑖 and correlated 𝜃_𝑖 ‣ Appendix OA2 Additional discussions ‣ Part II Additional discussions and empirical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters"). Suppose (Y1:n,θ1:n,Σ) follow some joint distribution Q0 under which Y1:n∣θ1:n,Σ∼𝒩(θ1:n,Σ). We observe (Y1:n,Σ). Consider a compound decision problem with a separable decision rule, such that

Let (Yi,θi,σi2)∼H0​i under Q0. Assume Q0 is such that the posterior mean 𝔼H0​i\[ℓ(a,θi)∣Yi,σi\] exists almost surely. Consider the decision rule 𝜹 that minimizes posterior risk under θi|Yi,σi over the action space

#### OA2.2. Alternatives to close

Let us turn to a few specific alternative methods that consider failure of precision independence. We argue that they do not provide a free-lunch improvement over our assumptions.

###### Alternative 1 (Working with t\-ratios).

We may consider normalizing σi away by working with t\-ratios Ti≡Yiσi|(σi,θi)∼𝒩⁡(θi/σi,1). The resulting problem is homoskedastic by construction. It is natural to consider performing empirical Bayes shrinkage assuming that θiσi​∼i.i.d.​H0, and use, say, σi​𝐄H^n​\[θiσi∣Ti\] as an estimator for the posterior mean of θi ([Jiang and Zhang, 2010](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib33)). However, without imposing θi/σi𝑦σi (which we discuss in [Remark 2](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#Thmrmk2 "Remark 2 (Other transformations). ‣ 2.4.3. Additional remarks ‣ 2.4. Discussions ‣ 2. Model and proposed method ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters")), such an approach approximates the optimal decision rule within a restricted class on a different objective.

Let us restrict decision rules to those of the form δi,t-stat​(Yi,σi)\=σi​h​(Yi/σi). The oracle Bayes choice of h is h⋆​(Ti)\=𝔼⁡\[σi​θi∣Ti\]𝔼⁡\[σi2∣Ti\]. However, h⋆ is not the posterior mean of θi/σi given the t\-ratio Ti, unless σi2𝑦θi/σi. On the other hand, the loss function that does rationalize the posterior mean h⁡(Ti)\=𝔼⁡\[θi/σi∣Ti\] is the precision-weighted compound loss L(𝜹,θ1:n)\=1n∑i\=1nσi−2(δi−θi)2. Thus, rescaling posterior means on t\-ratios achieves optimality for a weighted objective among a restricted class of decision rules δi,t-stat. ■

###### Alternative 2 (Variance-stabilizing transforms).

Second, we may consider a variance-stabilizing transform when the underlying micro-data are Bernoulli and θi is a Bernoulli mean ([Efron and Morris, 1975](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib30); [Brown, 2008](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib6)). Specifically, we rely on the asymptotic approximation

<table id="A2.Ex9a" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table"><tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline"><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A2.Ex9a.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sqrt{n_{i}}(Y_{i}-\theta_{i})\underset{n_{i}\to\infty}{\overset{d}{\longrightarrow}}\mathcal{N}(0,\theta_{i}(1-\theta_{i}))." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msqrt><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></msqrt><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>Y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>θ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><munderover accent="true" accentunder="true"><mo stretchy="false">⟶</mo><mrow><msub><mi mathsize="0.700em">n</mi><mi mathsize="0.710em">i</mi></msub><mo mathsize="0.700em" stretchy="false">→</mo><mi mathsize="0.700em" mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow><mo mathsize="0.700em">𝑑</mo></munderover><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒩</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>θ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>θ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow></semantics></math></td><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody></table>

A variance-stabilizing transform can disentangle the dependence: Let Wi\=2​arcsin⁡(Yi) and ωi\=2​arcsin⁡(θi), and, by the delta method,

<table id="A2.Ex10a" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table"><tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline"><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A2.Ex10a.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\sqrt{n_{i}}\left({W_{i}-\omega_{i}}\right)\underset{n_{i}\to\infty}{\overset{d}{\longrightarrow}}\mathcal{N}(0,1).\hskip 10.00002pt\text{
Thus, approximately, }W_{i}\mid\omega_{i},n_{i}\sim\mathcal{N}\left({\omega_{i},\frac{1}{n_{i}}}\right)." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msqrt><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></msqrt><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>ω</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><munderover accent="true" accentunder="true"><mo stretchy="false">⟶</mo><mrow><msub><mi mathsize="0.700em">n</mi><mi mathsize="0.710em">i</mi></msub><mo mathsize="0.700em" stretchy="false">→</mo><mi mathsize="0.700em" mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow><mo mathsize="0.700em">𝑑</mo></munderover><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒩</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">.</mo><mtext>&nbsp;Thus, approximately,&nbsp;</mtext><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">∣</mo><msub><mi>ω</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>∼</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒩</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>ω</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mfrac><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow></semantics></math></td><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody></table>

One might consider an empirical Bayes approach on the resulting Wi. Note that Wi may still violate precision independence, since ωi may not be independent of ni. Moreover, squared error loss on estimating ωi\=2​arcsin⁡(θi) is different from squared error loss on estimating θi. We do not know of any guarantees for the loss function on θi, 1n​∑i\=1n(δi−sin2⁡(ωi/2))2, when we perform empirical Bayes analysis on ωi. ■

###### Alternative 3 (Treating the standard error as estimated).

Lastly, if the researcher has access to micro-data, [Gu and Koenker (2017)](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib71) and [Fu et al. (2020)](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib87) propose empirical Bayes strategies that treat σi as noisy as well, in which we know the likelihood of (Yi,σi). This approach allows for dependence between θi and σi but assumes independence between (θi,σi) and some other known parameter. To describe their model, we introduce more notation. Let Yi​j,j\=1,…,ni, denote the micro-data for population i, where, for each i, we are interested in the mean of Yi​j. Let Yi denote their sample mean and Si2 denote their sample variance, where σi2\=Si2/ni. Let σi​02 denote the true variance of observations from population i.

Both papers work under Gaussian assumptions on the micro-data. This parametric assumption37 on the micro-data—which is stronger than we require—implies that Yi𝑦Si2|(σi​0,θi,ni) with marginal distributions:

ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td><td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="A2.Ex11a.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒩</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>θ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><msubsup><mi>σ</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em"
