rspace="0em">​</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>θ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>∼</mo><mrow><mi>Gamma</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mstyle><mo>,</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>σ</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow></mfrac></mstyle><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow></semantics></math></td><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody></table>

They then propose empirical Bayes methods treating 𝐘i≡(Yi,Si2) as noisy estimates for parameters 𝜽i≡(θi,σi​02). This formulation allows 𝜽i to have a flexible distribution, and thus allows for dependence between θi and σi​02. However, since the known sample size ni enters the likelihood of 𝐘i, this approach still assumes that ni𝑦𝜽i. ■

###### Alternative 4 (f\-modeling).

A final alternative is to exploit Tweedie’s formula ([Efron, 2022](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib3)), which implies that an estimate of the conditional distribution Yi|σi is all one needs for computing the posterior means ([Brown and Greenshtein, 2009](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib22); [Liu et al., 2020](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib23); [Luo et al., 2023](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib11)). However, conditional density estimation is a challenging problem, and most available methods do not exploit the restriction that Yi|σi is a Gaussian convolution. ■

This discussion is not to say that close is necessarily preferable to these alternatives. It highlights that the possible dependence between θi and σi cannot be easily resolved. Existing alternatives compromise on optimality, use a different loss function, or implicitly assume θi is independent from components of σi2 (e.g., ni). Of course, depending on the empirical context, these may well be reasonable features.

#### OA2.3. Transformation-based rationalization of the location-scale assumption ([2.4](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#S2.Ex7 "Equation 2.4 ‣ 2.3. Conditional location-scale modeling of precision dependence ‣ 2. Model and proposed method ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters"))

The following lemma shows that, essentially, only affine transforms preserve exponential family structure on Yi. Exponential family structure is important since generalizations of Tweedie’s formula holds for such distributions ([Efron, 2011](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib84)), and thus they connect posterior means to the marginal distribution of the data. If some affine transform yields precision independence—so as to allow for methods that assume precision independence—then the location-scale assumption ([2.4](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#S2.Ex7 "Equation 2.4 ‣ 2.3. Conditional location-scale modeling of precision dependence ‣ 2. Model and proposed method ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters")) must hold.

###### Lemma OA2.2.

Let Yi|θi,σi∼𝒩⁡(θi,σi2) and (θi,σi) drawn i.i.d. Consider h⁡(Yi,σi) such that h⁡(⋅,σi) is differentiable and strictly increasing. Let Zi\=h⁡(Yi,σi). Then the distribution of Zi, parametrized by θi, is an exponential family

only if h⁡(Yi,σi)\=a⁡(σi)+b⁡(σi)​Yi.

Moreover, suppose θi|σi has finite first and second moments. When ([OA2.2](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A2.Ex12a "Lemma OA2.2. ‣ OA2.3. Transformation-based rationalization of the location-scale assumption () ‣ Appendix OA2 Additional discussions ‣ Part II Additional discussions and empirical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters")) holds for some h⁡(Yi,σi)\=a⁡(σi)+b⁡(σi)​Yi, the distribution of Zi\=h⁡(Yi,σi) is of the form

###### Proof.

The first part of the statement follows immediately from [Lemma OA2.3](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A2.Thmlemma3 "Lemma OA2.3. ‣ OA2.3. Transformation-based rationalization of the location-scale assumption () ‣ Appendix OA2 Additional discussions ‣ Part II Additional discussions and empirical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters"). For the second part, it is easy to see that τi≡τ⁡(θi,σi)\=θi​b​(σi)+a⁡(σi). If τ⁡(θi,σi)|σi does not depend on σi, then 𝔼⁡\[τ∣σi\],Var⁡(τ∣σi) are constant in σi. This means that b⁡(σi)\=1/Var⁡(θi∣σi) and a⁡(σi)\=−𝔼⁡\[θi∣σi\]​b​(σi). Rearrange, we have

### Appendix OA3 Additional empirical exercises

#### OA3.1. Positivity of s0​(⋅) in the Opportunity Atlas data

Hence Si is an overestimate of the successive averages of s0​(σ). [Figure OA3.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A3.F1 "In OA3.1. Positivity of 𝑠_0⁢(⋅) in the Opportunity Atlas data ‣ Appendix OA3 Additional empirical exercises ‣ Part II Additional discussions and empirical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters") plot the estimated conditional expectation of Si given σi, using a sample of (S1,S3,S5,…) so that the Si’s used are mutually independent. We see in [Figure OA3.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A3.F1 "In OA3.1. Positivity of 𝑠_0⁢(⋅) in the Opportunity Atlas data ‣ Appendix OA3 Additional empirical exercises ‣ Part II Additional discussions and empirical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters") that for many measures of economic mobility, we can reject 𝔼⁡\[Si∣σi\]≥0, indicating some underdispersion in the data.

#### OA3.2. Simulation exercises setup

This section describes the details of the simulation exercises in [Section 4](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#S4 "4. Empirical illustration ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters").

We first consider details on data preprocessing:

1.  (1)
    
    The data used is the publicly available tract-level data from [Chetty et al. (forthcoming)](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib66).
    
2.  (2)
    
    Limit to Census tracts in the 20 largest Commuting Zones, ranked by the number of tracts in the dataset. They are: Phoenix, San Francisco, Los Angeles, Bridgeport, Washington DC, Miami, Tampa, Atlanta, Chicago, Boston, Detroit, Minneapolis, Philadelphia, Newark, New York, Cleveland, Pittsburgh, Houston, Dallas, and Seattle.
    
3.  (3)
    
    For a given outcome variable, we truncate to tracts with σi2 in the bottom 99.5% with all available covariates in [Table OA3.2](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A3.T2 "In OA3.2. Simulation exercises setup ‣ Appendix OA3 Additional empirical exercises ‣ Part II Additional discussions and empirical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters"). [Table OA3.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A3.T1 "In OA3.2. Simulation exercises setup ‣ Appendix OA3 Additional empirical exercises ‣ Part II Additional discussions and empirical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters") displays the sample sizes used.

The covariates used are listed in [Table OA3.2](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A3.T2 "In OA3.2. Simulation exercises setup ‣ Appendix OA3 Additional empirical exercises ‣ Part II Additional discussions and empirical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters"). The “number of children” variables are included in both levels and logs. This set of covariates is not precisely the same as what is used in [Bergman et al. (2024)](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib65). [Bergman et al. (2024)](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib65) additionally use economic mobility estimates for a later birth cohort, which are not included in the publicly released version of the Opportunity Atlas. The “number of children” variables are used by ([Chetty et al., forthcoming](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib66)) as a population weighting variable; they contain some information on the implicit micro-data sample sizes ni.

###### Notes.

This table links the covariates to their codebook labels in [Chetty et al. (forthcoming)](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib66). See their [Codebook for Table 9](https://opportunityinsights.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/07/Codebook-for-Table-9.pdf) and [Codebook for Table 4](https://opportunityinsights.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/07/Codebook-for-Table-4.pdf) for the corresponding precise definitions of each covariate ([Opportunity Insights, 2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib5)). ∎

We now describe the data-generating process for the calibrated simulation exercise. For a given outcome variable,

1.  (CS-1)
    
    Let Y~i denote the raw estimates. Residualize Y~i against some covariates Xi to obtain β and residuals Yi.
    
2.  (CS-2)
    
    Estimate the conditional moments m0,s0 on (Yi,σi) via local linear regression, described in [Appendix SM3](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A3a "Appendix SM3 Estimating 𝜂_0 by local linear regression ‣ Part IV Additional theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters").
    
3.  (CS-3)
    
    Partition σ into vingtiles. Within each vingtile j, estimate an npmle Gj over the data in that vingtile
    
    <table id="A3.Ex3" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table"><tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline"><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A3.Ex3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\left({\frac{Y_{i}-m_{0}(\sigma_{i})}{s_{0}(\sigma_{i})},\frac{\sigma_{i}}{s_{0}(\sigma_{i})}}\right)." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo>(</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>Y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><mrow><msub><mi>m</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>σ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>σ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mfrac><msub><mi>σ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>σ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow></semantics></math></td><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody></table>
    
4.  (CS-4)
    
    Normalize Gj to have zero mean and unit variance by shifting its support and dividing the support by its standard deviation.
    
5.  (CS-5)
    
    Sample τi∗|σi∼Gj if observation i falls within vingtile j.
    
6.  (CS-6)
    
    Let ϑi∗\=s0​(σi)​τi∗+m0​(σi)+β′​Xi and let Y~i∗|ϑi∗,σi∼𝒩⁡(ϑi∗,σi2).
    

The estimated β,m0,s0 will serve as the basis for the true data-generating process in the simulation, and as a result we do not denote it with hats. [Figure OA3.2](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A3.F2 "In OA3.2. Simulation exercises setup ‣ Appendix OA3 Additional empirical exercises ‣ Part II Additional discussions and empirical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters") shows an overlay of real and simulated data for one of the variables we consider. Visually, at least, the simulated data resemble the real estimates.

Figure OA3.2. A draw of real vs. simulated data for estimates of top-20 probability for Black individuals

Finally, we describe details for the policy exercise. Fix a given outcome variable:

1.  (CB-1)
    
    Let Y~i,σi denote the observed data.
    
2.  (CB-2)
    
    Define Y~i,1\=Yi+13​σi​Wi and Y~i,2\=Yi−3​σi​Wi as the coupled bootstrap draws, for ω\=1/9. Correspondingly, let σi,1\=10/9​σi and σi,2\=10​σi.
    

For the policy exercise, we separate the units into Commuting Zones (CZs). For each CZ separately, we treat the data as (Y~i,1,σi,1,Xi) within that CZ. We compute decision rules by only using data within the CZ (including the residualization by covariates). For the selection exercise, we select by top third within each CZ.

#### OA3.3. Different simulation setup

Figure OA3.3. Analogue of [Figure 4](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#S4.F4 "In 4.1. Calibrated simulation ‣ 4. Empirical illustration ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters") for the data-generating process in [Section OA3.3](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A3.SS3 "OA3.3. Different simulation setup ‣ Appendix OA3 Additional empirical exercises ‣ Part II Additional discussions and empirical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters"). Here the results average over 100 replications.

We have also conducted a Monte Carlo exercise where we replace [(CS-3)](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A3.I2.i3 "In OA3.2. Simulation exercises setup ‣ Appendix OA3 Additional empirical exercises ‣ Part II Additional discussions and empirical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters")–[(CS-5)](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A3.I2.i5 "In OA3.2. Simulation exercises setup ‣ Appendix OA3 Additional empirical exercises ‣ Part II Additional discussions and empirical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters") with the following step:

-   •
    
    For each σi, let
    
    <table id="A3.Ex4" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table"><tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline"><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A3.Ex4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha_{i}=\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2}\frac{m_{0}(\sigma_{i})-\min_{i}m_{0}(\sigma_{i})}{\max_{i}m_{0}(\sigma_{i})-\min_{i}(\sigma_{i})}\in[1/2,1]" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>α</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo>+</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mfrac><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>m</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>σ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>min</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><msub><mi>m</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>σ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>max</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><msub><mi>m</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>σ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><msub><mi>min</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>σ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mfrac></mrow></mrow><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow></semantics></math></td><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody></table>
    
    We sample τi∗|σi as a scaled and translated Weibull distribution with shape αi. The scaling and translation ensures that τi|σi has mean zero and variance one. Because we choose the Weibull distribution, the shape parameter αi corresponds exactly to α in [Assumption 2](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#Thmas2 "Assumption 2. ‣ 3.1.1. Assumptions for regret upper bound ‣ 3.1. Regret rate in squared error ‣ 3. Theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters"). Our choices of αi implies that τi|σi has thicker tails than exponential and does not have a moment-generating function.
    

The Weibull distribution has thicker tails and is skewed, and as a result, npmle\-based methods tend to greatly outperform methods based on assuming Gaussian priors. [Figure OA3.3](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A3.F3 "In OA3.3. Different simulation setup ‣ Appendix OA3 Additional empirical exercises ‣ Part II Additional discussions and empirical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters") shows the analogue of [Figure 4](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#S4.F4 "In 4.1. Calibrated simulation ‣ 4. Empirical illustration ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters") for this data-generating process. Indeed, we see that independent-npmle improves over independent-gauss considerably, and similarly for close\-npmle and close\-gauss.

#### OA3.4. Treating σi symmetrically with covariates

Here, we consider close with covariates ([3.1.2](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#S3.Ex11 "3.1.2. MSE regret results ‣ 3.1. Regret rate in squared error ‣ 3. Theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters")). In principle, we could model m0​(σi,Xi),s0​(σi,Xi) fully nonparametrically. However, such a model may be difficult to estimate given there are 9 additional covariates. Alternatively, we consider an additive model for the covariates:38

For each covariate and for σ, the functions gk​(⋅),hk​(⋅) are approximated with cubic splines with knots at the 25th, 50th, and 75th percentiles of the covariate.

We estimate m0​(⋅) by least squares projection of Yi onto the basis functions in (σi,Xi). We estimate s02​(⋅) by least squares projection of (Yi−m^​(σi,Xi))2−σi2 onto the basis functions in (σi,Xi). We truncate fitted values for s02 at zero. In practice, a substantial portion of them are negative (cf. [Section OA3.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A3.SS1 "OA3.1. Positivity of 𝑠_0⁢(⋅) in the Opportunity Atlas data ‣ Appendix OA3 Additional empirical exercises ‣ Part II Additional discussions and empirical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters")). Additionally, we consider a similar procedure, but one in which g0​(⋅),h0​(⋅) are constant. We think of this procedure as independent-gauss with flexible controls for the covariates.

  

###### Notes.

“Flexible” denotes procedures that use the additive model ([OA3.4](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A3.Ex5 "OA3.4. Treating 𝜎_𝑖 symmetrically with covariates ‣ Appendix OA3 Additional empirical exercises ‣ Part II Additional discussions and empirical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters")) for Xi. “x residualized” refers to procedures that, like those in the main text, residualize against the covariates in a pre-processing step. The percentage in orange shows the proportion of units with strictly positive estimated conditional variance s^2​(σi,Xi) for the flexible procedures. ∎

Figure OA3.4. Analogue of [Figure 5](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#S4.F5 "In 4.2. Validation exercise via coupled bootstrap ‣ 4. Empirical illustration ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters") for the setup in [Section OA3.4](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A3.SS4 "OA3.4. Treating 𝜎_𝑖 symmetrically with covariates ‣ Appendix OA3 Additional empirical exercises ‣ Part II Additional discussions and empirical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters").

We repeat the coupled bootstrap-based ranking exercise in [Figure 5](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#S4.F5 "In 4.2. Validation exercise via coupled bootstrap ‣ 4. Empirical illustration ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters"). However, here, due to considerably more flexible procedures, we no longer consider a within-Commuting Zone version of the exercise. Rather, we estimate everything on all the tracts, and select the top third over all tracts.

[Figure OA3.4](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A3.F4 "In OA3.4. Treating 𝜎_𝑖 symmetrically with covariates ‣ Appendix OA3 Additional empirical exercises ‣ Part II Additional discussions and empirical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters") plots the results of this exercise, analogous to [Figure 5](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#S4.F5 "In 4.2. Validation exercise via coupled bootstrap ‣ 4. Empirical illustration ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters"). We find that, compared to the residualize-then-shrink approach in the main text, modeling Xi’s additionally well can have large benefits. We caution that, since much of the conditional signal variance s02 appears to be quite small once we use ([OA3.4](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A3.Ex5 "OA3.4. Treating 𝜎_𝑖 symmetrically with covariates ‣ Appendix OA3 Additional empirical exercises ‣ Part II Additional discussions and empirical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters")) for the covariates, empirical Bayes posterior means are not very different from using m^0​(σi,Xi) directly. Importantly, for this application, including σi in modeling m0,s0 remains important. The approach that simply models Xi’s flexibly for m0,s0 but omits σi does not outperform the close approaches in the main text.

we have that, P⁡\[An,Subn​(G^n)\>Cℋ∗​εn\]≤9n. The constants in Δn,Mn affects the conclusion of the statement only through affecting the constant Cℋ∗.

###### Proof.

We first show that the specification of Δn and Mn means that the requirements of [Assumption SM1.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A1.Thmas1 "Assumption SM1.1. ‣ Appendix SM1 An oracle inequality for the likelihood ‣ Part III Important preliminary results for ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters") are satisfied. Among the requirements of [Assumption SM1.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A1.Thmas1 "Assumption SM1.1. ‣ Appendix SM1 An oracle inequality for the likelihood ‣ Part III Important preliminary results for ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters"):

1.  (1)
    
    is satisfied since the polynomial part of Δn converges to zero slower than n−1/2, but converges to zero faster than any logarithmic rate. Mn is a logarithmic rate.
    
2.  (2)
    
    is satisfied since α≤2.
    

We also observe that by Jensen’s inequality,

#### SM1.2. Proof of [Theorem SM1.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A1.Thmtheorem1a "Theorem SM1.1. ‣ Appendix SM1 An oracle inequality for the likelihood ‣ Part III Important preliminary results for ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters")

##### SM1.2.1. Decomposition of Subn​(G^n)

##### SM1.2.2. Taylor expansion of ψi​(Zi,η^,G^n)−ψi​(Zi,η0,G^n)

Define Δm​i\=m^i−m0​i, Δs​i\=s^i−s0​i, and Δi\=\[Δm​i,Δs​i\]′. Recall ∥η^−η0∥∞\=max⁡(∥s−s0∥∞,∥m−m0∥∞) as in ([A.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A1.E1 "Equation A.1 ‣ Appendix A Proof outline for ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters")). Since ψi​(Zi,η,G) is smooth in (mi,si)∈ℝ×ℝ\>0, we can take a second-order Taylor expansion:

We further decompose the first-order terms into an empirical process term and a mean-component term. By [Lemma OA1.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A1.Thmlemma1 "Lemma OA1.1. ‣ Appendix OA1 Review of notation and proofs of and ‣ Part I Proof of ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters"), ([SM1.4](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A1.E4 "Equation SM1.4 ‣ SM1.1. Derivative computations ‣ Appendix SM1 An oracle inequality for the likelihood ‣ Part III Important preliminary results for ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters")), and ([SM1.5](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A1.E5 "Equation SM1.5 ‣ SM1.1. Derivative computations ‣ Appendix SM1 An oracle inequality for the likelihood ‣ Part III Important preliminary results for ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters")), for the choice ρn in ([OA1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A1.Ex16a "Appendix OA1 Review of notation and proofs of and ‣ Part I Proof of ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters")) we have that the denominators to the first derivatives can be truncated at ρn, as fi,G^n≥ρn/νi so that the truncation does not bind:

    Large deviation of U¯2​k is further controlled by applying Dudley’s tail bound ([Vershynin, 2018](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib79)), since the entropy integral over S is well-behaved. The covering number N is controlled via [Proposition SM1.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A1.Thmprop1 "Proposition SM1.1. ‣ SM1.8. Complexity of 𝒫(ℝ) under moment-based distance ‣ Appendix SM1 An oracle inequality for the likelihood ‣ Part III Important preliminary results for ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters") and [Proposition SM1.2](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A1.Thmprop2 "Proposition SM1.2. ‣ SM1.8.4. Putting together ‣ SM1.8. Complexity of 𝒫(ℝ) under moment-based distance ‣ Appendix SM1 An oracle inequality for the likelihood ‣ Part III Important preliminary results for ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters"), which are minor extensions to Lemma 4 and Theorem 7 in [Jiang (2020)](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib85). The covering number is of a manageable size since the induced distributions fG,νi are very smooth.
    
3.  (3)
    
    Since D¯k,i​(G0,η0,0)\=0. U3​m,U3​s are effectively also empirical process terms, without the additional randomness in G^n. Thus the projection-to-ω\-net argument above is unnecessary for U3​m,U3​s, whereas the bounding follows from the same Dudley’s chaining argument. [Lemma SM1.4](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A1.Thmlemma4a "Lemma SM1.4. ‣ SM1.6. Bounding 𝑈_{3⁢𝑚},𝑈_{3⁢𝑠} ‣ Appendix SM1 An oracle inequality for the likelihood ‣ Part III Important preliminary results for ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters") bounds U3​k.
    
4.  (4)
    
    For the second derivative terms R1,R2, we observe that the second derivatives take the form of functions of posterior moments under either G^n or G0. The posterior moments under prior G^n is bounded within constant factors of Mnq since the support of Gn is restricted. The posterior moments under prior G0 is bounded by |Zi|q, for 𝔼|Zi|q≲ℋMnq as we show in [Lemma SM1.14](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A1.Thmlemma14 "Lemma SM1.14. ‣ SM1.9. Auxiliary lemmas ‣ Appendix SM1 An oracle inequality for the likelihood ‣ Part III Important preliminary results for ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters"), thanks to the simultaneous moment control for G0. These second derivatives are bounded in [Lemmas SM1.5](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A1.Thmlemma5a "Lemma SM1.5. ‣ SM1.7. Bounding 𝑅_1,𝑅_2 ‣ Appendix SM1 An oracle inequality for the likelihood ‣ Part III Important preliminary results for ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters") and [SM1.6](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A1.Thmlemma6a "Lemma SM1.6. ‣ SM1.7. Bounding 𝑅_1,𝑅_2 ‣ Appendix SM1 An oracle inequality for the likelihood ‣ Part III Important preliminary results for ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters").
    

(1) and (4) above bounds U1​k,R1,R2 under An. (2) and (3) bounds U2​k,U3​k probabilistically by bounding P⁡\[An,Uj​k\>t\]. By a union bound in [Lemma SM1.13](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A1.Thmlemma13 "Lemma SM1.13. ‣ SM1.9. Auxiliary lemmas ‣ Appendix SM1 An oracle inequality for the likelihood ‣ Part III Important preliminary results for ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters"), we can simply add the rates.

Doing so, we find that the first term in ϵn ([SM1.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A1.Ex2b "Equation SM1.1 ‣ Theorem SM1.1. ‣ Appendix SM1 An oracle inequality for the likelihood ‣ Part III Important preliminary results for ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters")) comes from U1​s, which dominates U1​m. The second term comes from U2​k. The third term comes from R1, which dominates R2; this term also dominates a term in the bound for U2​k. The fourth term comes from U3​s. The leading terms in ϵn dominate κn, recalling [Assumption 1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#Thmas1 "Assumption 1. ‣ 3.1.1. Assumptions for regret upper bound ‣ 3.1. Regret rate in squared error ‣ 3. Theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters"). This completes the proof.

#### SM1.7. Bounding R1,R2

###### Lemma SM1.5.

Recall R1​i from ([SM1.15](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A1.E15a "Equation SM1.15 ‣ SM1.2.2. Taylor expansion of 𝜓_𝑖⁢(𝑍_𝑖,𝜂̂,𝐺̂_𝑛)-𝜓_𝑖⁢(𝑍_𝑖,𝜂_0,𝐺̂_𝑛) ‣ SM1.2. Proof of ‣ Appendix SM1 An oracle inequality for the likelihood ‣ Part III Important preliminary results for ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters")). Then, under [Assumptions 1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#Thmas1 "Assumption 1. ‣ 3.1.1. Assumptions for regret upper bound ‣ 3.1. Regret rate in squared error ‣ 3. Theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters"), [2](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#Thmas2 "Assumption 2. ‣ 3.1.1. Assumptions for regret upper bound ‣ 3.1. Regret rate in squared error ‣ 3. Theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters"), [4](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#Thmas4 "Assumption 4. ‣ 3.1.1. Assumptions for regret upper bound ‣ 3.1. Regret rate in squared error ‣ 3. Theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters"), [3](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#Thmas3 "Assumption 3. ‣ 3.1.1. Assumptions for regret upper bound ‣ 3.1. Regret rate in squared error ‣ 3. Theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters"), and [SM1.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A1.Thmas1 "Assumption SM1.1. ‣ Appendix SM1 An oracle inequality for the likelihood ‣ Part III Important preliminary results for ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters"), if ∥η^−η0∥∞≤Δn and Z¯n≤Mn, then R1​i≲ℋΔn2Mn2logn.

###### Proof.

Observe that R1​i≲σℓ,σu,s0​ℓ,s0​umax(Δm​i2,Δs​i2)⋅∥Hi(η~i,G^n)∥∞, where ∥⋅∥∞ takes the largest entry from a matrix by magnitude. By assumption, the first term is bounded by Δn2. By [Lemma SM1.11](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A1.Thmlemma11 "Lemma SM1.11. ‣ SM1.9. Auxiliary lemmas ‣ Appendix SM1 An oracle inequality for the likelihood ‣ Part III Important preliminary results for ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters"), the second derivatives are bounded by Mn2​log⁡n. Hence ∥Hi(η~i,G^n)∥∞≲ℋMn2logn. This concludes the proof. ∎

#### SM1.8. Complexity of 𝒫⁡(ℝ) under moment-based distance

The following is a minor generalization of Lemma 4 and Theorem 7 in [Jiang (2020)](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib85). In particular, [Jiang (2020)](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib85)’s Lemma 4 reduces to the case q\=0 below, and [Jiang (2020)](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib85)’s Theorem 7 relies on the results below for q\=0,1. The proof largely follows the proofs of these two results of [Jiang (2020)](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib85).

We first state the following fact readily verified by differentiation.

###### Proof.

The proof strategy is as follows. First, we discretize \[−M,M\] into a union of small intervals Ij. Fix G. There exists a finitely supported distribution Gm that matches moments of G on every Ij. It turns out that such a Gm is close to G in terms of d∞,M(q). Next, we discipline Gm by approximating Gm with Gm,ω, a finitely supported distribution supported on the fixed grid {k​ω:k∈ℤ}∩\[−M,M\]. This shows that there exists a Gm,ω with finite support on a grid that approximates G in d∞,M(q). Finally, the set of all Gm,ω’s may be approximated by a finite set of distributions, and we count the size of this finite set.

##### SM1.8.1. Approximating G with Gm

First, let us fix some ω<φ⁡(q)∧φ⁡(1) to be chosen. Let a\=νuνℓ​φ+​(ω)≥1. Let Ij\=\[−M+(j−2)​a​νℓ,−M+(j−1)​a​νℓ\] be such that

where Ij is a width a​νℓ interval. Let j∗\=⌈2​Ma​νℓ+2⌉ be the number of such intervals.

<table id="A1.Ex108" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table"><tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline"><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A1.Ex108.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m=(2k^{*}+q+1)j^{*}+1" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathsize="0.900em">m</mi><mo mathsize="0.900em">=</mo><mrow><mrow><mrow><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">(</mo><mrow><mrow><mn mathsize="0.900em">2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi mathsize="0.900em">k</mi><mo mathsize="0.900em">∗</mo></msup></mrow><mo mathsize="0.900em">+</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">q</mi><mo mathsize="0.900em">+</mo><mn mathsize="0.900em">1</mn></mrow><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi mathsize="0.900em">j</mi><mo mathsize="0.900em">∗</mo></msup></mrow><mo mathsize="0.900em">+</mo><mn mathsize="0.900em">1</mn></mrow></mrow></semantics></math></td><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody></table>

##### SM1.8.2. Disciplining Gm onto a fixed grid

Now, consider a gridding of Gm via Gm,ω. We construct Gm,ω to be the following distribution. For a draw ξ∼Gm, let ξ~\=ω​sgn⁡(ξ)​⌊|ξ|/ω⌋. We let Gm,ω be the distribution of ξ~. Gm,ω has at most m\=(2​k∗+q+1)​j∗+1 support points since Gm has at most that many, and all its support points are multiples of ω.

##### SM1.8.3. Covering the set of Gm,ω

Let Δm−1 be the (m−1)\-simplex of probability vectors in m dimensions. Consider discrete distributions supported on the support points of Gm,ω, which can be identified with a subset of Δm−1. This bound holds for all sufficiently small δ. Since δ​log⁡(1/δ)q/2 is increasing over (0,e−q/2∧e−1) and the right-hand side does not vanish over the interval, we can absorb larger δ’s into the constant. ∎

As a consequence, we can control the covering number in terms of dk,∞,M for k∈{m,s}.

###### Proposition SM1.2.

Consider d∞,M(q) in [Proposition SM1.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A1.Thmprop1 "Proposition SM1.1. ‣ SM1.8. #### SM1.9. Auxiliary lemmas

See [OA1.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A1.Thmlemma1 "Lemma OA1.1. ‣ Appendix OA1 Review of notation and proofs of and ‣ Part I Proof of ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters")

###### Proof.

For (1), observe that since s^,s0 are bounded away from 0 and ∞ under [Assumption 4](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#Thmas4 "Assumption 4. ‣ 3.1.1. Assumptions for regret upper bound ‣ 3.1. Regret rate in squared error ‣ 3. Theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters"), |Z^i|∨1≲ℋ(1+Δn)Mn+Δn≲(1+Δn)Mn. Hence by [Assumption SM1.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A1.Thmas1 "Assumption SM1.1. ‣ Appendix SM1 An oracle inequality for the likelihood ‣ Part III Important preliminary results for ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters"), |Z^i|∨1≲ℋMn.

For (2), we note by Theorem 5 in [Jiang (2020)](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib85),

<table id="A1.Ex164" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table"><tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline"><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A1.Ex164.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f_{\hat{G}_{n},\hat{\nu}_{i}}(\hat{Z}_{i})\geq\frac{1}{n^{3}\hat{\nu}_{i}}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi mathsize="0.900em">f</mi><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathsize="0.900em">G</mi><mo mathsize="1.280em">^</mo></mover><mi mathsize="0.900em">n</mi></msub><mo mathsize="0.900em">,</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathsize="0.900em">ν</mi><mo mathsize="1.280em">^</mo></mover><mi mathsize="0.900em">i</mi></msub></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">(</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathsize="0.900em">Z</mi><mo mathsize="0.900em">^</mo></mover><mi mathsize="0.900em">i</mi></msub><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo mathsize="0.900em">≥</mo><mfrac><mn mathsize="0.900em">1</mn><mrow><msup><mi mathsize="0.900em">n</mi><mn mathsize="0.900em">3</mn></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathsize="0.900em">ν</mi><mo mathsize="0.900em">^</mo></mover><mi mathsize="0.900em">i</mi></msub></mrow></mfrac></mrow></semantics></math></td><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody></table>

thanks to the choice κn in [Assumption 1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#Thmas1 "Assumption 1. ‣ 3.1.1. Assumptions for regret upper bound ‣ 3.1. Regret rate in squared error ‣ 3. Theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters"). That is,

Claim (3) is immediate by calculating log(1/ρn)\=(3logn+CℋMn2Δn)∨log(e2​π)≲ℋlogn and applying [Assumption SM1.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A1.Thmas1 "Assumption SM1.1. ‣ Appendix SM1 An oracle inequality for the likelihood ‣ Part III Important preliminary results for ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters")(1) to obtain that ΔnMn2≲ℋ1. ∎

###### Lemma SM1.11.

Under the assumptions in [Lemma OA1.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A1.Thmlemma1 "Lemma OA1.1. ‣ Appendix OA1 Review of notation and proofs of and ‣ Part I Proof of ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters") and [Assumption 4](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#Thmas4 "Assumption 4. ‣ 3.1.1. Assumptions for regret upper bound ‣ 3.1. Regret rate in squared error ‣ 3. Theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters"), suppose η~i lies on the line segment between η0 and η^i and define ν~i,m~i,s~i,Z~i accordingly. Then, the second derivatives ([SM1.7](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A1.Ex8a "Equation SM1.7 ‣ SM1.1. Derivative computations ‣ Appendix SM1 An oracle inequality for the likelihood ‣ Part III Important preliminary results for ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters")), ([SM1.9](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A1.Ex9b "Equation SM1.9 ‣ SM1.1. Derivative computations ‣ Appendix SM1 An oracle inequality for the likelihood ‣ Part III Important preliminary results for ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters")), evaluated at η~i,G^n,Z~i, satisfy

###### Proof.

First, we show that

###### Lemma SM1.12.

Suppose Z has simultaneous moment control 𝔼​\[|Z|p\]1/p≤A​p1/α. Then

Regret rate in squared error ‣ 3. Theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters"), then

###### Lemma SM1.13.

Let E be some event and assume that

<table id="A1.Ex200" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table"><tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline"><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A1.Ex200.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\operatorname{P}(E,A&gt;a)\leq p_{1}\hskip 9.24994pt\operatorname{P}(E,B&gt;b)\leq p_{2}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi mathsize="0.900em">P</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">(</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">E</mi><mo mathsize="0.900em">,</mo><mrow><mi mathsize="0.900em">A</mi><mo mathsize="0.900em">&gt;</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">a</mi></mrow><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo mathsize="0.900em">≤</mo><mrow><msub><mi mathsize="0.900em">p</mi><mn mathsize="0.900em">1</mn></msub><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mi mathsize="0.900em">P</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">(</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">E</mi><mo mathsize="0.900em">,</mo><mrow><mi mathsize="0.900em">B</mi><mo mathsize="0.900em">&gt;</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">b</mi></mrow><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo mathsize="0.900em">≤</mo><msub><mi mathsize="0.900em">p</mi><mn mathsize="0.900em">2</mn></msub></mrow></semantics></math></td><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody></table>

Then P(E,A+B\>a+b)≤p1+p2

###### Proof.

Note that A+B\>a+b implies that one of A\>a and B\>b occurs. Hence

<table id="A1.Ex201" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table"><tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline"><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A1.Ex201.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\operatorname{P}(E,A+B&gt;a+b)\leq\operatorname{P}(\left\{{E,A&gt;a}\right\}\cup\left\{{E,B&gt;b}\right\})\leq p_{1}+p_{2}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathsize="0.900em">P</mi><mrow><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">(</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">E</mi><mo mathsize="0.900em">,</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">A</mi><mo mathsize="0.900em">+</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">B</mi><mo mathsize="0.900em">&gt;</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">a</mi><mo mathsize="0.900em">+</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">b</mi><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">)</mo></mrow><mo mathsize="0.900em">≤</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">P</mi><mrow><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">(</mo><mrow><mo>{</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">E</mi><mo mathsize="0.900em">,</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">A</mi><mo mathsize="0.900em">&gt;</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">a</mi><mo>}</mo></mrow><mo mathsize="0.900em">∪</mo><mrow><mo>{</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">E</mi><mo mathsize="0.900em">,</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">B</mi><mo mathsize="0.900em">&gt;</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">b</mi><mo>}</mo></mrow><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">)</mo></mrow><mo mathsize="0.900em">≤</mo><msub><mi mathsize="0.900em">p</mi><mn mathsize="0.900em">1</mn></msub><mo mathsize="0.900em">+</mo><msub><mi mathsize="0.900em">p</mi><mn mathsize="0.900em">2</mn></msub></mrow></semantics></math></td><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody></table>

by union bound. ∎

###### Lemma SM1.14.

Let τ∼G0 where G0 satisfies [Assumption 2](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#Thmas2 "Assumption 2. ‣ 3.1.1. Assumptions for regret upper bound ‣ 3.1. Regret rate in squared error ‣ 3. Since G0 is mean zero and variance 1, by Chebyshev’s inequality, G0​(\[−M,M\])≥G0​(\[−2,2\])≥3/4. Hence 𝔼\[|τ|p∣Z\=z\]≲p,α,A0Mp≲p,α,A0(|z|∨1)p, since we have bounded pth moments by [Assumption 2](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#Thmas2 "Assumption 2. ‣ 3.1.1. Assumptions for regret upper bound ‣ 3.1. Regret rate in squared error ‣ 3. Theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters"). ∎

### Appendix SM2 A large-deviation inequality for the average Hellinger distance

###### Theorem SM2.1.

For some n≥7, let τ1,…,τn|(ν12,…,νn2)​∼i.i.d.​G0 where G0 satisfies [Assumption 2](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#Thmas2 "Assumption 2. ‣ 3.1.1. Assumptions for regret upper bound ‣ 3.1. Regret rate in squared error ‣ 3. Theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters"). Let νu\=maxi⁡νi and νℓ\=mini⁡νi. Assume Zi|τi,νi2∼𝒩⁡(τi,νi2). Fix positive sequences γn,λn→0 with γn,λn≤1 and constant ϵ\>0. Fix some positive constant C∗. Consider the set of distributions that approximately maximize the likelihood

Let γ\=2+α2​α+β. We first note that, for εn in ([SM1.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A1.Ex4a "Corollary SM1.1. ‣ Appendix SM1 An oracle inequality for the likelihood ‣ Part III Important preliminary results for ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters")), the choices

#### SM2.1. Proof of [Theorem SM2.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A2.Thmtheorem1 "Theorem SM2.1. ‣ Appendix SM2 A large-deviation inequality for the average Hellinger distance ‣ Part III Important preliminary results for ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters")

##### SM2.1.1. Decompose B⁡(t,λn,ϵ)

## Part IV Additional theoretical results

### Appendix SM3 Estimating η0 by local linear regression

This section details how we estimate η0\=(m0​(⋅),s0​(⋅)) by local linear regression in [Section 4](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#S4 "4. Empirical illustration ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters"). It also outlines a detailed procedure and verifies that this procedure satisfies the conditions we require for the conditional moment estimation, when the true η0 belong to a Hölder class of order p\=2: m0​(σ),s0​(σ)∈CA12​(\[σℓ,σu\]).

In our empirical application, we estimate m0,s0 by nonparametrically regressing Yi on xi≡log10⁡(σi).39 Our procedure takes the following steps, which simply use kernel-based nonparametric regression procedures implemented by [Calonico et al. (2019)](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib63) to estimate m0 and s0 and truncate the estimated s0 below at some data-driven point. Nonparametric regression is frequently applied to visualize data and to estimate causal effects in regression discontinuity settings.

1.  (E-1)
    
    Use the default procedure [Calonico et al. (2019)](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib63) to estimate local linear regression of Yi on xi (Epanechnikov kernel, IMSE direct plug-in bandwidth). The resulting estimated conditional mean is m^​(⋅).
    
2.  (E-2)
    
    Let R^i2\=(Yi−m^​(xi))2. Use the above local linear regression procedure again to estimate the conditional mean of R^i2 on xi, and let v^​(x) be the estimated conditional mean. Let
    
    <table id="A3.Ex1a" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table"><tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline"><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A3.Ex1a.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{s}^{2}(\sigma_{i})=\hat{v}(x_{i})-\sigma_{i}^{2}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msup><mover accent="true"><mi mathsize="0.900em">s</mi><mo mathsize="0.900em">~</mo></mover><mn mathsize="0.900em">2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">(</mo><msub><mi mathsize="0.900em">σ</mi><mi mathsize="0.900em">i</mi></msub><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo mathsize="0.900em">=</mo><mrow><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathsize="0.900em">v</mi><mo mathsize="0.900em">^</mo></mover><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">(</mo><msub><mi mathsize="0.900em">x</mi><mi mathsize="0.900em">i</mi></msub><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo mathsize="0.900em">−</mo><msubsup><mi mathsize="0.900em">σ</mi><mi mathsize="0.900em">i</mi><mn mathsize="0.900em">2</mn></msubsup></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em" mathsize="0.900em">.</mo></mrow></semantics></math></td><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody></table>
    
3.  (E-3)
    
    Since v^​(xi) is a linear smoother, it can be written as
    
    <table id="A3.Ex2a" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table"><tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline"><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A3.Ex2a.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{v}(x)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\ell_{i}(x)\hat{R}_{i}^{2}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathsize="0.900em">v</mi><mo mathsize="0.900em">^</mo></mover><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">(</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">x</mi><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo mathsize="0.900em" rspace="0.111em">=</mo><mrow><munderover><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em" movablelimits="false" stretchy="true">∑</mo><mrow><mi mathsize="0.900em">i</mi><mo mathsize="0.900em">=</mo><mn mathsize="0.900em">1</mn></mrow><mi mathsize="0.900em">n</mi></munderover><mrow><msub><mi mathsize="0.900em" mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mi mathsize="0.900em">i</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">(</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">x</mi><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi mathsize="0.900em">R</mi><mo mathsize="0.900em">^</mo></mover><mi mathsize="0.900em">i</mi><mn mathsize="0.900em">2</mn></msubsup></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em" mathsize="0.900em">.</mo></mrow></semantics></math></td><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody></table>
    
    for some weights ℓi​(x). Let an estimate of the effective sample size be
    
    <table id="A3.Ex3a" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table"><tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline"><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A3.Ex3a.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{n}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{1}{\sum_{j=1}^{n}\ell_{i}^{2}(x_{j})}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi mathsize="0.900em">p</mi><mi mathsize="0.900em">n</mi></msub><mo mathsize="0.900em">=</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn mathsize="0.900em">1</mn><mi mathsize="0.900em">n</mi></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><munderover><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em" movablelimits="false" stretchy="true">∑</mo><mrow><mi mathsize="0.900em">i</mi><mo mathsize="0.900em">=</mo><mn mathsize="0.900em">1</mn></mrow><mi mathsize="0.900em">n</mi></munderover><mfrac><mn mathsize="0.900em">1</mn><mrow><msubsup><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em" stretchy="true">∑</mo><mrow><mi mathsize="0.900em">j</mi><mo mathsize="0.900em">=</mo><mn mathsize="0.900em">1</mn></mrow><mi mathsize="0.900em">n</mi></msubsup><mrow><msubsup><mi mathsize="0.900em" mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mi mathsize="0.900em">i</mi><mn mathsize="0.900em">2</mn></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">(</mo><msub><mi mathsize="0.900em">x</mi><mi mathsize="0.900em">j</mi></msub><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mfrac></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em" mathsize="0.900em">.</mo></mrow></semantics></math></td><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody></table>
    
4.  (E-4)
    
    Let the estimated conditional variance be
    
    <table id="A3.Ex4a" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table"><tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline"><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A3.Ex4a.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{s}^{2}(\sigma_{i})=\tilde{s}^{2}(\sigma_{i})\vee\frac{2}{p_{n}+2}\left({\hat{v}(x_{i})\vee\min_{j=1,\ldots,n}\sigma_{j}^{2}}\right)" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msup><mover accent="true"><mi mathsize="0.900em">s</mi><mo mathsize="0.900em">^</mo></mover><mn mathsize="0.900em">2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">(</mo><msub><mi mathsize="0.900em">σ</mi><mi mathsize="0.900em">i</mi></msub><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo mathsize="0.900em">=</mo><mrow><mrow><msup><mover accent="true"><mi mathsize="0.900em">s</mi><mo mathsize="0.900em">~</mo></mover><mn mathsize="0.900em">2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">(</mo><msub><mi mathsize="0.900em">σ</mi><mi mathsize="0.900em">i</mi></msub><mo mathsize="0.900em">n</mi></msub><mo mathsize="0.900em">+</mo><mn mathsize="0.900em">2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathsize="0.900em">v</mi><mo mathsize="0.900em">^</mo></mover><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">(</mo><msub><mi mathsize="0.900em">x</mi><mi mathsize="0.900em">i</mi></msub><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo mathsize="0.900em">∨</mo><mrow><munder><mi mathsize="0.900em">min</mi><mrow><mrow><mi mathsize="0.900em">j</mi><mo mathsize="0.900em">=</mo><mn mathsize="0.900em">1</mn></mrow><mo mathsize="0.900em">,</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em" mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo mathsize="0.900em">,</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">n</mi></mrow></munder><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><msubsup><mi mathsize="0.900em">σ</mi><mi mathsize="0.900em">j</mi><mn mathsize="0.900em">2</mn></msubsup></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></semantics></math></td><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody></table>
    
    where the additional truncation by mini\=1,…,n⁡σi2 deals with the unlikely scenario that v^​(xi) is negative. Note that, in theory, the population analogue v⁡(xi)\=𝔼⁡\[Ri2∣xi\]\=s02​(σi)+σi2≥σi2. See [Remark SM3.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A3.Thmrmk1 "Remark SM3.1 (The truncation rule in ()). ‣ Appendix SM3 Estimating 𝜂_0 by local linear regression ‣ Part IV Additional theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters") for a heuristic rationale of the above truncation rule.
    

The rest of the section analyzes the theoretical properties of a similar procedure for analyzing m0​(⋅),s0​(⋅) and connects them to the requirements in [Assumption 4](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#Thmas4 "Assumption 4. ‣ 3.1.1. Assumptions for regret upper bound ‣ 3.1. Regret rate in squared error ‣ 3. Theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters"). The product of this analysis is [Theorem SM3.2](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A3.Thmtheorem2 "Theorem SM3.2. ‣ Appendix SM3 Estimating 𝜂_0 by local linear regression ‣ Part IV Additional theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters"), which verifies the same regret bound as in [Theorem 1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#Thmtheorem1 "Theorem 1. ‣ 3.1.2. MSE regret results ‣ 3.1. Regret rate in squared error ‣ 3. Theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters"), where we estimate m0,s0 with the procedure we outline below.

There are a few minor inconveniences of the above procedure that we strengthen below:

-   •
    
    We would like to control for the fact that the bandwidths h^n for the local linear regression is data-driven. However, to establish uniform behavior in h^n, we would like to restrict it to satisfy the optimal convergence rate almost surely: For some C\>0,
    
    <table id="A3.Ex5a" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table"><tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline"><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A3.Ex5a.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="C^{-1}n^{-1/5}\leq\hat{h}_{n}\leq Cn^{-1/5}\text{ almost surely.}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathsize="0.900em">C</mi><msup><mrow></mrow><mrow><mo mathsize="0.900em">−</mo><mn mathsize="0.900em">1</mn></mrow></msup><mi mathsize="0.900em">n</mi><msup><mrow></mrow><mrow><mo mathsize="0.900em">−</mo><mn mathsize="0.900em">1</mn><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em" stretchy="true" symmetric="true">/</mo><mn mathsize="0.900em">5</mn></mrow></msup><mo mathsize="0.900em">≤</mo><mover accent="true"><mi mathsize="0.900em">h</mi><mo mathsize="0.900em">^</mo></mover><msub><mrow></mrow><mi mathsize="0.900em">n</mi></msub><mo mathsize="0.900em">≤</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">C</mi><mi mathsize="0.900em">n</mi><msup><mrow></mrow><mrow><mo mathsize="0.900em">−</mo><mn mathsize="0.900em">1</mn><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em" stretchy="true" symmetric="true">/</mo><mn mathsize="0.900em">5</mn></mrow></msup><mtext mathsize="0.900em">&nbsp;almost surely.</mtext></mrow></semantics></math></td><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody></table>
    
-   •
    
    We would like to ensure that the estimated functions m^,s^ are Hölder continuous almost surely. Since m0​(x),s0​(x) are Hölder continuous,40 we do not significantly incur estimation error if we project to Hölder continuous functions.
    

We enforce these properties in the below procedure that we analyze. We anticipate the projection steps to be unnecessary in practice and hold with high probability in theory. Precisely, we add the steps [(LLR-2)](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A3.I3.i2a "In Appendix SM3 Estimating 𝜂_0 by local linear regression ‣ Part IV Additional theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters"), [(LLR-7)](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A3.I3.i7 "Item (LLR-7) ‣ Appendix SM3 Estimating 𝜂_0 by local linear regression ‣ Part IV Additional theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters"), [(LLR-4)](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A3.I3.i4 "Item (LLR-4) ‣ Appendix SM3 Estimating 𝜂_0 by local linear regression ‣ Part IV Additional theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters"), and [(LLR-11)](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A3.I3.i11 "Item (LLR-11) ‣ Appendix SM3 Estimating 𝜂_0 by local linear regression ‣ Part IV Additional theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters") to the procedure in [(E-1)](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A3.I1.i1a "In Appendix SM3 Estimating 𝜂_0 by local linear regression ‣ Part IV Additional theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters")–[(E-4)](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A3.I1.i4 "In Appendix SM3 Estimating 𝜂_0 by local linear regression ‣ Part IV Additional theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters"). We also make the dependence on the selected bandwidths explicit:

1.  (LLR-1)
    
    Fix some kernel K⁡(⋅). Use the direct plug-in procedure of [Calonico et al. (2019)](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib63) to estimate a bandwidth h^n,m.
    
2.  (LLR-2)
    
    For some Ch\>1, project h^n,m to some interval \[Ch−1n−1/5,Chn−1/5\] so as to enforce that it converges at the optimal rate:41
    
    <table id="A3.Ex6" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table"><tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline"><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A3.Ex6.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\hat{h}_{n,m}\leftarrow(\hat{h}_{n,m}\vee C_{h}^{-1}n^{-1/5})\wedge C_{h}n^{-1/5}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathsize="0.900em">h</mi><mo mathsize="0.900em">^</mo></mover><mrow><mi mathsize="0.900em">n</mi><mo mathsize="0.900em">,</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">m</mi></mrow></msub><mo mathsize="0.900em" stretchy="false">←</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">(</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathsize="0.900em">h</mi><mo mathsize="0.900em">^</mo></mover><mrow><mi mathsize="0.900em">n</mi><mo mathsize="0.900em">,</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">m</mi></mrow></msub><mo mathsize="0.900em">∨</mo><msubsup><mi mathsize="0.900em">C</mi><mi mathsize="0.900em">h</mi><mrow><mo mathsize="0.900em">−</mo><mn mathsize="0.900em">1</mn></mrow></msubsup><msup><mi mathsize="0.900em">n</mi><mrow><mo mathsize="0.900em">−</mo><mn mathsize="0.900em">1</mn><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em" stretchy="true" symmetric="true">/</mo><mn mathsize="0.900em">5</mn></mrow></msup><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">)</mo></mrow><mo mathsize="0.900em">∧</mo><msub><mi mathsize="0.900em">C</mi><mi mathsize="0.900em">h</mi></msub><msup><mi mathsize="0.900em">n</mi><mrow><mo mathsize="0.900em">−</mo><mn mathsize="0.900em">1</mn><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em" stretchy="true" symmetric="true">/</mo><mn mathsize="0.900em">5</mn></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" mathsize="0.900em">.</mo></mrow></semantics></math></td><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody></table>
    
3.  (LLR-3)
    
    Using h^n,m, estimate m0 with the local linear regression estimator m^raw under kernel K⁡(⋅) and bandwidth h^n,m.
    
4.  (LLR-4)
    
    Project the resulting estimator m^ to the Hölder class CA32​(\[0,1\]):
    
    <table id="A3.Ex7" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table"><tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline"><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A3.Ex7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{m}\in\argmin_{m\in C_{A_{3}}^{2}([0,1])}\lVert m-\hat{m}_{\mathrm{raw}}\rVert_{\infty}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathsize="0.900em">m</mi><mo mathsize="0.900em">^</mo></mover><mo mathsize="0.900em">∈</mo><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathsize="0.900em">arg</mi><mo lspace="0.150em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">min</mi></mrow><mrow><mi mathsize="0.900em">m</mi><mo mathsize="0.900em">∈</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi mathsize="0.900em">C</mi><msub><mi mathsize="0.900em">A</mi><mn mathsize="0.900em">3</mn></msub><mn mathsize="0.900em">2</mn></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">(</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">[</mo><mrow><mn mathsize="0.900em">0</mn><mo mathsize="0.900em">,</mo><mn mathsize="0.900em">1</mn></mrow><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">]</mo></mrow><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em">⁡</mo><msub><mrow><mo fence="true" mathsize="0.900em" rspace="0em">∥</mo><mrow><mi mathsize="0.900em">m</mi><mo mathsize="0.900em">−</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathsize="0.900em">m</mi><mo mathsize="0.900em">^</mo></mover><mi mathsize="0.900em">raw</mi></msub></mrow><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" mathsize="0.900em" rspace="0em">∥</mo></mrow><mi mathsize="0.900em" mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em" mathsize="0.900em">.</mo></mrow></semantics></math></td><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody></table>
    
    We obtain m^ through this procedure.
    
5.  (LLR-5)
    
    Form estimated squared residuals R^i2\=(Yi−m^​(xi))2.
    
6.  (LLR-6)
    
    Repeat [(LLR-1)](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A3.I3.i1a "In Appendix SM3 Estimating 𝜂_0 by local linear regression ‣ Part IV Additional theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters") on data (R^i2,xi) to obtain a bandwidth h^n,s.
    
7.  (LLR-7)
    
    Repeat [(LLR-2)](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A3.I3.i2a "In Appendix SM3 Estimating 𝜂_0 by local linear regression ‣ Part IV Additional theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters") to project h^n,s.
    
8.  (LLR-8)
    
    Using h^n,s, estimate v⁡(x)\=𝔼⁡\[Ri2∣X\=x\] with the local linear regression estimator v^ under kernel K⁡(⋅).
    
9.  (LLR-9)
    
    Since v^ is a local linear regression estimator, it can be written as a linear smoother v^​(x)\=∑i\=1nℓi​(x,h^n,s)​R^i2. Let an estimate of the effective sample size be
    
    <table id="A3.Ex8" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table"><tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline"><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A3.Ex8.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{n}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{1}{\sum_{j=1}^{n}\ell_{i}^{2}(x_{j},\hat{h}_{n,s})}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi mathsize="0.900em">p</mi><mi mathsize="0.900em">n</mi></msub><mo mathsize="0.900em">=</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn mathsize="0.900em">1</mn><mi mathsize="0.900em">n</mi></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><munderover><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em" movablelimits="false" stretchy="true">∑</mo><mrow><mi mathsize="0.900em">i</mi><mo mathsize="0.900em">=</mo><mn mathsize="0.900em">1</mn></mrow><mi mathsize="0.900em">n</mi></munderover><mfrac><mn mathsize="0.900em">1</mn><mrow><msubsup><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em" stretchy="true">∑</mo><mrow><mi mathsize="0.900em">j</mi><mo mathsize="0.900em">=</mo><mn mathsize="0.900em">1</mn></mrow><mi mathsize="0.900em">n</mi></msubsup><mrow><msubsup><mi mathsize="0.900em" mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mi mathsize="0.900em">i</mi><mn mathsize="0.900em">2</mn></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">(</mo><msub><mi mathsize="0.900em">x</mi><mi mathsize="0.900em">j</mi></msub><mo mathsize="0.900em">,</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathsize="0.900em">h</mi><mo mathsize="0.900em">^</mo></mover><mrow><mi mathsize="0.900em">n</mi><mo mathsize="0.900em">,</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">s</mi></mrow></msub><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mfrac></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em" mathsize="0.900em">.</mo></mrow></semantics></math></td><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody></table>
    
10.  (LLR-10)
     
     Truncate the estimated conditional standard deviation:
     
     <table id="A3.Ex10" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table"><tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline"><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A3.Ex10.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{s}_{\mathrm{raw}}(x)=\sqrt{\hat{v}(x)-\sigma^{2}(x)}\vee\sqrt{\frac{2}{p_{n}+2}\hat{v}(x)}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathsize="0.900em">s</mi><mo mathsize="0.900em">^</mo></mover><mi mathsize="0.900em">raw</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">(</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">x</mi><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo minsize="0.900em">(</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">x</mi><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo mathsize="0.900em">−</mo><mrow><msup><mi mathsize="0.900em">σ</mi><mn mathsize="0.900em">2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">(</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">x</mi><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></msqrt><mo mathsize="0.900em">∨</mo><msqrt><mrow><mfrac><mn mathsize="0.900em">2</mn><mrow><msub><mi mathsize="0.900em">p</mi><mi mathsize="0.900em">n</mi></msub><mo mathsize="0.900em">+</mo><mn mathsize="0.900em">2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mover accent="true"><mi mathsize="0.900em">v</mi><mo mathsize="0.900em">^</mo></mover><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">(</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">x</mi><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">)</mo></mrow></mrow></msqrt></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em" mathsize="0.900em">.</mo></mrow></semantics></math></td><td class="ltx_eqn_cell 11.  (LLR-11)

To ensure we always have a positive estimate of s0, we truncate at a particular point ([(LLR-10)](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A3.Ex10 "Item (LLR-10) ‣ Appendix SM3 Estimating 𝜂_0 by local linear regression ‣ Part IV Additional theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters")). This truncation rule is a heuristic (and improper) application of results from the literature on estimating non-centrality parameters. We digress and discuss the truncation rule in the next remark.

###### Remark SM3.1 (The truncation rule in ([(LLR-10)](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A3.Ex10 "Item (LLR-10) ‣ Appendix SM3 Estimating 𝜂_0 by local linear regression ‣ Part IV Additional theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters"))).

The truncation rule in ([(LLR-10)](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A3.Ex10 "Item (LLR-10) ‣ Appendix SM3 Estimating 𝜂_0 by local linear regression ‣ Part IV Additional theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters")) is an ad hoc adjustment without affecting asymptotic performance.42 It is based on a literature on the estimation of non-central χ2 parameters ([Kubokawa et al., 1993](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib62)). Specifically, let Ui​∼i.i.d.​𝒩​(λi,1) and let V\=∑i\=1pUi2 be a noncentral χ2 random variable with p degrees of freedom and noncentrality parameter λ\=∑i\=1pλi2. The UMVUE for λ is V−p, which is dominated by its positive part (V−p)+. [Kubokawa et al. (1993)](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib62) derive a class of estimators of the form V−ϕ⁡(V,p) that dominate (V−p)+ in squared error risk. An estimator in this class is (V−p)∨2p+2​V.43

This setting is loosely connected to ours. Suppose m0 is known, and we were using a Nadaraya–Watson estimator with uniform kernel. Then, for a given evaluation point x0, we would be averaging nearby Ri2’s. Each Ri is conditionally Gaussian, Ri|(θi,σi)∼𝒩⁡(θi−m0​(σi),σi2) with approximately equal variance σi2≈σ​(x0)2. If there happens to be p0 Ri2’s that we are averaging, the Nadaraya–Watson estimator is of the form

<table id="A3.Ex13" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table"><tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline"><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A3.Ex13.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{v}(x_{0})=\frac{\sigma(x_{0})^{2}}{p_{0}}\sum_{i=1}^{p}\left({\frac{R_{i}}{\sigma(x_{0})}}\right)^{2}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathsize="0.900em">v</mi><mo mathsize="0.900em">^</mo></mover><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">(</mo><msub><mi mathsize="0.900em">x</mi><mn mathsize="0.900em">0</mn></msub><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo mathsize="0.900em">=</mo><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi mathsize="0.900em">σ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mrow><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">(</mo><msub><mi mathsize="0.900em">x</mi><mn mathsize="0.900em">0</mn></msub><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">)</mo></mrow><mn mathsize="0.900em">2</mn></msup></mrow><msub><mi mathsize="0.900em">p</mi><mn mathsize="0.900em">0</mn></msub></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><munderover><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em" movablelimits="false" rspace="0em" stretchy="true">∑</mo><mrow><mi mathsize="0.900em">i</mi><mo mathsize="0.900em">=</mo><mn mathsize="0.900em">1</mn></mrow><mi mathsize="0.900em">p</mi></munderover><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mfrac><msub><mi mathsize="0.900em">R</mi><mi mathsize="0.900em">i</mi></msub><mrow><mi mathsize="0.900em">σ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">(</mo><msub><mi mathsize="0.900em">x</mi><mn mathsize="0.900em">0</mn></msub><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac><mo>)</mo></mrow><mn mathsize="0.900em">2</mn></msup></mrow></mrow></mrow></semantics></math></td><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody></table>

Conditional on σi2,θi, the quantity ∑i\=1p(Riσ⁡(x0))2 is (approximately) noncentral χ2 with p degrees of freedom and noncentrality parameter

Here, we apply this truncation rule (improperly) to the case where v^​(x0) is a weighted average of the squared residuals, with potentially negative weights due to higher-order polynomials in the local polynomial regression. To do so, we would need to plug in an analogue of p0. We note that when independent random variables Vi have unit variance, the weighted average has variance equal to the squared length of the weights

Since a simple average has variance equal to 1/n, we can take (∑i\=1nℓi2​(x))−1 to be an effective sample size. Our rule simply takes the average effective sample size over evaluation points in ([(LLR-9)](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A3.Ex8 "Item (LLR-9) ‣ Appendix SM3 Estimating 𝜂_0 by local linear regression ‣ Part IV Additional theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters")) and use it as a candidate for p. ■

The goal in this section is to control the following probability as a function of t\>0

for some constants β,Cℋ to be chosen. Since we treat x1,…,xn as fixed (fixed design), we shall do so placing some assumptions on sequences of the design points x1:n as a function of n. These assumptions are mild and satisfied when the design points are equally spaced. They are also satisfied with high probability when the design points are drawn from a well-behaved density f⁡(⋅).

Before doing so, we introduce some notation on the local linear regression estimator. We shall maintain the following assumptions on the design points. The following assumptions introduce constants (Ch,n0,λ0,a0,K0,K⁡(⋅),c,C,CK,VK) which we shall take as primitives like those in ℋ. The symbols ≲,≳,≍ are relative to these constants, and we will not keep track of exact dependencies through subscripts.

###### Assumption SM3.1.

For some constant Ch\>1, the data-driven bandwidth hn is almost surely contained in the set Hn≡\[Ch−1n−1/5∨12​n,Chn−1/5\].

[Assumption SM3.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A3.Thmas1 "Assumption SM3.1. ‣ Appendix SM3 Estimating 𝜂_0 by local linear regression ‣ Part IV Additional theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters") is automatically satisfied by the projection steps [(LLR-2)](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A3.I3.i2a "In Appendix SM3 Estimating 𝜂_0 by local linear regression ‣ Part IV Additional theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters") and [(LLR-7)](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A3.I3.i7 "Item (LLR-7) ‣ Appendix SM3 Estimating 𝜂_0 by local linear regression ‣ Part IV Additional theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters").

###### Assumption SM3.2.

The sequence of design points (xi:i\=1,…,n) satisfy:

1.  (1)
    
    There exists a real number λ0\>0 and integer n0\>0 such that, for all n≥n0, any x∈\[0,1\], and any h~∈\[Ch−1n−1/5∨12​n,Chn−1/5\], the smallest eigenvalue λmin​(Bn​x​(h~))≥λ0.
    
2.  (2)
    
    There exists a real number a0\>0 such that for any interval I⊂\[0,1\] and all n≥1,
    
    <table id="A3.Ex19" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table"><tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline"><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A3.Ex19.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbbm{1}(x_{i}\in I)\leq a_{0}\left({\lambda(I)\vee\frac{1}{n}}\right)" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mfrac><mn mathsize="0.900em">1</mn><mi mathsize="0.900em">n</mi></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><munderover><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em" movablelimits="false" stretchy="true">∑</mo><mrow><mi mathsize="0.900em">i</mi><mo mathsize="0.900em">=</mo><mn mathsize="0.900em">1</mn></mrow><mi mathsize="0.900em">n</mi></munderover><mrow><mn mathsize="0.900em">𝟙</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi mathsize="0.900em">x</mi><mi mathsize="0.900em">i</mi></msub><mo mathsize="0.900em">∈</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">I</mi></mrow><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo mathsize="0.900em">≤</mo><mrow><msub><mi mathsize="0.900em">a</mi><mn mathsize="0.900em">0</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mrow><mi mathsize="0.900em">λ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">(</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">I</mi><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo mathsize="0.900em">∨</mo><mfrac><mn mathsize="0.900em">1</mn><mi mathsize="0.900em">n</mi></mfrac></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></semantics></math></td><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody></table>
    
    where λ⁡(I) is the Lebesgue measure of I.
    
3.  (3)
    
    The kernel K is supported on \[−1,1\] and uniformly bounded by some positive constant K0.
    
4.  (4)
    
    There exists c,C,n0\>0 such that for all n\>n0, the choice of pn in ([(LLR-9)](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A3.Ex8 "Item (LLR-9) ‣ Appendix SM3 Estimating 𝜂_0 by local linear regression ‣ Part IV Additional theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters")) satisfies c​n4/5≤pn​(h~)≤C​n4/5 for all h~∈\[Ch−1n−1/5∨12​n,Chn−1/5\].
    

[Assumption SM3.2](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A3.Thmas2 "Assumption SM3.2. ‣ Appendix SM3 Estimating 𝜂_0 by local linear regression ‣ Part IV Additional theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters")(1–3) is nearly the same as Assumption (LP) in [Tsybakov (2008)](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib72). The only difference is that [Assumption SM3.2](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A3.Thmas2 "Assumption SM3.2. ‣ Appendix SM3 Estimating 𝜂_0 by local linear regression ‣ Part IV Additional theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters")(1) requires the lower bound λ0 to hold uniformly over a range of bandwidth choices, relative to LP-1 in [Tsybakov (2008)](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib72), which requires λ0 to hold for some deterministic sequence hn. This is a mild strengthening of LP-1: Note that if xi are drawn from a Lipschitz-continuous, everywhere-positive density f⁡(x), then for h→0,n​h→∞,

[Assumption SM3.2](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A3.Thmas2 "Assumption SM3.2. ‣ Appendix SM3 Estimating 𝜂_0 by local linear regression ‣ Part IV Additional theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters")(2)–(3) are the same as (LP-2)–(LP-3) in [Tsybakov (2008)](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib72). (2) expects that the design points are sufficiently spread out, and (3) is satisfied by, say, the Epanechnikov kernel.

###### Assumption SM3.3.

The kernel satisfies the following VC subgraph-type conditions. Let
