for k\=1,2. For any finitely supported measure Q,

<table id="A3.Ex23" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table"><tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline"><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A3.Ex23.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N(\epsilon,\mathcal{F}_{k},L_{2}(Q))\leq C_{K}(1/\epsilon)^{V_{K}}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi mathsize="0.900em">N</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">(</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">ϵ</mi><mo mathsize="0.900em">,</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic" mathsize="0.900em">ℱ</mi><mi mathsize="0.900em">k</mi></msub><mo mathsize="0.900em">,</mo><mrow><msub><mi mathsize="0.900em">L</mi><mn mathsize="0.900em">2</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">(</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">Q</mi><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo mathsize="0.900em">≤</mo><mrow><msub><mi mathsize="0.900em">C</mi><mi mathsize="0.900em">K</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mrow><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">(</mo><mrow><mn mathsize="0.900em">1</mn><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em" stretchy="true" symmetric="true">/</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">ϵ</mi></mrow><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">)</mo></mrow><msub><mi mathsize="0.900em">V</mi><mi mathsize="0.900em">K</mi></msub></msup></mrow></mrow></semantics></math></td><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody></table>

for CK,VK that do not depend on Q.

[Assumption SM3.3](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A3.Thmas3 "Assumption SM3.3. ‣ Appendix SM3 Estimating 𝜂_0 by local linear regression ‣ Part IV Additional theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters") is satisfied for a wide range of kernels, e.g. the Epanechnikov kernel. By Lemma 7.22 in [Sen (2018)](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib61), reproduced as [Lemma SM3.2](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A3.Thmlemma2 "Lemma SM3.2 (Lemma 7.22(ii) in ( ) ). ‣ SM3.1. Auxiliary lemmas ‣ Appendix SM3 Estimating 𝜂_0 by local linear regression ‣ Part IV Additional theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters") below, so long as the function t↦tk−1​K​(t) is bounded (assumed in [Assumption SM3.2](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A3.Thmas2 "Assumption SM3.2. ‣ Appendix SM3 Estimating 𝜂_0 by local linear regression ‣ Part IV Additional theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters")(3)) and of bounded variation (satisfied by any absolutely continuous kernel function), the covering number conditions hold by exploiting the finite VC dimension of subgraphs of these functions.

We now state and prove the main results in this section. The key to these arguments is [Proposition SM3.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A3.Thmprop1 "Proposition SM3.1. ‣ SM3.1. Auxiliary lemmas ‣ Appendix SM3 Estimating 𝜂_0 by local linear regression ‣ Part IV Additional theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters") on the bias and variance of local linear regression estimators. [Proposition SM3.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A3.Thmprop1 "Proposition SM3.1. ‣ SM3.1. Auxiliary lemmas ‣ Appendix SM3 Estimating 𝜂_0 by local linear regression ‣ Part IV Additional theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters") is uniform in both the evaluation point x and the bandwidth h, as long as the latter converges at the optimal rate.

###### Theorem SM3.1.

Suppose the conditional distribution θi|σi and the design points σ1:n satisfy [Assumptions 3](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#Thmas3 "Assumption 3. ‣ 3.1.1. Assumptions for regret upper bound ‣ 3.1. Regret rate in squared error ‣ 3. Theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters"), [2](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#Thmas2 "Assumption 2. ‣ 3.1.1. Assumptions for regret upper bound ‣ 3.1. Regret rate in squared error ‣ 3. Theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters"), and [SM3.2](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A3.Thmas2 "Assumption SM3.2. ‣ Appendix SM3 Estimating 𝜂_0 by local linear regression ‣ Part IV Additional theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters"). Moreover, suppose m0,s0 satisfies [Assumption 4](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#Thmas4 "Assumption 4. ‣ 3.1.1. Assumptions for regret upper bound ‣ 3.1. Regret rate in squared error ‣ 3. Theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters")(1) with p\=2. Suppose the kernel K⁡(⋅) satisfies [Assumption SM3.3](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A3.Thmas3 "Assumption SM3.3. ‣ Appendix SM3 Estimating 𝜂_0 by local linear regression ‣ Part IV Additional theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters"). Let m^,s^ denote the estimators computed by [(LLR-1)](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A3.I3.i1a "In Appendix SM3 Estimating 𝜂_0 by local linear regression ‣ Part IV Additional theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters") through [(LLR-11)](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A3.I3.i11 "In Appendix SM3 Estimating 𝜂_0 by local linear regression ‣ Part IV Additional theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters"). Then, there exists some n0\>0 such that

1.  (1)
    
    P⁡(m^,s^∈CA32​(\[0,1\]))\=1

###### Proof.

The first claim is true automatically by the projection to the Hölder space.

The third claim is true for all n\>n0 automatically by [(LLR-11)](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A3.I3.i11 "In Appendix SM3 Estimating 𝜂_0 by local linear regression ‣ Part IV Additional theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters"), since pn≥c​n4/5 and n−4/5≳n−1. For n≤n0, note that ∑iℓi​(x,h)\=∑iℓi​(x,h)​u​((xi−x)/h)′​u​(0)⏟1\=∥u⁡(0)∥2\=1 for all h,x. Hence

regardless of h. As a result, the truncation point for s^2 is at least of order 1n. This is sufficient for s^≥c/n.

Now, we show the second claim. Since we assume that m0,s0 lies in the Hölder space with s0\>s0​ℓ, then projection to the Hölder space (and truncation by OPEN2/(2+pn)​mini​σi2) worsens performance by at most a factor of two for all sufficiently large n. The projection to the Hölder space ensures that ∥η^−η0∥∞ is bounded a.s. for all n, so that we can remove “for all sufficiently large n” at the cost of enlarging a constant so as to accommodate the first finitely many values of n. By Lemma 1.3 in [Tsybakov (2008)](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib72), the term ∑i\=1n|ℓi​(x,h^n,s)| is bounded uniformly in h and x by a constant. Note that

<table id="A3.Ex38" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table"><tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline"><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A3.Ex38.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{\xi}_{i}\equiv R_{i}^{2}-v_{0}(x_{i})" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathsize="0.900em">ξ</mi><mo mathsize="0.900em">~</mo></mover><mi mathsize="0.900em">i</mi></msub><mo mathsize="0.900em">≡</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi mathsize="0.900em">R</mi><mi mathsize="0.900em">i</mi><mn mathsize="0.900em">2</mn></msubsup><mo mathsize="0.900em">−</mo><mrow><msub><mi mathsize="0.900em">v</mi><mn mathsize="0.900em">0</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">(</mo><msub><mi mathsize="0.900em">x</mi><mi mathsize="0.900em">i</mi></msub><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></semantics></math></td><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody></table>

###### Theorem SM3.2.

Under the assumptions of [Theorem SM3.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A3.Thmtheorem1 "Theorem SM3.1. ‣ Appendix SM3 Estimating 𝜂_0 by local linear regression ‣ Part IV Additional theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters"), let η^\=(m^,s^) denote estimators computed by [(LLR-1)](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A3.I3.i1a "In Appendix SM3 Estimating 𝜂_0 by local linear regression ‣ Part IV Additional theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters") through [(LLR-11)](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A3.I3.i11 "In Appendix SM3 Estimating 𝜂_0 by local linear regression ‣ Part IV Additional theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters"). #### SM3.1. Auxiliary lemmas

###### Proposition SM3.1.

Consider the local linear regression of data Yi\=f0​(xi)+ξi on the design points xi, for i\=1,…,n. Suppose f0 belongs to a Hölder class of order two: f0∈CL2​(\[0,1\]) for some L\>0. Suppose that the design points satisfy [Assumption SM3.2](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A3.Thmas2 "Assumption SM3.2. ‣ Appendix SM3 Estimating 𝜂_0 by local linear regression ‣ Part IV Additional theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters") and the (possibly data-driven) bandwidths hn satisfy [Assumption SM3.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A3.Thmas1 "Assumption SM3.1. ‣ Appendix SM3 Estimating 𝜂_0 by local linear regression ‣ Part IV Additional theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters"). Assume the kernel additionally satisfies [Assumption SM3.3](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A3.Thmas3 "Assumption SM3.3. ‣ Appendix SM3 Estimating 𝜂_0 by local linear regression ‣ Part IV Additional theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters").

Assume that the residuals ξi are mean zero, and there exists a constant Aξ\>0,α\>0 such that

<table id="A3.Ex51" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table"><tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline"><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A3.Ex51.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\max_{i=1,\ldots,n}(\mathbb{E}[|\xi_{i}|^{p}])^{1/p}\leq A_{\xi}p^{1/\alpha}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><munder><mi mathsize="0.900em">max</mi><mrow><mrow><mi mathsize="0.900em">i</mi><mo mathsize="0.900em">=</mo><mn mathsize="0.900em">1</mn></mrow><mo mathsize="0.900em">,</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em" mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo mathsize="0.900em">,</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">n</mi></mrow></munder><mo>⁡</mo><msup><mrow><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">(</mo><mrow><mi mathsize="0.900em">𝔼</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">[</mo><msup><mrow><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em" stretchy="true">|</mo><msub><mi mathsize="0.900em">ξ</mi><mi mathsize="0.900em">i</mi></msub><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em" stretchy="true">|</mo></mrow><mi mathsize="0.900em">p</mi></msup><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">]</mo></mrow></mrow><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn mathsize="0.900em">1</mn><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em" stretchy="true" symmetric="true">/</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">p</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><mo mathsize="0.900em">≤</mo><mrow><msub><mi mathsize="0.900em">A</mi><mi mathsize="0.900em">ξ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi mathsize="0.900em">p</mi><mrow><mn mathsize="0.900em">1</mn><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em" stretchy="true" symmetric="true">/</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">α</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></mrow></semantics></math></td><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody></table>

for all p≥2. Let ℓi​(x,h) be the weights corresponding to local linear regression, and define the bias part b⁡(x,hn)\=(∑i\=1nℓi​(x,hn)​f0​(xi))−f0​(xi) and the stochastic part v⁡(x,h)\=∑i\=1nℓi​(x,h)​ξi. Recall that Hn is the interval for hn in [Assumption SM3.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A3.Thmas1 "Assumption SM3.1. ‣ Appendix SM3 Estimating 𝜂_0 by local linear regression ‣ Part IV Additional theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters"). Then:

1.  (1)

###### Proof.

Note that (3) follows immediately from (1) and (2) since the bounds in (1) and (2) are uniform over all h∈Hn. We now verify (1) and (2).

1.  (1)
    
    This claim follows immediately from the bound for b⁡(x0) in Proposition 1.13 in [Tsybakov (2008)](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib72). The argument in [Tsybakov (2008)](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib72) shows that
    
    <table id="A3.Ex55" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table"><tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline"><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A3.Ex55.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sup_{x\in[0,1]}|b(x,h_{n})|\leq Ch_{n}^{2}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><munder><mo mathsize="0.900em" movablelimits="false">sup</mo><mrow><mi mathsize="0.900em">x</mi><mo mathsize="0.900em">∈</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">[</mo><mrow><mn mathsize="0.900em">0</mn><mo mathsize="0.900em">,</mo><mn mathsize="0.900em">1</mn></mrow><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">]</mo></mrow></mrow></munder><mrow><mo lspace="0em" maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em" stretchy="true">|</mo><mrow><mi mathsize="0.900em">b</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">(</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">x</mi><mo mathsize="0.900em">,</mo><msub><mi mathsize="0.900em">h</mi><mi mathsize="0.900em">n</mi></msub><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em" stretchy="true">|</mo></mrow></mrow><mo mathsize="0.900em">≤</mo><mrow><mi mathsize="0.900em">C</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi mathsize="0.900em">h</mi><mi mathsize="0.900em">n</mi><mn mathsize="0.900em">2</mn></msubsup></mrow></mrow><mo mathsize="0.900em">,</mo></mrow></semantics></math></td><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody></table>
    
    which is uniformly bounded by Cn−2/5 by [Assumption SM3.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A3.Thmas1 "Assumption SM3.1. ‣ Appendix SM3 Estimating 𝜂_0 by local linear regression ‣ Part IV Additional theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters").     We will do so by applying [Lemma SM3.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A3.Thmlemma1 "Lemma SM3.1. ‣ SM3.1. The analogue of f in [Lemma SM3.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A3.Thmlemma1 "Lemma SM3.1. ‣ SM3.1. Auxiliary lemmas ‣ Appendix SM3 Estimating 𝜂_0 by local linear regression ‣ Part IV Additional theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters") is
    
    <table id="A3.Ex76" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table"><tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline"><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A3.Ex76.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t\mapsto f(t;x,h)=\left({\frac{t-x}{h}}\right)^{k-1}K\left({\frac{t-x}{h}}\right)" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathsize="0.900em">t</mi><mo mathsize="0.900em" stretchy="false">↦</mo><mrow><mi mathsize="0.900em">f</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">(</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">t</mi><mo mathsize="0.900em">,</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">x</mi><mo mathsize="0.900em">,</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">h</mi><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo mathsize="0.900em">=</mo><mrow><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi mathsize="0.900em">t</mi><mo mathsize="0.900em">−</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">x</mi></mrow><mi mathsize="0.900em">h</mi></mfrac><mo>)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi mathsize="0.900em">k</mi><mo mathsize="0.900em">−</mo><mn mathsize="0.900em">1</mn></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">K</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi mathsize="0.900em">t</mi><mo mathsize="0.900em">−</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">x</mi></mrow><mi mathsize="0.900em">h</mi></mfrac><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></semantics></math></td><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody></table>
    
    for V2​n,k,k\=1,2. Naturally, the analogues of ℱ is
    
    <table id="A3.Ex77" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table"><tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline"><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A3.Ex77.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\mathcal{F}_{k}=\left\{{t\mapsto f(t;x,h):x\in[0,1],h\in H_{n}}\right\}\cup\{t\mapsto 0\}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic" mathsize="0.900em">ℱ</mi><mi mathsize="0.900em">k</mi></msub><mo mathsize="0.900em">=</mo><mrow><mo>{</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">t</mi><mo mathsize="0.900em" stretchy="false">↦</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">f</mi><mrow><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">(</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">t</mi><mo mathsize="0.900em">;</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">x</mi><mo mathsize="0.900em">,</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">h</mi><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em" rspace="0.278em">)</mo></mrow><mo mathsize="0.900em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">x</mi><mo mathsize="0.900em">∈</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">[</mo><mn mathsize="0.900em">0</mn><mo mathsize="0.900em">,</mo><mn mathsize="0.900em">1</mn><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">]</mo></mrow><mo mathsize="0.900em">,</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">h</mi><mo mathsize="0.900em">∈</mo><msub><mi mathsize="0.900em">H</mi><mi mathsize="0.900em">n</mi></msub><mo>}</mo></mrow><mo mathsize="0.900em">∪</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">{</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">t</mi><mo mathsize="0.900em" stretchy="false">↦</mo><mn mathsize="0.900em">0</mn><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">}</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" mathsize="0.900em">.</mo></mrow></semantics></math></td><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody></table>

###### Lemma SM3.1.

Suppose ξi are bounded by M≥1 and mean zero. Consider the process

<table id="A3.Ex87" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table"><tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline"><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A3.Ex87.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="V_{n}(f)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\sum_{i=1}^{n}f(x_{i})\xi_{i}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi mathsize="0.900em">V</mi><mi mathsize="0.900em">n</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">(</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">f</mi><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo mathsize="0.900em">=</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn mathsize="0.900em">1</mn><msqrt><mi mathsize="0.900em">n</mi></msqrt></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><munderover><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em" movablelimits="false" stretchy="true">∑</mo><mrow><mi mathsize="0.900em">i</mi><mo mathsize="0.900em">=</mo><mn mathsize="0.900em">1</mn></mrow><mi mathsize="0.900em">n</mi></munderover><mrow><mrow><mi mathsize="0.900em">f</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">(</mo><msub><mi mathsize="0.900em">x</mi><mi mathsize="0.900em">i</mi></msub><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi mathsize="0.900em">ξ</mi><mi mathsize="0.900em">i</mi></msub></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></semantics></math></td><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody></table>

over a class of real-valued functions f∈ℱ and evaluation points x1,…,xn∈\[0,1\]. Define the seminorm ∥⋅∥n relative to x1,…,xn by

<table id="A3.Ex88" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table"><tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline"><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A3.Ex88.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lVert f\rVert_{n}^{2}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}f(x_{i})^{2}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mo fence="true" mathsize="0.900em" rspace="0em">∥</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">f</mi><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" mathsize="0.900em">∥</mo></mrow><mi mathsize="0.900em">n</mi><mn mathsize="0.900em">2</mn></msubsup><mo mathsize="0.900em">=</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn mathsize="0.900em">1</mn><mi mathsize="0.900em">n</mi></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><munderover><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em" movablelimits="false" stretchy="true">∑</mo><mrow><mi mathsize="0.900em">i</mi><mo mathsize="0.900em">=</mo><mn mathsize="0.900em">1</mn></mrow><mi mathsize="0.900em">n</mi></munderover><mrow><mi mathsize="0.900em">f</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mrow><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">(</mo><msub><mi mathsize="0.900em">x</mi><mi mathsize="0.900em">i</mi></msub><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">)</mo></mrow><mn mathsize="0.900em">2</mn></msup></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em" mathsize="0.900em">.</mo></mrow></semantics></math></td><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody></table>

Suppose 0∈ℱ and ℱ has polynomial covering numbers:

###### Proof.

The process Vn​(f) has subgaussian increments with respect to ∥⋅∥n:

###### Proof.

First, note that learning m0 from (Yi,σi) is a nonparametric regression problem with heteroskedastic variances. This problem is more difficult than a corresponding problem with homoskedastic variances σℓ2+s02, since we may represent

<table id="A4.Ex2" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table"><tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline"><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A4.Ex2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Y_{i}=\theta_{i}+\sigma_{\ell}W_{i}+(\sigma_{i}^{2}-\sigma_{\ell}^{2})^{1/2}U_{i}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi mathsize="0.900em">Y</mi><mi mathsize="0.900em">i</mi></msub><mo mathsize="0.900em">=</mo><mrow><msub><mi mathsize="0.900em">θ</mi><mi mathsize="0.900em">i</mi></msub><mo mathsize="0.900em">+</mo><mrow><msub><mi mathsize="0.900em">σ</mi><mi mathsize="0.900em" mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi mathsize="0.900em">W</mi><mi mathsize="0.900em">i</mi></msub></mrow><mo mathsize="0.900em">+</mo><mrow><msup><mrow><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">(</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi mathsize="0.900em">σ</mi><mi mathsize="0.900em">i</mi><mn mathsize="0.900em">2</mn></msubsup><mo mathsize="0.900em">−</mo><msubsup><mi mathsize="0.900em">σ</mi><mi mathsize="0.900em" mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mn mathsize="0.900em">2</mn></msubsup></mrow><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn mathsize="0.900em">1</mn><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em" stretchy="true" symmetric="true">/</mo><mn mathsize="0.900em">2</mn></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi mathsize="0.900em">U</mi><mi mathsize="0.900em">i</mi></msub></mrow></mrow></mrow></semantics></math></td><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody></table>

for independent Gaussians Wi,Ui∼𝒩⁡(0,1). Let Vi\=θi+σℓ​Wi. Note that we can do no worse for estimating m0 with (Vi,σi) than with (Yi,σi), and estimating m0 from (Vi,σi) is a homoskedastic regression problem, where Vi∼𝒩⁡(m0​(σi),σℓ2+s02). It remains to show that the minimax rate for estimating m0 on the grid points σ1:n from (Vi,σi) is n−2p/(2p+1).

Since we simply have a nonparametric regression problem, we may translate and rescale so that the design points σ1:n are equally spaced in \[0,1\] (σi\=i/n) and the variance of Vi is 1—potentially changing the constant A1 for the Hölder smoothness condition. ###### Lemma SM4.3.

Consider the setup of [Theorem 3](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#Thmtheorem3 "Theorem 3. ‣ 3.2. Robustness to the location-scale assumption () ‣ 3. Theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters"). The minimax risk is achieved by the decision rule ([2.4.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#S2.Ex16 "2.4.1. Implementation ‣ 2.4. Discussions ‣ 2. Model and proposed method ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters")). That is, let δi∗ denote the decision rule ([2.4.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#S2.Ex16 "2.4.1. Implementation ‣ 2.4. Discussions ‣ 2. ###### Proof.

Choose σi\=1+i/n. Choose a constant s0​(σi)\=ϵ\>0 and some non-constant m0​(σi) normalized so that m0\=0. Thus s02≥1n​∑i\=1nm0​(σi)2≡K. Thus,

for some c\>0 for all ϵ\>0. Therefore, the numerator is bounded below by c. The denominator converges to zero as ϵ→0. With this choice, maxi⁡s02​(σi)/σi2<ϵ is eventually smaller than any positive C. Thus the ratio is arbitrarily large as we take ϵ→0. ∎

### Appendix SM5 Maximum posterior discrepancy of priors satisfying moment constraints

This section contains the main result of [Chen (2023)](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#bib.bib29) (arXiv:2303.08653) and supersedes that paper.44 The notation and setup is entirely self-contained.

Consider an observation X whose likelihood is X|θ∼𝒩⁡(θ,σ2) for some known σ2. There are two priors for θ, denoted by G0 and G1. Suppose both priors have zero mean and have finite variances bounded by V\>0. Consider the decision problem of estimating θ under squared error, with L⁡(a,θ)\=(a−θ)2. For the Bayesian with prior G1, the Bayes decision rule is the posterior mean 𝔼G1​\[θ∣X\] under the prior G1. This decision rule attains Bayes risk under the prior G0

<table id="A5.Ex1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table"><tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline"><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A5.Ex1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R(G_{1},\sigma;G_{0})\equiv\mathbb{E}_{\theta\sim G_{0}}\left[{(\mathbb{E}_{G_{1}}[\theta\mid X]-\theta)^{2}}\right]." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi mathsize="0.900em">R</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">(</mo><msub><mi mathsize="0.900em">G</mi><mn mathsize="0.900em">1</mn></msub><mo mathsize="0.900em">,</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">σ</mi><mo mathsize="0.900em">,</mo><msub><mi mathsize="0.900em">G</mi><mn mathsize="0.900em">0</mn></msub><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo mathsize="0.900em">≡</mo><mrow><msub><mi mathsize="0.900em">𝔼</mi><mrow><mi mathsize="0.900em">θ</mi><mo mathsize="0.900em">∼</mo><msub><mi mathsize="0.900em">G</mi><mn mathsize="0.900em">0</mn></msub></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>[</mo><msup><mrow><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">(</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi mathsize="0.900em">𝔼</mi><msub><mi mathsize="0.900em">G</mi><mn mathsize="0.900em">1</mn></msub></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">[</mo><mrow><mi mathsize="0.900em">θ</mi><mo lspace="0em" mathsize="0.900em" rspace="0.167em">∣</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">X</mi></mrow><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">]</mo></mrow></mrow><mo mathsize="0.900em">−</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">θ</mi></mrow><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">)</mo></mrow><mn mathsize="0.900em">2</mn></msup><mo>]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em" mathsize="0.900em">.</mo></mrow></semantics></math></td><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody></table>

We can think of R⁡(G1,σ,G0) as a measure of decision quality under disagreement. It measures the quality of G1’s decision from G0’s point of view. When G1≠G0, how large can R⁡(G1,σ,G0) be?

Since

it thus suffices to bound 𝔼G0​\[𝔼G1​\[θ∣X\]2\] modulo constants. That is, it suffices to bound the 2-norm ∥𝔼G1​\[θ∣X\]∥2 under the law X∼𝒩⁡(0,σ2)⋆G0.

The rest of the section shows that this quantity is uniformly bounded over all G0,G1,σ2\>0. Specifically, [Lemma SM5.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A5.Thmlemma1 "Lemma SM5.1. ‣ Appendix SM5 Maximum posterior discrepancy of priors satisfying moment constraints ‣ Part IV Additional theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters") shows that for all G0,G1 that are mean zero and have variance bounded by V, 𝔼G0​\[𝔼G1​\[θ∣X\]2\] is bounded by a constant that depends only on (V,σ2). This bound is large when σ2 is large. To improve this bound, [Theorem SM5.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A5.Thmtheorem1 "Theorem SM5.1. ‣ Appendix SM5 Maximum posterior discrepancy of priors satisfying moment constraints ‣ Part IV Additional theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters") then shows that, if G1 additionally satisfies some conditions on its tail behavior, 𝔼G0​\[𝔼G1​\[θ∣X\]2\] is bounded by a constant that depends only on V and the tail condition—and does not depend on σ.

Suppose G0,G1 have mean zero and variances bounded by V, then

To show a more powerful bound, we require a stronger condition on the tails of G1 and derive bounds that are independent of σ but are dependent on the tail conditions. In particular, assume

<table id="A5.Ex9" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table"><tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline"><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A5.Ex9.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\max\left({1-G_{1}(s),G_{1}(-s)}\right)\leq C_{G_{1}}s^{-k}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi mathsize="0.900em">max</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn mathsize="0.900em">1</mn><mo mathsize="0.900em">−</mo><mrow><msub><mi mathsize="0.900em">G</mi><mn mathsize="0.900em">1</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">(</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">s</mi><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo mathsize="0.900em">,</mo><mrow><msub><mi mathsize="0.900em">G</mi><mn mathsize="0.900em">1</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">(</mo><mrow><mo mathsize="0.900em">−</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">s</mi></mrow><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo mathsize="0.900em">≤</mo><mrow><msub><mi mathsize="0.900em">C</mi><msub><mi mathsize="0.900em">G</mi><mn mathsize="0.900em">1</mn></msub></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi mathsize="0.900em">s</mi><mrow><mo mathsize="0.900em">−</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">k</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></mrow></semantics></math></td><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody></table>

for some k\>2 and CG1\>0, for all s\>0. We will also assume that 𝔼G1​\[θ2∣X\] exists almost surely. Note that if 𝔼G1​|θ|2+ϵ<m, then k can be taken to be 2+ϵ and CG1 can be taken to be m by Markov’s inequality. In the rest of the proof, we let Ct<∞ denote a positive constant that depends only on t. Occurrences of Ct might correspond to different constant values.

###### Theorem SM5.1.

Suppose k\>2. There exists a constant Q<∞ that depends solely on (CG1,k,V) such that, uniformly for all (G0,G1) and σ∈ℝ, where (i) G0,G1 have mean zero and variance bounded by V and (ii) G1 satisfies ([SM5](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A5.Ex9 "Appendix SM5 Maximum posterior discrepancy of priors satisfying moment constraints ‣ Part IV Additional theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters")) with (CG1,k),

<table id="A5.Ex11" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table"><tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline"><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A5.Ex11.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{E}_{G_{0}}\left[{\mathbb{E}_{G_{1}}[\theta\mid X]^{2}}\right]\leq Q." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi mathsize="0.900em">𝔼</mi><msub><mi mathsize="0.900em">G</mi><mn mathsize="0.900em">0</mn></msub></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>[</mo><mrow><msub><mi mathsize="0.900em">𝔼</mi><msub><mi mathsize="0.900em">G</mi><mn mathsize="0.900em">1</mn></msub></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mrow><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">[</mo><mrow><mi mathsize="0.900em">θ</mi><mo lspace="0em" mathsize="0.900em" rspace="0.167em">∣</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">X</mi></mrow><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">]</mo></mrow><mn mathsize="0.900em">2</mn></msup></mrow><mo>]</mo></mrow></mrow><mo mathsize="0.900em">≤</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">Q</mi></mrow><mo lspace="0em" mathsize="0.900em">.</mo></mrow></semantics></math></td><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody></table>

###### Proof.

Assume that σ2≥1. For all σ2<1, we can apply [Lemma SM5.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A5.Thmlemma1 "Lemma SM5.1. ‣ Appendix SM5 Maximum posterior discrepancy of priors satisfying moment constraints ‣ Part IV Additional theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters") so that 𝔼G0​\[𝔼G1​\[θ∣X\]2\]≤6​V+4.

<table id="A5.Ex30" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table"><tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline"><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A5.Ex30.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="u=C\sigma\sqrt{\log(s)}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathsize="0.900em">u</mi><mo mathsize="0.900em">=</mo><mrow><mi mathsize="0.900em">C</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">σ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msqrt><mrow><mi mathsize="0.900em">log</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">(</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">s</mi><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">)</mo></mrow></mrow></msqrt></mrow></mrow></semantics></math></td><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody></table>

for some C≥2 to be chosen. On s\>K, u/σ\>2 and thus uσ−1\>u2​σ. Observe that by [Lemma SM5.2](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.14444v6#A5.Thmlemma2 "Lemma SM5.2. ‣ Appendix SM5 Maximum posterior discrepancy of priors satisfying moment constraints ‣ Part IV Additional theoretical results ‣ Empirical Bayes When Estimation Precision Predicts Parameters") and the fact that σ\>1,

Therefore,

<table id="A5.Ex55" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table"><tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline"><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A5.Ex55.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\overline{\Phi}(x)\leq\varphi(x)\sqrt{\frac{\pi}{2}}=\frac{1}{2}e^{-x^{2}/2}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathsize="0.900em" mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><mo stretchy="true">¯</mo></mover><mrow><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">(</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">x</mi><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">)</mo></mrow><mo mathsize="0.900em">≤</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">φ</mi><mrow><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">(</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">x</mi><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">)</mo></mrow><msqrt><mfrac><mi mathsize="0.900em">π</mi><mn mathsize="0.900em">2</mn></mfrac></msqrt><mo mathsize="0.900em">=</mo><mfrac><mn mathsize="0.900em">1</mn><mn mathsize="0.900em">2</mn></mfrac><msup><mi mathsize="0.900em">e</mi><mrow><mo mathsize="0.900em">−</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">x</mi><msup><mrow></mrow><mn mathsize="0.900em">2</mn></msup><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em" stretchy="true" symmetric="true">/</mo><mn mathsize="0.900em">2</mn></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" mathsize="0.900em">.</mo></mrow></semantics></math></td><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody></table>
